News.title: Crete wildfires live: Greece emergency as hurricane-force winds fan Rethymno flames
News.content:
A state of emergency has been declared in parts of Crete and elsewhere in Greece as firefighters battle intense wildfires, with hurricane-force winds fanning flames

A state of emergency has been declared in parts of Crete and elsewhere in Greece as firefighters battle intense wildfires.

The blazes in the Rethymno region of southern Crete have scorched around 4,500 hectares since Wednesday. Hurricane-force winds - which reached speeds of up to 125km/h (78mph) yesterday - grounded firefighting aircraft and hampered efforts to contain the flames. Firefighters resumed operations on the ground today without the use of aircraft for the third day in a row.

Thousands of people, including tourists, have been evacuated with fires are also raging on Paros, Andros and Kalymnos islands, parts of the Peloponnese and western mainland Greece.

Advice has been issued by the UK Government for Brits caught in areas affected, stating: "Be cautious if you are in or near an area affected by wildfires: follow @112Greece for official updates; follow the guidance of the emergency services; call the Greek emergency services on 112 if you are in immediate danger; contact your airline or travel operator who can assist you with return travel to the UK."

Fresh wildfire outbreaks in Greece, Portugal and Turkey come on top of devastating wildfires that are tearing through parts of France and Spain. Since yesterday, firefighters have responded to 169 wildfires across Turkey.

News.title: Burnham says Infantino 'wrong man' to lead Fifa as third confederation opposes World Cup plan
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Gianni Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa after a senior adviser to the president resigned and a third confederation opposed his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

Burnham was critical of the proposal when it was first announced, and told reporters on Friday: "This was an outrageous suggestion.

"The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation."

Burnham was speaking hours after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it "stands in solidarity" with counterparts in Europe and North, Central America and the Caribbean.

The AFC added Infantino's plan could not "realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward".

"The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world's leading football nations," it said.

"Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered."

Shortly after that statement, Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

The AFC's statement means Infantino's plans are unlikely to be approved by Fifa members if put to a vote.

Infantino had indicated the proposals would need a straight majority to go through - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour for the proposal.

Uefa - the body that governs European football - has 55 votes. Concacaf, which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, has 35 and Asia has 46.

Should all member associations back the stance of their governing body, that would mean 136 nations are against Infantino's plan.

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three attacks while in prison and possessing a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

The 19-year-old murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

In May 2025, it was reported boiling water had been thrown on a prison officer at Belmarsh. They were taken to hospital and discharged on the same day.

When Rudakubana was jailed, the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to him being under-18 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

On 23 July, the MoJ confirmed Rudakubana was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The decision to transfer him was criticised by a lawyer representing the families of victims.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.

Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.

The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.

Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.

Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.

Sainsbury's bought Argos â together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â in 2016 for Â£1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around Â£720m in 2024.

In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Robert said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.

He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat products

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.

Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops â and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.

News.title: Anthropic's Claude AI escapes test environment and hacks into three organisations
News.content:
US technology firm Anthropic says its AI models hacked into the systems of three organisations on their own, during a private security experiment.

The models found a weakness in what was supposed to be an isolated test environment and connected to the internet.

It comes just days after rival OpenAI said that its models had breached the systems of other companies, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.

The announcement prompted Anthropic to check whether its own systems had carried out similar attacks. It says it uncovered three cases which have since been reported to the affected companies.

Anthropic, which did not name the organisations, urged other AI labs to perform similar reviews to better understand the risks of their models' capabilities.

Anthropic said in a statement, external it reviewed more than 140,000 tests to find evidence Claude - its family of AI models - had managed to get online even though it was supposed to be in an isolated test environment, cut off from the internet.

The tests included exercises in which Claude was tasked with obtaining "secret" information hidden on another machine on the closed-off network.

It was then told to get the information by breaking into the machine and finding it - a common way that experts assess a model's hacking capabilities.

A "misconfiguration" on systems run by Anthropic and its testing partner left the models with live internet access.

Treating it all as still part of the same exercise, Claude then connected to the internet and breached the systems of three real organisations rather than just test ones, the San Francisco-based firm said.

Anthropic said the earliest incidents date back to April and that it is "approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone."

Neither Anthropic nor the organisations that were breached had noticed the intrusions at the time.

Anthropic said it could have reviewed its records more thoroughly and added that the findings gave the firm "cautious optimism" that such risks can be overcome with more investment and tighter measures.

News.title: Satellite images show impact of heatwaves and drought on UK landscape
News.content:
Satellite imagery shows the toll taken on the UK landscape from this year's long hot summer.

BBC Verify analysis of satellite data shows where in the UK has been most affected by heatwaves and a lack of rain.

We can see parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.

Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and have an impact on agriculture and food supplies.

Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told BBC Radio 4's Today programme areas without mayors would also benefit from investment because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.

Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.

But Labour backbencher Perran Moon said the government's plans were "discriminatory" and could create a "two-tier system".

The MP for Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall said the area would never have a mayor or become a combined authority and so risked not having access to devolved powers that other areas would have.

"What we're asking government to do is to provide us with the same powers, the same funding that mayoral combined authorities have without the requirement of becoming a combined authority or having a mayor."

The government has also announced that mayors will be given a fast-track route to building new tramways, roads and light rail in their areas.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the threshold at which local leaders need to seek approval for projects will rise to Â£500m, up from Â£200m.

News.title: UK petrol prices hit highest level since Iran war began
News.content:
While petrol has hit its highest price since the Iran war began, according to the RAC, diesel remains below the peak of 191.54p a litre it reached on 15 April.

In early July, the RAC said the average price of diesel sank to a low of 150.59p per litre for petrol and 164.52p per litre for diesel.

Since then the prices have risen, with petrol now at 159.97p a litre while diesel costs 178.97p a litre.

RAC head of policy Simon Williams said the price of diesel was likely to reach 185p a litre "in the next few weeks, barring any major oil price reduction".

Despite the conflict, petrol and diesel prices remain below the levels reached in the summer of 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, when petrol reached 191.5p a litre and diesel hit 199p.

Because transporting oil is a slow process, price movements in the wholesale markets take about a fortnight to show at the pump.

Fuel retailers have denied accusations of price gouging during the conflict. The official markets regulator said it had "not seen evidence of retailers actively changing their pricing strategies to take advantage of the crisis".

A government scheme called Fuel Finder, external lets drivers compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK.

Luke Bosdet, the head of policy at the AA, said the group had been surprised at the speed that prices had fallen and put it down to the scheme.

On 20 May, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said a planned 5p increase in fuel duty due in September would be postponed until 31 December because of the conflict.

News.title: What your summer reading list says about you
News.content:
You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.

But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?

"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the Ãcole Normale SupÃ©rieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality.

"When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain.

"Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."

Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.

Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.

During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:

Epic other-world adventures (action, adventure, science fiction, dystopian/post-apocalyptic, fantasy)

Everyday life and human relationships (comedy, romantic, drama, family, musical)

Threat and danger (true crime, crime/mystery/thriller, horror)

Facts and histories (documentary, biography, historical)

But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

News.title: Thames Water boss says leakage targets 'not realistic'
News.content:
Water companies have performance commitments on issues such as leakage.

It is illegal to release raw sewage into rivers and seas during "normal" weather conditions, but firms are allowed to do so when it rains heavily, to prevent homes being flooded.

Thames is the UK's largest water company, supplying water and wastewater services to 16 million customers across London and parts of southern England.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Weston said the company treats 4.3 billion litres of waste a day, and "99.5% of the time" it gets treated successfully, although "sometimes something goes wrong".

"We want to do better when it comes to pollutions," he said, but added, "the targets that the company is expected to make are not realistic.

"[For example], we have to hit a certain level of leakage, but it is so far in excess of what we are capable of doing, I think anyone would be capable of doing, however much money you invested, that it is not going to be achievable."

The chance of getting to zero pollution was "very, very slim", he added.

Ofwat told the BBC: "With around a fifth of water put into supply still lost through leakage, companies must deliver on the commitments they have been funded to achieve.

"Water company targets are intended to be ambitious and drive better outcomes for customers and the environment."

A spokesperson for the Environment Agency said: "[We] and the public expect Thames Water to comply with the law," adding that the agency would continue to hold companies to account where performance falls short.

James Wallace, chief executive of campaign group River Action, said: "Thames Water's tactics of opacity and deflection fool no-one. Telling the public to save water while this wasteful profit-obsessed corporation leaks 570 million litres of treated drinking water every day is offensive.

"There is nothing 'realistic' about accepting sewage pollution as inevitable. The choice is simple: keep propping up a failed privatised financial model, or put Thames Water into special administration and rebuild it as a public utility serving customers, rivers and the public."

News.title: High Court upholds decision to allow Chinese mega embassy
News.content:
A High Court challenge against the construction of a Chinese mega embassy in London has failed.

The decision to uphold planning permission for the site on the old Royal Mint, near the Tower of London, has dismayed campaigners from the Royal Mint Court Residents' Association (RMCRA), which represents families and businesses in about 100 properties.

The RMCRA fear the site poses an espionage threat and will be used to enforce "draconian" Chinese laws in the UK and to target dissidents.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) and the London Borough of Tower Hamlets defended the claim, saying they "conscientiously and carefully had regard" to the residents' concerns.

The association was also concerned about the Chinese government creating a fire risk by ignoring safety obligations, which it said would not be enforceable because of diplomatic immunity.

A High Court hearing was held earlier this month and two judges have now dismissed RMCRA's challenge.

Mrs Justice Lieven, sitting with Lord Justice Dingemans, said there was "no doubt" that the government took into account that it was the Chinese government applying for planning permission.

She also said that the RMCRA was not disadvantaged by not receiving a copy of a "blast assessment" at the time of the planning decision, which detailed the effect of a possible terrorist explosion.

The judge said: "There was no unfairness to the claimant by reason of these documents not having been disclosed."

The RMCRA say they intend to appeal against the High Court ruling.

News.title: British man accused of spying on Cyprus RAF base for Iran
News.content:
A British man has been arrested on suspicion of spying on a UK military base in Cyprus on behalf of the Iranian military.

Rashad Sultanov, 44, of Islington, north London, is accused of carrying out "hostile surveillance" on RAF Akrotiri and sharing information with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

Sultanov, who also holds Azerbaijani citizenship, was arrested by Cypriot police on 17 July and is in custody pending extradition proceedings.

The Crown Prosecution Service has said he will be charged under the National Security Act - the first time an alleged offence under the 2023 law has been investigated in an overseas territory.

News.title: BP puts North Sea business up for sale
News.content:
BP has said it is putting its North Sea business up for sale in a move that would end 60 years of production in the region by the oil giant.

The decision follows a review of BP's operations as it seeks to slim down the group. Its North Sea business has five production hubs - two in the central North Sea and three west of Shetland - and employs about 1,100 people.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.

Trump, some trade unions, industry figures and some Labour MPs all back increased drilling in the North Sea.

"The UK has been our home for more than 100 years and will continue to play an important role in our future," BP chief executive Meg O'Neill said.

"We're proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day," she said.

The company said it remained committed to operating the business safely and reliably throughout the sale process.

Its North Sea business produced 117,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2025, a small fraction of the oil giant's 2.3 million barrels of daily production.

News.title: TikToker faces police probe over secret filming using 'smart glasses'
News.content:
One of the most disturbing incidents occurs on Skye where he tells a UK-born Sikh shopkeeper of Indian heritage that there is "forced" diversity in Europe.

He goes on to refer to the Kalergi Plan - a far right conspiracy theory about a plot to "breed out the white race".

The woman, who was running the shop with help from her teenage daughter, politely suggests his comments are "slightly derogatory".

When he leaves, Margerison angrily describes her in his video commentary as "condescending" and complains that "they don't understand".

The woman, who was born in London and has lived in Skye for 20 years, told BBC Scotland News he initiated the conversation by asking "what are you doing here?" but edited this out of the published footage.

She said her encounter with Margerison, who is heavily built and well over 6ft tall, was "100% intimidating" and that she cried when she was later told by a friend that a secretly-filmed video had been published on TikTok.

"You're made to feel very small when you see a video like this," she said.

"And it's sad because everyone in the local community is really nice. This was really upsetting."

While in the Hebrides, Margerison also filmed an angry encounter with an elderly couple in a supermarket after they complained that he had "loudly and rudely" asked them to move out of his way.

He follows them around the store, at one point blocking their path, swears in front of them, accuses them of being "mental".

He also tells them he intends to post footage of them on TikTok which he says is "well within my rights".

News.title: Elderly victim of 'cruel' carer can't be left alone after being 'traumatised'
News.content:
An 81-year-old whose "cruel" carer was jailed after being caught on camera abusing her cannot be left alone because she is "traumatised," her daughter has said.

Louise Harris was given a three-month sentence after CCTV filmed her drunkenly screaming "I hope you die in your sleep... you horrible cow" at Elizabeth Anne Shipton in Pontardawe, Neath Port Talbot.

Elizabeth's daughter Tracy Faram Shipton called Harris's actions "horrific" and said her sentence for ill treatment and criminal damage was "laughable".

Despite this, the family is unable to appeal against it as, under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, external, the attorney general can only refer specific qualifying crimes to the Court of Appeal.

Harris, 42, was filmed on the family's video surveillance system, which was originally installed so Tracy and her brother could monitor their late father John in case he fell while caring for Elizabeth.

She had originally been charged with attempted robbery - a crime which would have qualified for sentencing to be appealed by the victim's family - but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) dropped that charge.

"Mum can't be left on her own at all now," Tracy added.

A CPS spokesman said: "We keep all cases under review and on this occasion concluded that our legal test was not met, as there was insufficient evidence to prosecute the defendant with attempted robbery and theft.

"We have written to the victim to explain our decision in more detail."

News.title: Famous Whale Bone Arch to be replaced by replica
News.content:
Whitby's famous Whale Bone Arch will be replaced by a bronze replica, it has been confirmed.

The clifftop structure, described as one of the town's "most recognisable and significant landmarks", is in need of replacement due to deterioration.

Real jawbones of dead whales were first raised on top of West Cliff in 1964 as a symbol of Whitby's maritime heritage. They were replaced with another genuine pair in 2002, but the new set will be more durable and less controversial.

Whitby's mayor Sandra Turner said: "Nobody wants to think a whale has been killed in this day and age, but at the same time it's Whitby's heritage. It's important we still have something up there which represents that."

North Yorkshire Council, which owns and maintains the 19ft (5.8m) tall arch, said it would be taken down in September to allow a replica of the same size to be moulded from the existing bones.

The new structure is expected to be installed early next year, according to the authority.

"Years of exposure to the weather on the coast has led to significant deterioration in the arch's condition, meaning the bones now need to be replaced," a spokesperson said.

Council executive member Mark Crane, whose responsibilities include harbours, said: "The new bronze arch will stand for generations, providing a lasting symbol of the town's unique maritime heritage and ensuring this iconic feature continues to inspire residents and visitors long into the future."

A statue of Captain Cook, which stands just a few feet away from the current whale bones, is also made from bronze.

At an estimated Â£70,000, the bronze replica was the most expensive option put forward by the council, which will cover its cost.

"Given the feelings with people in this modern-day era perhaps it's probably the best route to go," said Turner.

"The council did try to get a genuine set of jaw bones, but there's so much legislation to bring them out of one country to another.

"The biggest problem was locating a pair of jaw bones that were of the size and condition that was suitable."

News.title: Aerial footage shows wildfire tearing through Suffolk heathland
News.content:
The Suffolk wildfire has grown to an area equal to more than 200 football pitches, Suffolk's fire service says.

Checking into this quietly luxurious townhouse – among the Georgian terraces that once inspired the writers and artists of the Bloomsbury Group – feels more like being handed the keys to an old family residence than a hotel room

Location

A five-minute stroll from Russell Square, 15 minutes from both King's Cross and Euston, and neighbour to the British Museum, The Zetter Bloomsbury couldn't be better placed for a cultural weekend in the capital.

The hotel is in one of London's most storied neighbourhoods. Bloomsbury was once home to an influential circle of writers, artists and thinkers, including Virginia Woolf, EM Forster and John Maynard Keynes. It was a place where creativity, conversation and curiosity flourished – and that spirit still lingers in its leafy squares, independent bookshops and handsome Georgian terraces.



The vibe

The third opening from the boutique Zetter hotel group (the others are in Clerkenwell and Marylebone) feels entirely at home in this neighbourhood. Its greatest asset isn't its postcode but the feeling when you step through the front door. Outside is modern London; inside, time seems to soften. In antique-filled rooms, rich velvet furnishings and softly lit corners create the feeling of entering another era.

open image in gallery The Parlour, where antique treasures create the perfect setting for morning coffee ( Zetter Bloomsbury )

Artefacts thought to date back as far as the Egyptian, Greek and Roman periods mingle with more modern curiosities, including bowls reportedly recovered from the Titanic. The effect is less museum, more the home of a fascinating collector.

Service

The service at Zetter Bloomsbury is attentive, yet effortlessly makes you feel at home. As a solo traveller, I felt genuinely looked after as the team knew when to stop for a chat or simply check that I had everything I needed. One recommendation I was particularly grateful for was the perfectly mixed margarita – just the right companion for an evening in The Parlour bar and lounge.

Bed and bath

There are 68 rooms in total at Zetter Bloomsbury, spread across six floors, with five different categories, ranging from Cosy all the way up to eight suites, including the Terrace Suite (overlooking the hotel’s secluded garden). Even the entry-level rooms feel indulgent. Egyptian cotton linen, jewel-toned fabrics, antique furniture and carefully chosen curiosities mean no two rooms are the same.

open image in gallery Rooms are thoughtfully designed in jewel tones ( Zetter Bloomsbury )

Large Georgian sash windows flood the rooms with natural light during the day. As evening falls, carefully placed lighting creates an entirely different mood; intimate, cinematic and very grown-up.

Bathrooms feature generous rainfall showers stocked with Verden toiletries. Suites also come with freestanding baths in the bedrooms.



Food and drink

Breakfast is served in The Orangery, a bright conservatory overlooking the hotel's gardens. Filled with plants and artwork, it's a peaceful retreat. The a la carte offering spans everything from healthy bowls of chia muesli with Granny Smith apple, stem ginger and coconut, to a classic full English and Eggs Royale. All dietary requirements can be taken care of.

open image in gallery The Orangery brings the outside in with its garden views ( Zetter Bloomsbury )

Afternoon tea is also served in The Orangery. Delicate finger sandwiches filled with Coronation chicken and truffle egg mayonnaise give way to warm scones with jam and clotted cream before a procession of beautifully crafted pastries is served, including a rich chocolate délice layered with salted caramel and cocoa nibs. Add a glass of champagne and the hours happily slip away.

There is no formal restaurant at the Zetter Bloomsbury, but The Parlour serves coffees, light bites, bar snacks, and cocktails and wine come evening, and is perhaps the hotel's loveliest room. By day, sunlight pours through windows onto bookshelves, antiques and comfortable armchairs. By evening, antique lamps cast a warm amber glow across the room.

If you prefer a sink-in velvet sofa, you can take your drinks to the The Drawing Room (ground floor) or The Living Room (lower ground floor); both are beautiful lounges that can be hired for private events for up to 30 guests.

Facilities

There's a small well-equipped gym open 24 hours a day overlooking the gardens, with a rowing machine, bike, running machine, free weights and a bench. Yoga mats are available for guests wanting a slower start to the morning, and the hotel has two electric bikes that are available to borrow free of charge.

open image in gallery Snacks and drinks are served in The Parlour ( Rebecca Hope )



Accessibility

The hotel has two accessible bedrooms with adapted wet rooms and lift access.

Pet policy

Dogs are welcome in all rooms, with chew toys, a selection of treats, food bowls and a comfy dog bed in situ on arrival. Rooms also come with a guide to the best dog-friendly places in the area. There is a fee of £25 per pet, per stay.

Check-in/check-out

Check-in is 3pm, check-out is 11am.

Family-friendly?

There are several interconnecting rooms designed with families in mind; these are best suited to those with older children and teenagers. A free cot can be added to all rooms for under-twos.

At a glance

Best thing: Waking up in an impressive London townhouse with no reason to leave.

Perfect for: Romantic escapes and anyone with a penchant for beautiful interiors and old-world glamour.

Not right for: Minimalists.

Instagram from: The Drawing Room when you’re dressed for cocktails.

Address: 2 - 7 Monatague Street, London WC1B 5BP

Phone: +4420 7324 4488

Website: thezetter.com



Caroline was a guest of The Zetter Bloomsbury

News.title: Disgraced funeral director jailed over ‘dreadful’ treatment of bodies and ashes
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Disgraced funeral director Robert Bush has been jailed for 20 years in a case in which more than 200 victims described the devastating impact of his crimes.

Bush, 48, was jailed as Hull Crown Court for 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful burial.

He breached the trust of grieving families “on an almost industrial scale” by keeping bodies for months after they should have been cremated, giving out the wrong ashes, taking money for funeral plans without making any arrangements, and stealing charity donations collected at services.

He was sentenced on Friday for offences spanning 12 years at his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull. Mr Justice Hilliard said he would serve half of his sentence before being released on parole. Although there were proposals to reduce this to one third, this has been “paused”, he said.

The judge said that in the cases of 57 families who were given the wrong ashes or no ashes, about 40 of the deceased were kept for longer than a month before being cremated, including more than 200 days in one case.

He said that boxes of ashes were found in many areas of Bush’s premises and there appeared to be no proper system to record where they were: “The majority of the remains were stored in an undignified manner and the identification of remains was wholly inadequate.”

Telling Hull Crown Court about the terrible scenes police found at Legacy’s Hessle Road premises, he described how there were bodies on racks, two more lying on the floor and evidence of human putrefaction as well as excrement on the floor of a toilet. Adding: “The conditions were dreadful.”

The judge said these details have been “traumatic in the extreme” for the families.

Bush had told police he had been having issues with the refrigeration equipment and he could save money by not running all units.“I have no doubt there was plenty of money… if he had only chosen to apply it in that way,” Mr Justice Hilliard said.

He added that what the dead lacked in dignity at the hands of Robert Bush “is more than made up for by the dignity with which the relatives have conducted themselves on their behalf in these proceedings”.

Hull Crown Court heard that there were no sentencing guidelines and no maximum penalty for the offence of preventing a lawful burial, which accounted for 30 of the charges, and previous cases did not reflect what Bush was doing.

Over four days, the court heard more than 200 statements from victims, with many choosing to read theirs in person and breaking down in tears.

They included relatives of 31 people found at Legacy whose bodies should have been cremated, including the mother of an unborn baby who was found in a paper bag on the floor.

open image in gallery Funeral director Robert Bush outside court ( PA Wire )

The judge also heard from more than 50 people who found out they had been given the wrong ashes for their loved ones when police raided the funeral home and found urns and packaging labelled with their names.

The court heard that Bush’s offending came to light in March 2024 when he was on holiday in Arizona and asked the directors of another funeral firm to help with a body recovery while he was away.

A casual worker at Legacy told the two men “out of the blue” that bodies had been at the site “for years” and described it as “a horror scene”.

The men alerted the police, who searched the premises and found bodies stored on the racks of a cold storage area, with the vast majority “uncovered and in varying states of decomposition”.

open image in gallery Police outside a branch of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in 2024 ( PA Archive )

The court heard the rest of the site was in a “lamentable state”, with ashes in mouldy boxes and even strewn across the floor, photographs left out of coffins and jewellery not returned to families.

An investigation found that Bush had sold fraudulent funeral plans to more than 220 people, pocketing more than £500,000 in the process.

Some of those affected gave statements to the court, describing how he had conned them out of their savings and left them without the safety net of knowing their funerals had been paid for.

The court heard that Bush stole money from 12 charities by not passing on donations collected at services, including the Salvation Army, Macmillan Cancer Support, Help for Heroes, the RNLI and some local groups.

open image in gallery A court drawing of Robert Bush at his sentencing hearing, which stretched for five days ( PA )

An investigation into his finances revealed that over seven years when he was defrauding his customers, Bush spent £42,000 on holidays, £21,000 on motorcycle racing and £17,400 on home improvements.

Richard Wright KC, mitigating, said Bush had prioritised himself and his family over his customers, and was now treated as a “pariah – hated and despised”.

open image in gallery Mr Justice Hilliard sentencing funeral director Robert Bush, 48, to twenty years in prison for 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful burial, at Hull Crown Court, Kingston-upon-Hull. Picture date: Friday July 31, 2026. ( PA )

In April, Bush pleaded guilty to 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from the 12 charities.

He had already admitted 30 counts of fraud by false representation relating to bodies found at the site, and four “foetus allegations” of fraud, where he presented ashes to women falsely saying that they were “the remains of their unborn”.

Bush also pleaded guilty to a further charge of fraud, covering the ashes of 57 people between 2017 and 2024, and one of fraudulent trading relating to funeral plans between 2012 and 2024.

‘The hardest part is not knowing why’: Son of woman found in funeral home

A son whose mother’s body was left in Robert Bush’s funeral parlour for six months said the “hardest part is not knowing why he did it”.

Ron Marsh contacted Legacy Independent Funeral Directors when his mother Joyce Moulton died in September 2023, aged 98.

He said Bush was professional and the service he organised was “excellent”, but the family never received Mrs Moulton’s ashes – and attempts to contact Legacy went unanswered.

In March 2024, he was visited at his Surrey home by police family liaison officers who told him his mother’s body had been found during a raid at Legacy’s premises in Hull.

Mr Marsh, 79, said: “I was gobsmacked. It was just not anything I ever thought happened, would happen, and certainly not happen to my mum.

“I couldn’t comprehend something like that happening, so it was a struggle for me to understand what had happened, why it had happened, and why he had allowed it to happen.”

He went on to say: “It was very traumatic, very upsetting. It’s probably not a strong enough word, but I can’t think of one.

“But I just would like to know what the hell he thought he was doing, because the complete disregard for the dignity of 30 people, and their families, I can’t understand how someone could do it.

“And, unfortunately, I don’t think we’re going to get the chance to ask him, because he’s pleaded guilty, so he doesn’t have to take the stand.

“It will be interesting to see what the mitigating circumstances are that his defence puts up, but as far as I’m concerned, he is a very despicable man with absolutely no morals or human compassion.”

Mr Marsh said his mother was “a grafter” who worked while raising him and his brother as a single parent, before marrying her second husband.

She returned to her home city of Hull to be near her siblings after being widowed in 1990.

Mrs Moulton had dementia and died in hospital in September 2023, two weeks after falling at home.

Mr Marsh contacted Bush after seeing business cards for Legacy at the morgue, and being told by a morgue attendant that “they’re very good”.

“He was professional, courteous, a businessman,” he said.

“We had the service. It was excellent. You could not have wished for a better service.

“When we paid the bill, he said: ‘Your mother will be cremated within the next two to three days.’ I thought that’s it, done deal.”

When the family had not received Mrs Moulton’s ashes by December, Mr Marsh attempted to contact Bush, but his phone calls and emails went unreturned.

After finding out that Bush had never cremated Mrs Moulton’s body, her family have had a second funeral paid for by Hull City Council, and her ashes have been scattered in one of their memorial gardens.

Mr Marsh said: “At the time, it looked like he was a genuine, bona fide, funeral director – three funeral homes, a successful person, and the service itself was very professional.

“But it has left me wondering, how many times has this happened somewhere else, maybe not to the extent of 30 odd bodies, but have other funeral people not carried out their duties, as they should do?

“Because there is no legislation with regard to funeral directors, and therefore, there’s no checking to see that once a funeral service has been had, if it’s not at the crematorium or at the church, that body has actually been either cremated or buried.

“So it still gets to me and I think it will for the rest of my life.

“But it’s the not knowing why he did it that is really more upsetting than anything else. And I don’t think we’ll ever know.”

Mr Marsh paid tribute to his mother as “pugnacious, but generous to a fault”.

He said: “When she went back up to Hull, and in the bungalow, there were a load of what she termed old people, albeit she was in her 80s, but there were old people around her who needed help, and she used to do the shopping for them.

“She always wanted to help people, and she was quite fearless.”

Prime Minister backs calls for regulation of funeral home sector

The sentencing comes as Andy Burnham backed the regulation of funeral homes and mortuaries.

The Prime Minister offered his sympathies to the families of victims of Robert Bush.

A separate independent inquiry into the crimes of David Fuller, who abused at least 100 dead women and girls in hospital mortuaries in south-east England, recommended regulation of the funeral sector to prevent similar crimes being committed again.

Speaking on a visit to Sheffield, Mr Burnham said: “I do back those calls, and there were recommendations in the Fuller Report that will be implemented because we have seen appalling situations like this before.

“I feel for the families and I know it’ll be a difficult day for them with these matters in court again. I was truly horrified when I heard what had happened. Appalling for any family to go through that. This needs a proper response in terms of the regulation needed, to make sure no family goes through that again.

“People, I think, would assume that the highest standards apply to this area and we’ve got to make sure that they do apply and that there can’t be any repeat of what we’ve seen.”

President Donald Trump on Friday unleashed a tirade against one of the Republican senators who have blocked a vote on Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination to formally lead the Department of Justice, writing that the $1.776 billion “weaponization” fund that has driven opposition to his nominee among GOP holdouts should move forward.

In a fiery and lengthy early morning post on Truth Social, Trump called out Texas Republican John Cornyn, one of the two GOP senators who’ve thus far blocked Blanche’s nomination from receiving a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee. He claimed Cornyn “never had a problem” with the plan to compensate convicted criminals — including Jan. rioters — who were prosecuted under Democrats until after he’d opposed the Texan in this year’s GOP primary.

“John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund,’ which will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed by the Crooked Joe Biden Administration, until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent in Texas, who easily won the Nomination for the United States Senate,” he said.

Continuing, the president claimed the thousands of convicts — some of whom assaulted police or committed other acts of violence during the riot he fomented at the U.S. Capitol in January 2021 — had been treated worse than any other group in U.S. history and were “suffering still” despite his decision to pardon them all en masse on his first day back in power last year.

“They are suffering still, many ruined, and I felt that they should be given compensation for what has been done to them,” he said. “I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined!”

Trump is lashing out once more at the Texas senator who has held up his ex-criminal defense lawyer’s bid to become attorney general ( AP )

He added that “millions of people” — including Cornyn — had agreed with him and accused the Texas senator of changing his mind out of spite over his primary loss to a Trump-backed challenger while demanding that Blanche be “immediately approved.”

Despite his increasingly shrill calls for Cornyn and Tillis to drop their opposition to Blanche, it’s unlikely that either will budge from their opposition in light of Trump’s assertion that he still wants the “weaponization” fund to move forward, as it directly contradicts Blanche’s sworn testimony from his confirmation hearing in which he called the plan “dead.”

The president’s latest tirade in support of Blanche comes less than a day after he said he’d consider pulling his former criminal defense attorney’s nomination rather than concede to Cornyn and North Carolina’s Thom Tillis, both of whom have demanded written assurances from Blanche that the “weaponization” fund plan will not be carried out in any form.

Both GOP holdouts have also objected to Blanche’s purported immunization of Trump and his family and businesses from any Internal Revenue Service audit or investigation.

On Thursday, he called his ex-criminal defense attorney a “star” who “has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time”and vowed to keep Blanche in place as acting attorney general regardless of what the senate does with his nomination.

“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” he said.

But Cornyn later posted to X that opposition to Blanche on account of the IRS deal he struck with Trump could be deeper than just he and his Tar Heel State colleague.

“POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis,” he said.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu confronted vice president JD Vance over his criticism of Israel during a recent trip to the US, according to a new report.

Netanyahu made his seventh state visit to the US this week to attend the funeral of his close friend Lindsey Graham and had meetings with President Donald Trump, defence secretary Pete Hegseth and Vance.

The vice president has been the most vocal critic of Israel in the Trump administration and recently accused the country of “trying to kill your way out of solving every single national security problem”.

In a one-to-one meeting at Blair House in Washington on Tuesday, Netanyahu addressed his criticism in a “frank and candid conversation”, an Israeli official told Axios.

A US official confirmed the nature of the discussion saying: “The conversation was direct.”

open image in gallery The conversation was ‘frank and direct’ according to sources ( Getty )

A second US official told the publication that the talk was a “cordial and productive conversation about Middle East issues that are important to both countries.”

They denied that the conversation was confrontational in nature and said: “The vice president and the prime minister agreed to continue pursuing opportunities for Israel and the United States to cooperate in areas of mutual interest and shared goals.”

In June, Vance hit back at Israeli politicians who had attacked the US deal with Iran, saying: “If I was in the cabinet of the Israeli government, I might not be attacking the only powerful ally that I have anywhere left in the entire world.”

He suggested that disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein had connections to the “highest levels of Israeli intelligence”, claims which Netanyahu and Israeli officials have consistently denied.

open image in gallery Vance has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu ( Reuters )

Vance also told Joe Rogan earlier this month that he believed that Israeli politicians had been influencing the US to move away from diplomacy and continue with a more belligerent campaign against Iran.

At the start of the war in March, reports suggested that Netanyahu and Vance held a tense phone call in which the vice president said that the Israeli leader’s predictions that Iran would capitulate were too optimistic.

But last month, Vance reiterated the close relationship between the US and Israel saying that while Netanyahu has “certainly got some things wrong” he would still say that “he’s been a good partner”.

"We're gonna keep on working together,” he told CBS. “But where interests diverge, the United States is gonna pursue the best interests of our nation, and that's how it's gonna be."

The Independent has contacted JD Vance’s representatives and the White House for comment.

Stuart Fails to Save the Universe episode two sees the return of a major Big Bang Theory star — but not as fans remember them.

Set after the events of the original sitcom, HBO Max’s new spin-off follows Stuart Bloom (Kevin Sussman), the comic book store owner from The Big Bang Theory, as he accidentally destroys a multiverse device created by Sheldon Cooper and Leonard Hofstadter.

With the help of familiar faces Bert (Brian Posehn), Barry Kripke (John Ross Bowie) and Denise (Lauren Lapkus), Stuart sets off on a mission across alternate realities to restore order to the universe, encountering new versions of characters fans will recognize from The Big Bang Theory along the way.

The latest episode, which aired Thursday night, sees the group enter a reality in which all humans have a device implanted on their necks that delivers an electric shock whenever they argue or get aggressive.

This eventually leads them into a 30-month reeducation facility designed to eliminate conflict. But after completing the program, they are unexpectedly abducted and taken to an abandoned warehouse.

open image in gallery John Ross Bowie, Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn star in the new ‘Big Bang Theory’ spin-off, ‘Stuart Saves the Universe’ ( HBO Max )

It’s here, once their hoods are removed, that Kaley Cuoco’s Penny reveals herself.

Rather than the blonde, aspiring actress-turned-pharmaceutical sales rep from The Big Bang Theory, this alternate version of Penny has brunette hair and leads a resistance movement against their AI-controlled world alongside her ex-boyfriend Zack (Brian Thomas Smith).

“A big part of it was offering them a challenge to do something entirely different,” co-creator and executive producer Chuck Lorre told Variety of bringing back some original The Big Bang Theory characters in new forms.

open image in gallery Kaley Cuoco reprises her role as Penny in ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ — but with a very different look ( Colin Remas Brown/HBO Max )

open image in gallery In ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe,’ Penny leads a resistance movement against an AI-controlled world ( Colin Remas Brown/HBO Max )

“As you’ve seen in Episode 2, Kaley’s not playing the server in the Cheesecake Factory. It’s still Penny, and now she’s a badass guerrilla leader. That was part of the design from the very beginning. In a multiverse environment, these characters could recur as themselves, but with an entirely different backstory.”

The Big Bang Theory ran from 2007 to 2019 on CBS and made global stars of its core cast members, Cuoco, Jim Parsons (Sheldon), Johnny Galecki (Leonard), Kunal Nayyar (Raj Koothrappali), Mayim Bialik (Amy Farrah Fowler) and Simon Helberg (Howard Wolowitz).

It followed a group of socially awkward scientists and their friends as they navigated relationships, careers and everyday life in Pasadena, California.

The wildly popular show reportedly ended because Parsons turned down $50 million to return for a 13th and 14th season.

Stuart Fails to Save the Universe airs Thursdays at 9 p.m. ET on HBO Max.

News.title: The families traumatised by ‘evil’ funeral director Robert Bush: ‘My uncle was left in a body bag for 6 months’
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

After news broke that a funeral home in Hull had been discovered with 35 bodies, Mark Hotham’s family had a “gut feeling” that he was one of Robert Bush’s victims.

The 87-year-old was the last person to be identified after police made the gruesome discovery at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in March 2024.

By that time, he had been lying dead for over half a year, with his family unsure who was in the coffin at his funeral.

“Bless him, he wasn’t changed at all and had been left in the clothes he had died in,” his nephew Nigel Hotham told The Independent. “They had left his emergency fall assistance pendant around his neck. He was just left in a body bag for six months.”

Bush, 48, had abused the trust placed in him by families on an “almost industrial scale” by keeping bodies for months after they should have been cremated, giving out the wrong ashes, stealing charity donations and taking money for fraudulent funeral plans.

He was jailed on Friday at Hull Crown Court for 20 years. Passing sentence, Mr Justice Hilliard said Bush’s offending had caused “anguish and pain on a scale beyond comprehension” and that “no sentence can put right the harm the defendant has done.”

He added Bush was motivated by “financial greed” and had a “heartless side to him too”.

open image in gallery Mark Hotham's body was found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors six months after his death ( Family handout )

Upon being told by police that his uncle was one of the bodies, Mr Hotham said: “A sergeant who I knew rang me and said, ‘Nig, I think we’ve got Mark.’

“That line will stick in my head for the rest of my life. My throat went really dry, the room was spinning and I felt sick. I phoned my sister who lives in Lincolnshire and she became hysterical.”

The five-day sentencing has been a traumatic process, with Mr Hotham left shocked after Bush walked past them “nonchalantly” before entering the dock.

Police were called to Legacy after concerns were raised about the treatment of the deceased, and discovered 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes.

open image in gallery Funeral director Robert Bush, centre, arrives at Hull Crown Court ( PA Wire )

“I despise him, I don’t forgive him and I never, ever will,” Mr Hotham said.

In emotional scenes, more than 80 people told Hull Crown Court how “evil” and “callous” Bush had devastated their lives, with the judge told the funeral home was akin to a “horror scene”.

Jasmine Beverley and her partner Ben were left distraught after their son Sunny was “born sleeping”. They had left his body at Legacy alongside a photograph and a blue fleece blanket.

They were handed his ashes inside an envelope in March 2023, but his remains were discovered in a brown paper bag almost two years after he was born.

Through tears, she told Bush: “I trusted you with the most precious person in my life.”

open image in gallery Bush has now been jailed for his crimes ( Humberside Police )

They were not the only bereaved parents to have their trust abused by Bush, who pleaded guilty to four “foetus fraud” allegations.

During this period, he spent more than £42,000 on holidays while he was defrauding scores of customers.

He also spent £9,000 on camping and almost £7,000 on motorcycle racing in the year he told Ms Beverley her unborn baby had been cremated, with one of his victims describing him as a “cruel conman”.

Financial records submitted to the court showed that between 2017 and 2024, when he was arrested, Bush spent more than £42,000 on holidays, £21,000 on motorcycle racing and £17,400 on home improvements.

Despite his friendly facade, certain families had expressed concerns about the service their loved ones had received. Jim Porter’s daughter Tina Thomas noticed at his funeral that the coffin did not look big enough for him.

The 80-year-old’s body was later recovered from Legacy with his hospital identification bands still on his wrist and ankle.

open image in gallery The bodies were discovered by chance while Bush was on holiday in Arizona ( PA )

Another woman had noticed Bush’s strange behaviour while organising a funeral for her father Shane Atkinson, in which he made comments like: “It’s been a pleasure working with your dad this week. I’ve had a lot of fatties in this week, it’s been hard work, and your dad is little.”

There were gasps in court as forensic scientist Dr Richard Lloyd described the “lamentable state” of the mortuary in Hessle Road, with unidentified ashes in mouldy boxes.

Dr Lloyd said the first stages of cleansing did not appear to have been carried out on any of the deceased, and it appeared “bodies were simply abandoned… for nature to take its course”.

The court heard there was a large quantity of unidentified clothing, which probably should have been for dressing the deceased, meaning this “last office” service was routinely not carried out.

Bush had also stolen money from 12 charities by not passing on donations collected at his funeral services, including the Salvation Army, Macmillan Cancer Support, Help for Heroes, the RNLI and some local groups.

open image in gallery Bush also stole from 12 charities and pocketed funeral donations ( Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire )

Echoing calls from families, one of the industry bodies representing funeral directors said it was time for statutory regulation.

Andrew Judd, chief executive of the National Association of Funeral Directors, told The Independent: “The problem we have is that membership of our trade association or some of the other ones is entirely elective.

“We are resolute that people will join and remain in our membership because they have nothing to hide and they want to be the best we can be and the services we provide help with that.

“Membership of our association comes with strings attached. If anyone is in active membership, they are subject to routine unannounced inspections.

“Currently, if a funeral director chooses not to join the trade association, nobody has access to their business and there is no mandatory requirement for inspection.”

Earlier this year, Richard Elkin and Hayley Bell were jailed for four years by a judge who heard details of decomposing bodies covered in maggots and lying in their own fluids at their funeral business in Gosport, Hampshire.

Families involved in this case called for government action. They were supported by Gosport’s Tory MP Caroline Dinenage, who raised the issue in parliament, saying: “The case highlighted that the funeral sector is nothing better than a lawless Wild West.”

Rob Key has no doubt Stephen Fleming is the right man to revive England’s Test team and declared he “wouldn’t be surprised” if Ben Stokes was tempted out of retirement to play a role.

As managing director of men’s cricket at the England and Wales Cricket Board, Key is attempting to pick up the pieces of a turbulent summer that has seen former skipper Stokes walk away from international duty and Brendon McCullum axed as red-ball coach.

Key’s own position has come under heavy scrutiny but, having retained his job, he has identified former New Zealand captain Fleming and returning captain Joe Root as the partnership to bring stability and success back to a side that had clearly lost its way.

open image in gallery Stephen Fleming will take over as Test coach later this year (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Archive )

McCullum remains an important part of the picture at the helm of the white-ball team and plenty still believe Stokes could re-enter the fray in time for next year’s Ashes campaign.

Speaking at Lord’s to launch his latest vision for England, Key would not rule out a headline-grabbing return for the Durham all-rounder.

Asked if Fleming had raised the idea, he said: “We haven’t got round to that at the moment, but it would be a great story.”

Pressed by Sky Sports on whether Stokes himself had given any indication, a smiling Key added: “No, he hasn’t but I wouldn’t be surprised. Anything’s possible with Ben.

“No (bridges have been burned)… not at all. Not as far as I’m concerned.”

Fleming, 53, was a highly respected tactician and man manager during his long stint as New Zealand captain – during which time he forged a strong bond with McCullum.

open image in gallery Brendon McCullum will continue to lead the Test team (Gary Oakley/PA) ( PA Wire )

That relationship could serve the ECB well as they attempt to avoid the tensions that have marred previous attempts to install a split coaching regime – with Andy Flower and Ashley Giles failing to gel and Matthew Mott playing second fiddle to McCullum when they attempted a job share.

There has, though, been consternation about Fleming not taking charge of the forthcoming series against Pakistan. Having just concluded a long stint in charge of Chennai Super Kings he will take a break before arriving in the country in September, leaving him seven Tests and no home series before the Ashes.

Key was bullish on that, insisting: “My job is to get the best person. It wasn’t a stipulation for any of the candidates that you had to be there for Pakistan. Had that been the case, that would have limited the field drastically.

“A month ago this was probably not on a lot of people’s radar – certainly myself and Stephen Fleming, as well. In life, you have a lot of things that you have to do, that you can’t do, that have been planned a long way in advance, that are really important for him as well.

“So that wasn’t a stipulation that you had to be in there, as I said, that would have narrowed the field considerably if it was.

“In Stephen and Joe, I think we’ve got the two best people to take what is a side with a huge amount of potential. I’m as optimistic as ever that we’ve got the best people to take English cricket forward.”

open image in gallery Joe Root returns for a second spell as England captain (Ben Whitley/PA) ( PA Wire )

Four of England’s last six Test coaches have been imported from overseas, Fleming following in the footsteps of McCullum, Trevor Bayliss and Andy Flower, in what appears an indictment over the domestic production line.

Key accepted there had been slow progress on that score but indicated new opportunities for homegrown candidates to join the setup could be imminent, with Glamorgan’s Richard Dawson a leading contender.

“It’s not happened quick enough, but that’s a massive part of what we’re going to try and do going forward,” he said.

“One of the first things Stephen spoke about was that. We have a duty as well to bring coaches through, to upskill and to give them experiences. It’s a problem we’re all trying to solve, it’s just not a quick fix.

“When you go for jobs like this…the remit is you get the best person possible and in my opinion, that’s Stephen Fleming. Next time you don’t want someone to go, ‘Well, I have to appoint an English coach’. What you want is the English coaches to be top of that list.”

News.title: Senior dating: a guide to finding love later in life
News.content:
Whether you’re a widow, widower or divorcee, the thought of online dating in later life can feel daunting. However, more and more people are turning to the internet to find romance. Roughly 16 per cent of UK adults are using online dating services to meet a partner, according to Statista. Among them, there are lots of singles over 50 using dating sites.

So here’s how to navigate your senior dating online, with expert advice from psychologist and dating coach Dr Pam Spurr, and sex and relationship coach Angela Vossen.

How do I know if I'm ready to date again as a senior?

Coming out of any relationship is hard. If you’re hoping to date after a divorce, bereavement or break up, it can take a long time to feel ready to date again. Dr Spurr advises taking your time.

“Many people feel bruised, even traumatised, after coming out of a long-term relationship or having been bereaved,” she explains. “Your feelings naturally vary from day to day about whether you're ready to get back out to look for love – or even for fun. A crucial factor is if you've come to the point where you have more good days compared to bad days”.

Dr Spurr explains that good days are the days on which you feel more optimistic about life generally, and you find your thoughts turning to meeting someone new. “That's an important sign that you are healing,” she says. “However, if you're still feeling deeply insecure or are riddled with self-doubt about your worthiness, take your time. When you feel worthy, you will find someone worthy of you”.

Feeling heartbroken? Learn how to get over a break up

How to start senior dating online

If you’re new to online dating, it can feel intimidating at first. The secret is taking things step by step so that you do things at your own pace. The first step, however, should be choosing a senior dating site that will help match you with like-minded people. This will narrow your search and ensure your dating experience is more successful.

Step 1: Create an online profile

Once you’ve decided on a dating site or app and signed up, you’ll be asked to write a dating profile. This should reflect who you are along with your passions, values and what you seek in a partner.

Try to be authentic rather than creating a fantasy version of yourself. If you exaggerate your accomplishments, your date will only feel deceived once they get to know you. Likewise, don’t be tempted to use a photo of yourself from 10 years ago.

What are you waiting for? |  Single and looking to find true love? Sign up today for Telegraph Dating and join more than 220,000 like-minded people. Join today

Step 2: Spark meaningful chats with potential dates

Once you have signed up to a senior dating site and created a profile, you will be free to start looking at other people’s profiles and sending messages to anyone that catches your attention. But how can you initiate a conversation after an introduction?

“When messaging people on dating sites, ask open-ended questions to spark meaningful chats,” says Angela. A good example would be, ‘I can see you enjoy travel. What place have you always wanted to visit but haven’t yet?’ or “tell me more about your love of tennis? Did you watch the US Open?” If things go really well and the chat seems to flow naturally, you may decide to organise a phone chat or ask them out on a date. An initial chat over the phone can help gauge how well you get on and how easily the conversation flows. If this goes well, meeting in person may feel less nerve wracking and a little less ‘blind’.

Step 3: Prioritise your safety

“While most people are well intentioned online, it’s important to protect your safety,” advises Ms Vossen. “Keep personal details private (like where you live or your social media profiles) until you’ve met in person and built trust”. You should also arrange first dates in public places, share your plans with a friend, and trust your instincts if something feels off.

If the first date or two doesn’t quite hit the mark, try not to be too disappointed and remember that you can say no to another date. Ms Vossen says: “Be patient – online dating takes time, but with practice, you’ll gain confidence and enjoy the journey”.

Traditional ways to meet senior singles

Of course, couples continue to meet in a manner that predates online dating sites. If you’re keen to join the older dating scene but find the online world overwhelming, there are plenty of ways to meet people in real life.

1. Holidays and group trips

We are often our best selves on holiday, so it’s the ideal place to find a single senior woman or to meet men if the opportunity presents itself. Why not organise a trip on which you meet new people while doing what you love, whether that’s cycling, walking, sightseeing or just travelling around a new part of the world. There are many escorted tours that cater to specific age groups and interests. They also take away the stress of organising a trip yourself.

“An organised holiday or trip can be a great place to meet someone new and there are many organisations offering these for the over 50s,” says Dr Spur. “A word of caution though, you can spend a lot of money and there's no guarantee that you will meet that special person. However, if it's a place you've wanted to travel to then go with the mindset that you're going to have a great trip. If you meet someone, that's an added bonus”.

2. Activities and social groups

Whether you enjoy walking, reading or volunteering, taking up a new hobby or joining a social group is a great way to enhance your social life and increase your chances of meeting a new romantic interest.

“Joining a club or taking up a hobby can be a fantastic way of meeting singles who enjoy the same pastimes,” says Dr Spur. “You're doing an activity you enjoy knowing that there might also be someone there that will catch your eye”.

If you do meet someone that you’re interested in at a social event, Dr Spur advises starting with a simple ‘hello’ and an easy question such as how long they've been doing that particular activity or hobby. “This can open-up a friendly conversation that might lead to flirting down the line,” she says.

Start online dating for seniors today

Whichever way you decide to start looking for love, approach it in a way that you feel comfortable with. Signing up to an online dating service is a great way to meet other seniors. Remember, it’s never too late to begin a new chapter.
