The defender also won three European Cups, two Intercontinental Cups and four Italian Supercups during his career and his contributions to Milan saw the club retire the No 6 jersey.

On the international stage, Baresi was part of the Italy squad that won the World Cup in 1982, as well as featuring in the 1994 World Cup, which ended in a penalty-shoot-out defeat to Brazil in the final.

A post on the official Milan X account said: "The entire history of AC Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi.

"His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club's DNA, just as his iconic No 6 shirt is.

"The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi's family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own."

In a further statement on the club website, Milan added: "Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan, is incredibly difficult.

"But everyone at the club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi's memory. We must be strong and gather every bit of energy, even at this saddest of times.

Image: Franco Baresi made 719 appearances for AC Milan

"We lost Franco only a few months after his last public appearance in a packed San Siro, at the Milan Winter Olympics opening ceremony, an event on the world stage he helped make unforgettable.

"In memory of Franco, we stand united, knowing he'll guide and push us throughout our Rossoneri journey. Forever. Because Baresi is forever."

Baresi made 81 appearances for Italy and Italian Football Federation president Giovanni Malago described him as an "extraordinary champion".

"Italian football has lost one of its legends," Malago said in a statement on the FIGC website.

"An extraordinary champion who wore only two jerseys throughout his career: AC Milan and the Azzurri. A romantic choice, one that earned him a place in the hearts of fans and millions of Italians."

AC Milan great Paolo Maldini - who spent 25 years with the club - described Baresi as the "greatest player" he played with.

Image: Baresi in action for Italy at the 1994 World Cup

Maldini said on Instagram: "You taught me to fight until my very last breath, and showed me the meaning of devotion to the jersey and the value of being a true leader. You did this through your example, every single day: few words, but countless actions.

"You protected me when I was a child, guided me as a young man, and inspired me as an adult. You were the greatest player I ever had the honour of playing with.

"Sending a warm embrace to your entire family, especially your wife Maura and your sons, Edoardo and Giannandrea.

"We will miss you, captain. But the light of your star will continue to guide us forever."

Former Italy goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon shared his memories of his debut for Parma competing against Baresi.

"On November 19, 1995, I made my Serie A debut against Milan. I was 17 years old, and on the other side was the captain of that team: Franco Baresi," Buffon posted on X.

"For a boy my age, finding myself on the field against champions like him was something incredible. From that day on, I had an even clearer understanding of what it meant to represent football with class, leadership, and respect.

"Goodbye Franco. Rest in peace."

Sports.title: Are Bournemouth set to strike defender gold again with Silva?
Sports.content:
There was a time when Antonio Silva's rise to the top appeared an inevitability. He was only 18 years old when he scored his first Champions League goal for Benfica in a 4-3 win over Juventus. He played at the 2022 World Cup for Portugal soon after that.

Since then, Silva has been linked with Europe's biggest clubs but it is Bournemouth who look set to sign him after agreeing a deal with Benfica. In truth, excluded from Portugal's squad this summer, his momentum has stalled. But, aged 22, there is time for this move to ignite his career.

Sure, there are grander destinations. But Bournemouth have emerged as one of the best recruiters of talent - proving themselves particularly adept at developing defenders. Silva is entitled to believe he can be the next to flourish for the Cherries.

Illia Zabarnyi and Dean Huijsen left for Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid, respectively, just one year ago. Marcos Senesi has since moved to Tottenham. Silva is special enough to impress every bit as much as his predecessors on the south coast.

Speaking to Joao Nuno Fonseca, Silva's coach during his days with Benfica's development team, there is confidence that Bournemouth boss Marco Rose may have a gem in his hands. "Marco will not have any problems with him," Fonseca tells Sky Sports.

"Antonio is a very good person and the type of player that is easy to coach. He is very attentive. At Benfica, he listened to every detail that we gave him. He was very mature and that had a huge impact because it is difficult to reach the first team at Benfica."

Silva did that swiftly in part because of this mentality. "You give him feedback and he applies it directly in games. He understands everything." It made for a precocious talent in his teenage years, boasting an appreciation of time and space that belied his years.

"The key aspect of his game is his anticipation. Antonio reads the game really well. He is an anticipation-based defender rather than a reactive one. You see a lot of reactive centre-backs. He is not one of those. Antonio understands what will happen next."

Fonseca notes that the feet are good too. But it is the mind that saw Silva rise so quickly. "The technical skills are there, of course. But the key difference is understanding the game, in possession and out of possession. He knows what to do in those moments."

He praises the timing of his tackles. "He is one of the best in this technical aspect." And Silva's statistics show a defender who is aggressive in winning interceptions and aerial duels. Important qualities given that Bournemouth will expect him to be proactive.

In possession, Silva has the confidence to play forwards rather than simply recycling possession. "He is a modern ball-playing centre-back, very comfortable receiving the ball on either foot." There is variety to his use of the ball, chipped passes and more.

"One of the best things he has is the diagonal switches that he can do without looking," says Fonseca. "He is very, very talented at that." Expect that to be a significant feature at Bournemouth, who are looking to retain elements of Andoni Iraola's vertical approach.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch some of Bournemouth's best team goals under Andoni Iraola

It is why Rose is regarded as the continuity candidate. Iraola is on record as an admirer of the former Borussia Dortmund coach who honed his ideas in the Red Bull school where looking forward and pressing high up the pitch are viewed as non-negotiables.

"I think it will work fantastically because of the way Antonio reads situations," says Fonseca. "Marco will demand anticipation, a defender who looks for forward passes that break the lines and find those spaces in behind. Antonio will adapt very quickly."

The Premier League will still be different. Even after four years at Benfica - perhaps especially after four years at Benfica - it will feel a step up. "This move is fantastic for him because he will evolve and mature much more as a player in the Premier League."

Did he stay in Portugal too long? "He needed to move earlier, in my opinion," concedes Fonseca. "He stayed longer than expected. The decision that he made not to leave Benfica last year did not help him because he needed exposure to new experiences."

He explains: "We used to say at Benfica that while life starts at Benfica it does not end at Benfica. You need to move forward if you want to play on the world stage." But a season with Jose Mourinho, an unbeaten league campaign no less, is hardly a waste.

And Fonseca does not place too much weight on the decision of Roberto Martinez to omit him from the World Cup squad in favour of his Benfica team-mate Tomas Araujo. "The decision of the Portugal head coach does not mean he is not capable," he says.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A look at the changes at Bournemouth as the club prepares for the Europa League

"Antonio is very capable and is completely ready to play in the Premier League. But it will be a different challenge for him. The challenge in England is week by week, not just waiting for the European games like he could at Benfica. The focus must be there."

Maybe there will be mistakes, lessons to learn even for a 22-year-old player who has already racked up an astonishing 181 appearances for Benfica in all competitions. "In the Premier League, the margin of error is very small. He needs to have that in mind."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at some of the best bits from Bournemouth's Rayan last season

But the overriding feeling is that this is an opportunity for Silva - and will be a coup for Bournemouth. "Antonio is a very complete centre-back who would help any team in the world. At this moment, it is going to be Bournemouth." A stepping stone to greatness?

"He has all the qualities to make the next move, but he cannot think like that. This move is the most important of his career. He will be in the Premier League. If he wants to move forward, he needs to focus completely and give 100 per cent for Bournemouth."

That is perhaps the lesson of Silva's journey so far. The hype came early. The next step is set to arrive later than expected. But at 22, there remains ample time for him to fulfil the promise that made him one of European football's most coveted young defenders.

Bournemouth have shown repeatedly that they can provide the perfect environment for talented centre-backs to take that next leap. Antonio Silva is now poised to have the opportunity to prove that his journey to the top remains on course. It is simply set to take a different route.

Sports.title: Meet Bahoya... the Bundesliga's fastest player attracting PL interest
Sports.content:
Why Bahoya’s profile is so in-demand

Premier League managers are being forced to come up with new solutions to combat the craze of man-to-man marking that has swept the English top-flight. The challenge is breaking the defensive chain, because once you do, more often than not, chaos ensues.

Having a player with the capacity to consistently beat their man is kryptonite against man-to-man marking. Only four Premier League players completed more take-ons per 90 in the league last season than Bahoya, while only two outperformed him in the Bundesliga.

Jeremy Doku is the gold standard for this metric. The word often associated with the Belgium winger is “unpredictable”, and that is exactly how Bahoya’s U17s coach at Angers describes the 21-year-old.

Like Doku, Bahoya’s unpredictability is not limited to his one-vs-one supremacy. “He can make runs from deep, play between the lines, and wide on the touchline,” Manu Guidicelli tells Sky Sports. “He can go right or left for a dribble – and above all, he can finish the actions.”

Having the capacity to drag your marker into areas of the pitch they do not want to be is another effective method of unlocking man-to-man marking. Guidicelli taught Bahoya how he could exploit his speed advantage in these scenarios at Angers.

“We made him understand he had this ability, and he quickly understood," says Guidicelli, who highlighted Bahoya's footballing IQ as one of his strengths, "and then he scored more goals. When he made those runs from deep, it was hard for defenders to catch up with him."

Asked about Bahoya's acceleration, Dina Ebimbe says: "It's too much. Maybe you can catch him after a while, but at the start, you're definitely not going to see him again. His steps are so quick and he can change direction very fast.”

Winning duels and making interceptions can be an even more effective way of creating an offensive advantage. Bahoya has made this another strength in his game after a lot of work since arriving in Frankfurt.

“He works a lot in the gym,” says Dina Ebimbe. "It changed everything for him because he was too slight when he joined. Everyone pushed him. He was always on the floor. He started work in the gym, and last season we saw his body was really different.”

Bahoya ranked in the top 11 per cent for duels won per 90 (8.9) and top 10 per cent for interceptions per 90 (0.88) among wingers in Europe’s top five leagues last season. His 2.1 tackles per 90 also placed him in the top 13 per cent of that same group.

"Jean-Matteo, in the athletic point, he's really top," says Dina Ebimbe. "He can run and make a lot of sprints. He's one of the fastest players in this league. And now he's becoming stronger."

Sports.title: West Ham in talks for Celtic midfielder Engels
Sports.content:
West Ham are in talks with Celtic over the signing of midfielder Arne Engels.

The 22-year-old also has interest from a number of Premier League clubs. Nottingham Forest saw multiple offers rejected for him on Deadline Day of the winter window.

But it is Championship side West Ham who are currently pursuing the Belgium international, who has two years to run on his contract.

Celtic's chief executive Michael Nicholson said a few weeks ago that the Hoops' transfer activity was proving difficult because they are competing with clubs in the Championship for targets.

Image: Engels has had interest from Premier League clubs this summer

Nicholson was speaking at Celtic's annual general meeting, in which manager Martin O'Neill said his squad was not strong enough to compete and is in major need of signings.

Celtic have since signed striker Kasper Hogh for a club-record fee from Bodo/Glimt.

It remains to be seen if any Premier League clubs will rival West Ham for Engels' signature.

Forest's top midfield target is Lucas Bergvall but they have been unable to strike an agreement with Spurs for the 20-year-old.

Sports.title: Infantino increasingly embattled after senior adviser resigns over World Cup sell-off plans
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino’s authority has been dealt a fresh blow after Carlos Cordeiro, one of his senior advisers, resigned with immediate effect in protest at proposals to sell a stake in the World Cup.

In the latest embarrassment for Infantino, who saw European FAs threaten to boycott future Fifa tournaments on Thursday, the former US Soccer chief Cordeiro criticised “a bad deal for football” and pointed out that the global governing body already sits on huge amounts of debt-free reserves.

“I cannot stand by while Fifa considers selling a stake in the World Cup,” Cordeiro said in his resignation statement. “I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.”

Cordeiro has worked for Fifa since 2021 as senior adviser to Infantino. He also operated as a senior adviser to the White House taskforce on this summer’s World Cup.

In resigning he said Fifa “already has the financial capacity to provide [additional financial] support from existing resources”. He added that Fifa would be “mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification” if it sold off a permanent stake.

In addition, Cordeiro questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process. “Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”

It adds to the pressure growing on Infantino and Fifa, which is facing calls for an urgent review of its governance after insisting that the planned World Cup sell-off will continue despite the threat of a boycott from all 55 European nations.

View image in fullscreen Carlos Cordeiro with Donald Trump and Gianni Infantin at the White House in 2018. Photograph: Evan Vucci/AP

In a strongly worded statement issued on Friday morning, the Asian Football Confederation backed Uefa’s and Concacaf’s opposition to the creation of a new commercial company, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), saying it “cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward”, and urging Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”.

Fifa had attempted to double down on its position overnight, releasing a statement at 4am UK time saying “we will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA [member association] has the ability to express its vote based on facts,” but it is now clear Infantino is facing united opposition to his proposals from around the globe.

Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC constitute 143 of Fifa’s 211 members, so if their coalition remains united there is no prospect of Infantino getting the votes he needs. The 56-year-old’s position as Fifa president is also under threat for the first time since he was elected in 2016, unless he backs down quickly.

While stopping short of matching Uefa’s boycott the AFC went further than Concacaf in clearly stating that the FFE proposal should be dropped. “The AFC stands in solidarity with Uefa and Concacaf in expressing serious concerns over Fifa’s proposal to introduce private investment into Fifa’s flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE,” its statement read. “The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game.

“Football should never have been placed in such a position. Against this backdrop, and in light of the clear positions expressed by Uefa and Concacaf as well as the unprecedented divisions that have emerged across the football world, the AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.

“The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world’s leading football nations. Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered.”

The AFC echoed Uefa and Concacaf’s complaints about a lack of consultation from Fifa, making clear that it is not the first time confederations and the Fifa council have been excluded from major decisions, most notably hosting arrangements for the 2030 and 2034 World Cups.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“The AFC sees this moment as a catalyst for strengthening institutional practices,” the statement continued. “While every Fifa MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote.

“It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.

“The AFC calls upon Fifa to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by Fifa’s statutory bodies.”

View image in fullscreen The hosts for the 2030 World Cup were announced at the Fifa Congress in Zurich in 2024. Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPA

Fifa had attempted to blame media reporting for the widespread opposition to its scheme, but it is now clear that will not wash with most of its member associations.

“We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation,” a Fifa statement read. “Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

“FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all Fifa member associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself.

“Nobody is selling football. This is not something Fifa would ever entertain. Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world. Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of Fifa.”

If Fifa was to refuse to back down, the first step of the threatened European boycott would come at next month’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland, with senior Women’s World Cup qualifiers to follow in October.

Sports.title: Franco Baresi, iconic Milan and Italy legend, dies aged 66
Sports.content:
The former Milan and Italy defender Franco Baresi, one of the most recognisable players of the ⁠golden era of Italian football in the 1980s and 1990s, has died at the age of 66.

“The entire history of ⁠AC Milan is in ⁠tears following the ​passing of Franco Baresi,” his former club said on Friday. “His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club’s DNA, just as his iconic No 6 shirt is.”

Last year Baresi’s former club, where he served as honorary vice-president, said he had undergone surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule, and had ⁠been prescribed recovery treatment by a cancer specialist.

In February, Baresi was one of the torchbearers for the Olympic ​flame at the opening ceremony for the Milano ‌Cortina Winter Games, appearing alongside ‌former Inter and Italy defender Giuseppe Bergomi, his longtime rival on the pitch.

Baresi is regarded as a Milan icon, having spent his entire 20-year career with the club, winning six Serie A titles and three top European trophies, and captaining the team for 15 seasons before retiring in 1997.

At the end of his playing career, Milan retired his No 6 shirt, making him the first player in the club’s history to receive that honour.

View image in fullscreen Baresi and Juventus captain Gianluca Vialli in 1992 in Turin. Photograph: Etsuo Hara/Getty Images

Baresi was part of the Italy squad that won the ‌1982 World Cup and captained the team to the 1994 final, which ended in a narrow penalty shootout loss to Brazil, with Baresi among the players who failed to ​score. He famously played the full 120 minutes just 25 days after knee surgery.

His loyalty to Milan was established early in his career, as he stayed with the club through two relegations to Serie B in the early 1980s and helped guide them back to the top flight on both occasions.

Baresi was the cornerstone of the Milan and ⁠Italy defences for nearly two decades, captaining the Serie A club during the most ​successful period in their history and ​earning 81 caps for the national ​team.

View image in fullscreen Franco Baresi playing for Italy against Malta during a World Cup qualifier in December 1992. Photograph: Colorsport/Rex

In an era dominated by physical defenders, Baresi distinguished himself through his reading of ​the game, redefining the ‌sweeper role by combining ​defensive authority with the ​ability to launch attacks from deep.

He marshalled a celebrated Milan backline featuring Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta and Mauro Tassotti, helping perfect the high defensive line and offside trap that underpinned the club’s 58-match unbeaten run in Serie A and earned Fabio Capello’s side the nickname “Gli Invincibili” (the Invincibles).

Sports.title: Who should win the men’s Ballon d’Or?
Sports.content:
Harry Kane

Seventy-three goals in 64 games for club and country – the second most prolific season by any player in history after Lionel Messi’s 82-goal campaign in 2011-12 – not bad for a man who once sat on the bench alongside Jamie Vardy in the Championship. Harry Kane was not a teenage prodigy like a few of the other players on this list but here he is crashing football’s top table at the age of 33.

It feels strange that a player who has scored at least 24 goals in each of the last 12 seasons, has won back-to-back Golden Boots in the Premier League, a World Cup Golden Boot and two European Golden Shoes, has never finished higher than 10th in Ballon d’Or voting.

The numbers were always there but now he is adding the silverware. Kane’s trophy drought ended when Bayern Munich won the Bundesliga last year and that triumph has opened the floodgates. Another Bundesliga title followed this season, alongside the DFB-Pokal and German Supercup.

England did not end their trophy drought at the World Cup but their captain scored six goals and overtook Gary Lineker as England’s top scorer at the tournament, ensuring he remained in contention for the Ballon d’Or.

Lamine Yamal

“It’s about being calm. When I’m in the area with the ball, I decide what happens,” said Lamine Yamal in February after he had scored the first hat-trick of his career in Barcelona’s 4-1 win against Villarreal. For most 19-year-olds this would sound like arrogance, but Yamal is not like most 19-year-olds.

He offered more proof of that this summer. The Spain forward became the first player to appear in a European Championship final and a World Cup final before turning 20 – and he won both. He only scored one goal at the World Cup, which was a modest return by his own lofty standards, but he was influential throughout. He won a gamechanging penalty in the semi-final against France, he made more successful take-ons than Messi across the tournament, and he had a hand in breaking down an Argentina side hellbent on baiting him into a physical duel in the final. He achieved all this after going into the tournament with a hamstring injury. Joe Hart captured the mood best after the final, saying: “Lamine Yamal is 19 years old. What a beautiful day for him. He’s 19 and has completed football.”

Add in the 24 goals and 18 assists he racked up in 45 appearances for Barcelona as they won La Liga and the Supercopa, and he has a strong case to go one better than his runners-up finish in last year’s Ballon d’Or.

Rodri

“We’ll see the real Rodri at the World Cup,” said Pep Guardiola last October, when the Manchester City captain returned to action after suffering an ACL injury. There were doubts that the 2023 Ballon d’Or winner would ever return to his best. But, as with most things in football, Guardiola was right.

Rodri was the heartbeat and the safety blanket in the Spain team, dictating every phase of the game, controlling possession and extinguishing almost every danger posed to his backline – Spain only conceded one goal in their eight matches at the tournament. Rodri completed 756 passes (more than anyone at the tournament) and he also topped the charts for touches, line-breaking passes and passes in the opposition third. In the final alone he completed 101 passes, completely strangling the life out of Argentina to the extent that they did not have a single shot on target.

He lifted the trophy as Spain’s captain, won the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player and earned a place in one of football’s most exclusive clubs as only the fourth man in history to have won the World Cup, European Championship, European Cup and Ballon d’Or, joining Gerd Müller, Franz Beckenbauer and Zinedine Zidane.

Kylian Mbappé

Kylian Mbappé went toe-to-toe with his old Paris Saint-Germain teammate Lionel Messi at the World Cup. They battled it out for the trophy, the Golden Boot, the Golden Ball and a place in the history books as the competition’s all-time leading scorer. He won two of the four. His two goals in the third-place playoff against England ensured he became the first man to win the Golden Boot twice. It also brought him to 22 goals in World Cups – one more than Messi – and made him the first man to reach double figures in a single edition since Müller in 1970.

And yet, it was not what Mbappé wanted. “I would have preferred not to be the top scorer and to have played in the final,” said the France captain. His domestic season was also prolific but disappointing, bringing goals and individual glory but no silverware. He scored 42 goals in 44 appearances, finishing the season as the top scorer in La Liga and the Champions League, but he did not win either trophy. The goals flowed but the medals did not follow. As Kane has discovered, goals alone are rarely enough to win the Ballon d’Or.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé has scored 22 goals in 22 matches at World Cups. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

Lionel Messi

Lionel Messi sat on the floor alone in a stadium of 80,000 people, boots off, staring into the distance as Spain’s substitutes streamed past him in celebration. It was not the fairytale image the Argentina captain had envisioned as he left the world stage. And, given his performances over the previous six weeks, it felt as if he deserved better even if his team did not.

Some expected Messi’s tournament to be a nostalgia act – a former great wheeled out for one last World Cup as he prepares for his 40th birthday. But then he went and scored a hat-trick in Argentina’s first game. He scored twice against Austria, then added another against Jordan. He stamped his authority on the tournament in the group stage and proceeded to drag Argentina through the knockouts: a goal against Cape Verde, a goal and an assist against Egypt, an assist against Switzerland, and two more assists to sink England in the semi-final. Had it not been for Mbappé’s brace in a bizarre third-place playoff, he would have collected the Golden Boot.

Could he win the Ballon d’Or having lost the World Cup final? In only four of the last 19 years has the award gone to a player who did not win the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa América in the same year. But three of them were won by Messi. A ninth Ballon d’Or is unlikely but the fact he is in this conversation at all – at 39 while playing in MLS having lost a final – is testament to his greatness.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Guimarães set for Arsenal? Newcastle to bring in Froholdt?
Sports.content:
Eddie Howe presumably won’t be reading this page for a while. Perhaps the now departed Newcastle boss will be seeking some beach time, looking out to sea and mentally preparing his audition for the England job while his assistant Jason Tindall works on trying to be as quick over the first few yards as Anthony Barry.

The Magpies fly out to La Manga on Friday for a pre-season training camp and it remains to be seen if Bruno Guimarães, a £75m Arsenal target, will turn up to the airport, meet them in Spain or send the lads a farewell on social media while house-hunting in London. Very latest reports suggest a deal to the champions has “moved closer” following Howe’s exit.

So what about the rest of the dwindling Magpies squad? The left-back Lewis Hall is being linked with Manchester United following the upheaveal at St James’ Park which has seen Howe depart in the wake of losing Sandro Tonali to Spurs and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona. And there are further reports suggesting the Brazil midfielder Joelinton may have the hump too and is seeking a move to Saudi Arabia.

Which brings us to the man seemingly set with the task of sorting out all this Tyneside turmoil. Matthias Jaissle, a 38-year-old German, has been a big hit with Al-Ahli – handily, Newcastle share the same Saudi Public Investment Fund owners – so the chatter has already started about the club’s likely new manager raiding his old team and bringing Ivan Toney back to the Premier League.

More realistic targets lie elsewhere and, with the exit of Guimarães in mind, Newcastle have a close eye on the FC Porto star Victor Froholdt. They reportedly watched the Denmark midfielder several times last season and would expect to pay about £70m for the 20-year-old, who already has 12 caps. Eintracht Frankfurt’s Hugo Larsson and the former Nottingham Forest man Danilo, now at Botafogo, are also being linked.

While Liverpool’s players argue among themselves about who should have the captain’s armband when Virgil isn’t about, the Reds could urgently do with beefing up the squad as the summer window drifts into August. With holes in central defence and at right-back, the ideal solution would be a player who could operate in both positions – an injury-free Joe Gomez, basically. Step forward Bournemouth’s James Hill, a player Andoni Iraola knows well. It could cost the Reds £40m to reacquaint the 24-year-old with Liverpool’s new head coach.

Curtis Jones, a prominent figure in armband-gate, continues to be linked with Inter, while transfer clue-hunters were sent into a right old tizzy when Dominik Szoboszlai said “if he comes back” when referring to his fellow midfielder Alexis Mac Allister during a post-match interview about Liverpool’s leadership group. The Argentinian has been linked with Real Madrid.

In terms of perfect fit, it surely doesn’t get any better than Cristian Romero to Atlético Madrid and it’s understood that the Spaniards have rekindled their interest in the Spurs centre-back.

Sports.title: Jaissle heads for Newcastle after success in Saudi Arabia that has eluded so many
Sports.content:
Taking over a big, underachieving port city club with a loyal fanbase that is desperate for success should not faze Matthias Jaissle. Should he take the role vacated by Eddie Howe, the 38-year-old German will leave Jeddah as a hero and arrive in the north-east as one of the most successful coaches in the history of Asian football.

A decade younger than Howe, Jaissle has achieved plenty, not only surviving in a Saudi Pro League that chews through coaches at a rapid rate but emerging victorious. It also helps that Al-Ahli and Newcastle share the same Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) owners.

Newcastle fans may know little about the former centre-back, whose playing career was cut short by injury, but that was also the case in Saudi Arabia when he arrived three years ago. Austria’s Bundesliga is not followed much in Asia, so two titles won with Red Bull Salzburg did not mean a great deal: neither did Jaissle’s association with Ralf Rangnick.

Fans were more focused on Al-Ahli’s recent return to the top flight, after a first season in the second tier, and were contemplating an influx of big-name players. A little different to the situation at St James’ Park with stars such as Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon already gone and others seemingly about to follow.

In Jeddah, Riyad Mahrez, Roberto Firmino, Édouard Mendy, Franck Kessié and others arrived in a summer when the club was acquired by PIF. For a team that had been in the doldrums a year earlier, it was quite a turnaround.

Despite all that Al-Ahli may have been the perfect club for Jaissle. The fans are famously passionate but had only one domestic league win since 1984. In Asia there had been two comprehensive Champions League final defeats. Compared to Al-Hilal, Al-Nassr and Al-Ittihad – also in the PIF stable – the Green corner of Jeddah had been relatively starved of success and, for a while, challenging again was enough.

For the then 35-year-old, dealing with such names did not seem a problem. His straight-talking style, with the foreign stars treated the same as the locals, drew a positive response. With his wealth of attacking talent Jaissle tried to win possession as high as possible to give players such as Mahrez the chance to shine. His preferred attack-minded, high-intensity playing style may move up a gear by the North Sea compared to the heat and humidity of the Red Sea.

View image in fullscreen Galeno (right) was a key signing for Al-Ahli under Jaissle and brought the best out of Ivan Toney in attack. Photograph: Reuters

In his first season Al-Ahli finished third, 11 points ahead of their fierce local rivals Al-Ittihad and, crucially, qualified for the AFC Champions League Elite. The second season was more difficult, for a while at least. After the departure of Allan Saint-Maximin, Jaissle wanted a replacement winger but, instead, Ivan Toney was signed and the England striker started slowly. Results dipped but were improving by January 2025 when the axe threatened to fall. Max Allegri was ready to take over, the kind of eye-catching coach that fans often want. But not in this case – members of the Green Army supported Jaissle, who had always taken time out to praise and talk to fans. A group of them appeared at the training ground with banners telling club management they should be the ones to go.

And it worked. Al-Ahli said Jaissle was staying with their full support. In came a winger, Galeno from Porto, and with the Brazilian getting the best out of Toney, Al-Ahli moved up a gear. They finished fifth in Jaissle’s second season but got more points. It was all about the Champions League, however. In the semi-finals, they defeated Al-Hilal, 19-time Saudi and four-time Asian winners. Then, in May 2025, in front of 60,000 fans in Jeddah, Kawasaki Frontale of Japan were defeated.

Then Al-Ahli did it again, winning the Asian title for a second time last May to become the first team since their Jeddah rivals, Al-Ittihad (in 2004 and 2005), to clinch successive Champions League crowns.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They also had a title challenge at home that only faded in the final weeks with Toney scoring 32 goals. In 34 games the team collected 81 points, 14 more than the previous season, and had Al-Nassr and Al-Hilal not been so consistent then it could have been a spectacular double.

The focus for the new season, due to start in August, was all about the Saudi Pro League title; but that should be someone else’s concern now.

Jaissle was recently linked with Al-Hilal and while that wouldn’t have gone down well with fans in Jeddah, he heads to Newcastle with the blessing of most. The German was always likely to return to Europe, and departs with success in Saudi Arabia, having won major titles. Many more experienced coaches have failed in that regard. Newcastle will be a different and tougher challenge.

He is not part of the elite any more but taking Newcastle closer to the Premier League’s top four would be a good start.

Sports.title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches
Sports.content:
The FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.

The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.

Across the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.

Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.

“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.

Sports.title: Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubs
Sports.content:
The Premier League has agreed on a proposal to reset financial distribution within English football’s top four divisions, one that would lead to an extra £1.5bn being shared across the pyramid over the next decade.

Clubs voted unanimously to support the so-called “new deal for football” at a meeting on Thursday, after discussions with the EFL. The offer will now be presented to the EFL’s board for consideration.

According to details originally published by Sky News, the Premier League’s offer would run for 10 years and result in an additional £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs on top of the £1.6bn currently distributed to clubs and communities every three years. Some of the money would be put into discrete funds – a “lifeboat” fund for clubs in immediate crisis and one that is directed exclusively at infrastructure.

To cover the extra costs, Premier League clubs have reportedly agreed to raise the transfer levy applied to all top-flight deals from 4% to 6%. The Guardian reported this week that Manchester City were initially opposed to increasing the levy.

The Premier League said in a statement that its clubs had “unanimously voted to approve a funded proposal for a new strategic partnership with the EFL”. It said it would now “look forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal” and remain “committed to finding a football-led solution”.

The EFL has yet to officially receive the offer but acknowledged “constructive” discussions with the Premier League and said its board would “review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League”.

This is the first time that Premier League clubs have officially agreed a proposal that could be put to the EFL since they were first asked to give more money to the rest of the pyramid five years ago. The Covid pandemic had revealed the precarious nature of finances at many EFL clubs and in 2022 the then sports minister Nigel Huddleston said the British public were already “out of patience” over a failure to reach an improved settlement.

The belief that the Premier League’s riches could be shared more effectively across the game helped lead in part to the creation of the Independent Football Regulator, which came into being last year. The regulator has played no direct part in the negotiations, but has a “backstop” power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

While there is cautious optimism that a deal can now finally be agreed, it is not a guarantee that the EFL will accept the Premier League’s offer, with sources suggesting it sees the proposal as being very similar to one that was mooted in 2023 but ultimately never approved by Premier League clubs. Both sides say they remain committed to ongoing dialogue.

Sports.title: Maxence Lacroix joins ‘beautiful club’ Chelsea as John Stones seals Inter deal
Sports.content:
Maxence Lacroix has joined Chelsea from Crystal Palace to become the club’s fifth signing of the summer. The France international, who won the FA Cup and Conference League with Palace, was the Blues’ main defensive target of the window.

Lacroix, 26, signs a six-year deal with Xabi Alonso’s side. “I am really happy to be part of this beautiful club,” said Lacroix, who played three times for France at the World Cup, including in their 6-4 bronze medal match defeat by England.

“Everyone knows the legend of Chelsea, its tradition of winning, and to be a part of that is a proud moment. I think it’s the best move for me because it’s the best club in the world. When I spoke with the manager, I saw that we have the same direction and desire for this club.

“We want to win. When you see the quality of the players here, everything we have around the club, it’s something that we can achieve. The ambition is to lift trophies, and I can’t wait to contribute.”

Chelsea had been looking to add experience to their back line having missed out on Rennes’ Jérémy Jacquet in January, with the player opting to join Liverpool. Levi Colwill, who is considered to be a key part of the club’s long-term plans, missed almost all of last season with an anterior cruciate ligament injury, with Wesley Fofana and Trevoh Chalobah forming the central-defensive partnership for much of the campaign.

After a dismal season that saw the club finish 10th, the club’s hierarchy has acknowledged a change in recruitment policy is needed, with a refocusing away from young, inexperienced players towards ones that can help the team compete for the title.

Lacroix, who made 55 appearances last season for Palace, has been one of the league’s most consistent defenders since moving to Selhurst Park from Wolfsburg in 2024.

The Blues confirmed the club-record arrival of Aston Villa forward Morgan Rogers last week, and have also added Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, striker Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and Sporting Lisbon’s Geovany Quenda.

Chelsea also look set to sign Brighton’s Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson after his contract with Brentford was terminated.

John Stones has joined Inter on a two-year contract, the Serie A club have announced.

The England centre-back was a free agent after leaving Manchester City and had attracted interest from clubs across Europe.

The 32-year-old ended his 10-year stay at City in June. He made 295 appearances for the club after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016 and won six Premier League titles, three FA Cups and a Champions League title.

Sports.title: Hayden Mullins leaves Fulham role after three years to take charge of EFL club
Sports.content:
Hayden Mullins leaves Fulham role after three years to take charge of EFL club

Hayden Mullins has departed Fulham to take up the manager's job at Newport County.

Mullins was the Cottagers' Under-21s boss, but he has joined the League Two side.

3 Mullins represented Reading, Crystal Palace, Portsmouth, West Ham and Notts County as a player

This will be the 47-year-old's second EFL job after being in charge of Colchester United from March 2021 to January 2022.

He was appointed as Fulham's Under-21s boss in 2023 but has now headed back into senior football.

He replaces former Leicester City left-back Christian Fuchs.

Fuchs left the Welsh side by surprise in June, and Chris Todd had been appointed as interim.

Meanwhile, assistant manager Mark Smith has departed the club.

But Mullins has now left Fulham after 101 games as Under-21s boss to take on the challenge of the League Two side.

In a statement, they said: "Newport County is delighted to announce the appointment of Hayden Mullins as the club's new manager.

"Mullins arrives at Rodney Parade with a wealth of experience from both his playing and coaching career, having represented clubs including Crystal Palace, West Ham United and Portsmouth before moving into management.

"Following his retirement, Mullins began his coaching journey at Reading before joining Watford in 2016, initially working with the club's academy before progressing to manage the under-23 side.

"During his time at Vicarage Road, Mullins twice stepped into the role of caretaker manager, taking charge of the first team following the departures of Quique Sánchez Flores in 2019 and Nigel Pearson in 2020.

"He later joined Colchester United as assistant head coach before being appointed the club's permanent head coach in May 2021.

"After his spell at Colchester, Mullins continued to broaden his coaching experience with the Turks and Caicos Islands national team before joining Fulham as under-21 head coach in July 2023.

"During his time at Craven Cottage, he enjoyed success by leading Fulham Under-21s to the Premier League Cup title in 2024, defeating Tottenham Hotspur Under-21s 4-0 in the final.

"Hayden Mullins will take charge of the first-team squad with immediate effect. His first match in the dugout will come on Saturday when Newport County face Yeovil Town in pre-season, before leading the side into Tuesday night's fixture against AS Roma at Rodney Parade."

3 Mullins is set for just his second full time job as an EFL manager

Why did Fuchs leave?

The Austrian departed Newport after just seven months and two days before pre-season was due to start.

His time in charge of the Welsh club was relatively successful as he led the club to safety.

They just avoided relegation to the National League by winning their final two games of the season.

But despite that, he still decided to resign, and there was no real explanation for why it happened.

3 Fuchs didn't last at Newport for very long Credit: Getty

In a statement, the club said: "Newport County can confirm that Christian Fuchs has made the decision to step away from his role as manager.

"During his time at Rodney Parade, Christian successfully guided Newport County to League Two survival, ensuring the club retained its EFL status at the end of the 2025-26 season.

"Everyone at Newport County would like to thank Christian for his hard work, commitment and professionalism during his time at the club.

"The club wishes Christian every success and happiness for the future."

And a month later, the club have their replacement.

Mullins has two pre-season games before the season starts against AFC Wimbledon in the Carabao Cup first round.

And the league game kicks off with a home tie against newly promoted Rochdale.

The final-day showdown between Celtic and Hearts brought a dramatic ending, with the Bhoys ultimately clinching a fifth consecutive league title.

Since then, there has been plenty of activity in Scotland’s top flight and Rangers in particular will hope that brings a change in fortunes.

Having finished third last season, the Rangers board decided to make changes both in the manager's hot-seat and the playing staff.

Derek McInnes almost led Hearts to a shock title success, but then decided to leave Tynecastle in order to take the reins at Ibrox.

McInnes has been well backed in the transfer market, with the ex-Aberdeen boss bringing Lawrence Shankland and Cammy Devlin with him from Hearts.

Rangers have also strengthened with moves from south of the border, with Sunderland midfielder Dan Neil and Hull goalkeeper Ivor Pandur also heading to Glasgow.

Former Everton defender Ben Godfrey has also joined on loan from Atalanta, while Belgium Under-21 international Tuur Rommens offers another option at full-back.

In contrast, Celtic have had a relatively quiet summer in the transfer market, with just two new arrivals to date.

The Hoops have signed two strikers before the new season, with Danish international Kasper Hogh and Qarabag forward Camilo Duran moving to Parkhead.

Martin O’Neill has lost two of his key players from last season’s title success, with Daizen Maeda and Kelechi Iheanacho joining Ipswich and Bursaspor respectively.

Hearts’ squad has been decimated after last term’s title bid and may struggle to finish the best of the rest behind the Old Firm.

Motherwell (5/4 for a top-six finish) look to be a team on the up, as long as their new manager, Alfred Johansson, can keep them on the right path.

Under Jens Berthel Askou, Well finished fourth last season and lost just three home games all campaign - the same number as both Celtic and Rangers.

To Finish Bottom - Falkirk @ 9/2

One of the stories of last season was Falkirk finishing in the top half having only been promoted from the Championship 12 months earlier.

It was such an impressive achievement, it’s led to speculation over the future of their manager John McGlynn.

The 64-year-old has been heavily linked with the vacant Scotland manager role, following Steve Clarke’s decision to step down after the World Cup.

McGlynn insists there has been no contact from the Scottish FA, but it does leave a cloud hanging over the Falkirk Stadium going into the new season.

The Bairns will fear ‘second-season syndrome’, especially having already been knocked out of the League Cup following defeats to Ayr United and Alloa Athletic in the group format.

Falkirk have also lost several key players during the close season, including forward Barney Stewart and midfielder Dylan Tait.

Sports.title: Roberto De Zerbi reveals exactly what he meant by ‘bomba’ in fresh Tottenham transfer update
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi reveals exactly what he meant by ‘bomba’ in fresh Tottenham transfer update

Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi has moved to clarify his 'bomba' comments earlier this week.

De Zerbi sent Spurs fans into a frenzy earlier this week as he teased an imminent 'bomba' following the club's pre-season penalty shootout win over Sydney FC.



2 De Zerbi hinted that Spurs were on the cusp of a big transfer earlier this week Credit: Getty

It's a phrase supporters use online that usually means a big transfer is about to take place.

"In the transfer market, when I want one player, I become like a shark, no chance to say no," De Zerbi said.

"The transfer market, it's not finished for sure, but we completed 60 per cent of our project in the transfer market.



"Now we have another bomba!"

Fans were speculating who De Zerbi was referring to, with Cody Gakpo, Omar Marmoush and Marcus Rashford previously linked with a move to the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

However, the Italian has since tempered expectations that a big-money arrival is on the cusp of linking up with the north London side.



"Bomba in Italian is different to English. You can write what you want. I said we have to compete in the transfer market," the 47-year-old said.

"We have some other players to complete the squad."

And when asked what a 'bomba' would be in Italian, De Zerbi replied: "Tonali, Fernandes, Senesi, Robertson are bomba. Top players for us."



2 Tonali was a 'bomba' according to De Zerbi Credit: Tottenham Hotspur FC

De Zerbi did admit, though, that Spurs are not done in the market this summer.

"I think two, maybe three, we have to see," the Spurs boss revealed when asked if the club could make any more signings.

Spurs' active summer

The capital outfit have been one of the more active teams in the market following their brush with relegation last season.



The club have added Martin Dubravka to the squad to provide cover for first choice goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky, who penned a new deal at the club earlier in the summer.

Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi joined on free transfers from Liverpool and Bournemouth, respectively, while Jan Paul van Hecke completed a £52million move to north London last month.

Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali also completed big money moves to the club having arrived from West Ham and Newcastle.

Attention now turns to the frontline, with Savinho among those targeted by the 2025 Europa League winners.

Sports.title: Tottenham made transfer mistake selling Will Lankshear – these two senior players should’ve gone instead
Sports.content:
Tottenham made transfer mistake selling Will Lankshear – these two senior players should’ve gone instead

Tottenham have been warned they may live to regret selling Will Lankshear this summer.

Middlesbrough signed the 21-year-old striker in a deal that could rise to £20m (£10m initially, with up to £10m in add-ons).



3 Lankshear was relegated with Oxford last season. Credit: Getty

Lankshear spent last season on loan at Oxford in the Championship, scoring 11 goals in 44 games.

He has long been touted as an exciting youth prospect at Spurs, having joined from Sheffield United in 2022.

The England youth international scored 23 goals for the Under-21 side that won the 2023-24 Premier League 2 title, and he was named the competition's Player of the Season.



"I feel like now is the best time in my career and I'm ready to hit the ground running and help this club," Lankshear told the Boro website.

"Middlesbrough is such a massive club over the years. I deem it to be a Premier League club.



"The project here really excites me. I can't wait to get started and be part of the journey, and get this club back where it belongs."

Tottenham forward options

Goals at both ends of the pitch were a big problem for Spurs last season.



In the Premier League, they scored 48 but conceded 57 with Richarlison their top scorer on just 11.

Manager Roberto De Zerbi has splashed out around £237m, signing the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes and Jan-Paul van Hecke.

However, little has been done to address their problems at the top end of the pitch.

3 De Zerbi has already made six new signings this summer Credit: Getty



De Zerbi has teased a transfer 'bomba' still this summer, which could be a new forward player.

The club’s options were a topic of discussion on the latest episode of Inside Spurs.

The panel were not happy that the only two striking options at the moment were Dominic Solanke and Richarlison.

Spurs fan and broadcaster Abbi Summers said: "We cannot go into this season with our striking options being Solanke and Richarlison.



"They're both so injury-prone and that can't be it for the level Spurs need to be at."

talkSPORT's Sonny Snelling argued that Lankshear should have stayed to be back-up to a new, big-name striker.

3 Richarlison has 32 goals in 133 Tottenham games Credit: Getty

He said: "We haven't seen Richarlison be fit or consistent. We haven't seen Solanke be fit or consistent.



"I think Solanke is the better of the two players and what I see is both players have attributes that De Zerbi would like, but both of them have negatives as well that De Zerbi won't like.

“I think the forward line is a bit of a mess anyway, because we're in a situation where ideally you go into a transfer window trying to improve your squad.

"If we're buying a player who doesn't really take that attacking line to the next level, I don't really see the point.

"But then you've got Mikey Moore still there. You've got Tel. You've got Odobert to come back from injury. You've got Kulusevski to come back from injury.



"Even if you bring the 10s, you've got Maddison who's still coming back. You've got Xavi Simons to come back. You've got Kudus to come back. How do they all fit in?

"You can't shift those injured players. So what you're doing is you're bringing in another forward, and then you've got a whole issue of who do you loan out?

"I know we've got a good fee for Will Lankshear, but I would have kept him and promoted him to the second-choice striker and got rid of Solanke and Richarlison and then got a stellar striker on top of that."

Tottenham begin their Premier League season on August 22 with a trip to Brentford.
