Sports.title: New Premier League substitution rule could see players banned for entering pitch
Sports.content:
New Premier League substitution rule could see players banned for entering pitch

The Premier League will be soon underway, but managers and players will need to navigate a host of major rule changes designed to stamp out time-wasting.

The PGMOL has confirmed a brand-new substitution law that could leave teams a player down.

3 No player received the sanction at the 2026 World Cup Credit: Getty

Refereeing chiefs have made it their mission to speed up the game following the implementation of new regulations at the World Cup.

They want to target the tactical thinking of footballers taking slow, deliberate walks across the pitch when their number is raised on the board.

The new rule will only allow a strict 10-second time limit for substituted players to leave the pitch.

Failure to do so will force clubs to play with only ten men, and could prove disastrous for teams protecting a tight lead late on.

What is the Premier League's 10-second substitution rule?

Under the new law, a player being substituted has exactly ten seconds to completely leave the pitch once the electronic board is displayed by the fourth official.

Additionally, players must exit using the nearest point on the boundary line, unless directed otherwise by the match officials for safety or security reasons.

If a player takes longer than the allocated time to cross the touchline, their replacement is barred from entering the field for at least one minute.

Their team must play temporarily with a reduced side until the first natural stoppage after that minute has elapsed.

3 Michael Oliver will be used to the rule after refereeing at the summer tournament Credit: Getty

Why is the Premier League enforcing it?

For years, Premier League managers have used late substitutions to disrupt momentum and run down the clock.

Previously, referees could only punish slow exits by showing a yellow card to the departing player.

The old sanction rarely discouraged teams from employing the tactic late in matches.

By forcing a club to play with a man down for over a minute, the PGMOL expects players to sprint off the pitch to avoid leaving their teammates vulnerable.

Following the successful introduction of the measures at the World Cup during the summer, the FA was keen to adopt the set of rules for English football.

The rule will also be implemented across the men's and women's professional game in England, including the EFL, WSL Football and the National League

3 Goalkeepers are often accused of faking injury to waste time, but this trial is designed to stop that Credit: Getty

What other rules have been introduced?

Goalkeepers will also be subjected to new regulations.

If play stops for a keeper injury, they must also leave the pitch upon restart like any other player - unless the stoppage involves a direct collision or is a serious issue.

Pro Ref released a statement saying: "The trial, championed collectively by Pro Ref, The FA, Premier League, EFL, WSL Football and the National League, will be implemented across the men's and women's professional game in England,

"And is designed to address occasions where goalkeeper injuries have been used to disrupt momentum, slow the game down or create opportunities for tactical instruction."

Meanwhile, any outfield player who receives on-pitch treatment must now remain off the field for a minimum of 60 seconds - doubled from the previous 30 seconds.

Additionally, referees will enforce a five-second countdown for throw-ins and goal-kicks, with a potential reversal of possession for delays.

VAR can now review second yellow card incidents, though a high threshold for intervention remains in place for other decisions.

There will also be increased focus on penalising holding in the box that materially impacts play.

Sports.title: Bournemouth land Marcos Senesi replacement in deal worth £25million
Sports.content:
Bournemouth are set to complete the signing of Antonio Silva from Portuguese side Benfica in a deal worth £25million.

The 22-year-old is set to undergo a medical, arriving as a replacement Marcos Senesi, who completed a free switch to Tottenham Hotspur last month.

2 Antonio Silva replaces Marcos Senesi at the Vitality Stadium

Silva has previously been linked with a high-profile Premier League switch with the Cherries winning the race to land the youngster.

The defender becomes Bournemouth's second summer signing following the capture of striker Alvaro Rodriguez from Elche.

Defence a priority for Premier League sides

Silva isn't the first central defender to have secured a high-profile Premier League move this summer.

Indeed, centre-back has been a priority position for a number of top-flight English teams in the off-season.

Along with the addition of Senesi, Spurs strengthened further at the back with the £52million capture of Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton.

And the Seagulls were happy to splash the cash to sign teenager Luka Vuskovic from the north London side as a Van Hecke successor.

Leeds United, meanwhile, spent big to bring in Tarik Muharemovic from Sassuolo after Pascal Struijk completed his switch to the AMEX Stadium.

Chelsea have also strengthened their backline having confirmed the signing of Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace on Thursday.

The Eagles are in the market for another centre-back to replace Lacroix, with Brest youngster Raphael Le Guen a rumoured target.

2 Senesi is one of a number of centre-backs to have moved this summer Credit: Getty

Bournemouth seek stability

The Cherries are seeking stability this summer having endured a defensive rebuild last year following the departures of Dean Huijsen, Illia Zabarnyi, Milos Kerkez and Kepa Arrizabalaga 12 months ago.

Even so, Bournemouth managed a European finish for the first time in their history.

Success, though, has seen their star players linked with a move away from the club.

Bournemouth rebuffed a £64million bid from Chelsea for prized midfielder Alex Scott earlier this month, talkSPORT understands.

The 22-year-old has two years left to run on his current deal at the Vitality Stadium, yet recently rejected a new contract offer from the south coast side.

Forwards Rayan and Eli Junior Kroupi have also been linked with summer exits, though the latter faces a lengthy spells on the sidelines having suffered a foot injury during pre-season.

Sports.title: Major FIFA figure quits with furious statement in ‘beginning of the end’ for Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Major FIFA figure quits with furious statement in ‘beginning of the end’ for Gianni Infantino

Gianni Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro has quit in protest over the FIFA president's plans to sell World Cup stakes.

A footballing civil war has unfolded in recent days after details emerged of Infantino's intention to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

5 Carlos Cordeiro is the first senior figure to step down in the wake of Gianni Infantino's controversial proposal Credit: AFP

5 FIFA president Gianni Infantino has publicly backed controversial plans for football's governing body

This could see FIFA's shares in their biggest tournaments, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup, sold off to the highest bidder.

Infantino's plans have been met with huge criticism, with UEFA nations unanimously agreeing to a boycott if these schemes go ahead.

CONCACAF and the AFC have also publicly opposed the plans, although that has not deterred FIFA, who still intend to press on.

talkSPORT's senior reporter Ben Jacobs has described the backlash as the 'beginning of the end' for Infantino.

As revealed on talkSPORT last night, Infantino has lost support from his inner circle, and the first key player has now fallen.

Cordeiro is a heavyweight figure within FIFA as a former US Soccer president and a former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs.

He announced his resignation in a scathing statement, where he outlined his strong opposition to the plans.

Cordeiro said: “As a Senior Advisor to the FIFA President, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup.

“Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.”

Carlos Cordeiro: Full statement Cordeiro said: "As Senior Advisor to the FIFA President, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup. "Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game. "Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away. That is why this proposal should be rejected. "FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt. The FIFA President himself has highlighted the $15 billion in revenue generated between 2022 and 2026. "If Member Associations believe additional investment is needed to develop the game, FIFA already has the financial capacity to provide that support from its existing resources. Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification. "Such economic success was not accidental. It was delivered by experienced football professionals who shattered FIFA's commercial records. Yet despite those achievements, FIF is now being asked to believe that outside investors are needed to unlock greater value. "I do not accept that proposition. The people who built this success have already demonstrated that FIFA possesses the expertise to continue growing both the game and its commercial future. "Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions. Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football? "These questions remain largely unanswered, and yet Member Associations are being asked to make a decision of enormous consequence in barely 50 days or risk being left behind. That is not a responsible way to determine the future of the world's game. "This proposal has become a defining question for FIFA's future. After careful consideration, I can no longer continue in my role as Senior Advisor to the FIFA President. I have therefore resigned with immediate effect. "FIFA's responsibility is not to maximize commercial returns at any cost. It is to protect and strengthen football for future generations. When those principles come into conflict, football must come first. "It has been the privilege of a lifetime to serve FIFA for more than five years and to work alongside dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game. I hope they, too, will speak up, because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."

Who is Carlos Cordeiro?

Cordeiro was appointed as Senior Advisor to FIFA for Global Strategy and Governance in 2021, before later being named as Senior Advisor to Infantino too.

5 Cordeiro was previously president of the United States Soccer Federation Credit: Getty

His name then became familiar around the world when he was appointed by Donald Trump to serve as the Senior Advisor to the White House's dedicated 2026 World Cup Task Force.

Cordeiro previously served as president of the United States Soccer Federation, holding the role between 2018 and 2020.

Following his appointment, FIFA cited Cordeiro's background in investment banking as a key factor, having been a partner at Goldman Sachs.

Football's governing body said at the time: "Cordeiro built a long career in business and global investment banking in Europe."

Tipping point

Cordeiro has now resigned after giving a damning assessment of Infantino's plans for FIFA to sell off 20 per cent of its new subsidiary, FFE.

The FFE would consolidate broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing, and licensing – including those for the World Cup and Club World Cup.

5 Infantino is facing a mass exodus at FIFA Credit: Getty

While FIFA would retain majority control of the subsidiary, Infantino then intends to see the rest sold, partly to each of FIFA’s 211 national associations in stakes worth around $20million (£15m), with another portion farmed out to private investment.

Infantino would be lined up to run FFE as its commissioner when his final FIFA presidency ends in 2031, assuming he is re-elected, which could then potentially see him earn tens of millions of pounds.

But with the under-fire football chief reliant on FIFA's 211 Member Federations to vote through his plans, he may struggle for support.

UEFA nations have unanimously agreed to a boycott if these schemes go ahead, in a strong show of opposition from European football's governing body.

CONCACAF have also 'rejected the proposal', with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) since calling for FIFA to 'undertake an urgent review of its governance' in the latest devastating blow.

This leaves Infantino's proposal in tatters, as he awaits learning the stance of CAF (Confederation of African Football), CONMEBOL, the governing body of soccer in South America and OFC (Oceania Football Confederation).

5 Infantino had already been under pressure for his relationship with the Trump administration Credit: Getty

Even if these confederations vote in favour of his proposal, UEFA, CONCACAF, and the AFC's decision to oppose Infantino's plans means 143 of FIFA's 211 member nations oppose his efforts.

For his plans to pass, Infantino needs 106 of FIFA's 211 members to vote in favour, which is currently in huge doubt.

It also raises questions over the long-term future of the FIFA president in his role, who has already come under fire this summer following the World Cup and the manner of Folarin Balogun's suspended ban.

The USA striker was cleared to play against Belgium in the last 16 after his red card ban was suspended for a year after intervention from US President Donald Trump.

Infantino has responded to the latest criticism of him in typical fashion - by accusing people of 'spreading hate'.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino's World Cup plot is unravelling as senior advisor QUITS and Asian Federation join leading nations in opposing controversial plan - denying deluded FIFA boss a majority
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino's divisive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup appears to be dead after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) joined UEFA and CONCACAF in opposing the plot - and his senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro has also now quit in protest. Carlos Cordeiro, a retired American investment banker and senior adviser to Infantino, has resigned from his role at FIFA - becoming the first internal figure to do so. It comes after UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC all opposed FIFA’s plans to generate £3.1billion in private investment in FIFA tournaments. 136 FIFA members are now publicly opposed to the FIFA Forward Enterprise, bringing the dissidents above the required 106 threshold to block the plans with dignitaries now joining the calls for Infantino to scrap his plans. Releasing a statement, Cordeiro - who served on the White House task force for the 2026 World Cup - distanced himself from Infantino’s plans and ripped into the proposals. He has called on his now former FIFA colleagues to follow suit and speak out against the plans, which he describes as a bad deal for football. Infantino had promised member associations a £30million incentive to force the deal through. 'As a Senior Advisor to the FIFA President, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup,’ Cordeiro said. 'Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.' Overnight, FIFA issued a statement, doubling down on plans to sell £3.1 billion in shares for FIFA tournaments after UEFA announced a boycott of competitions and CONCACAF - the North, Central, American and Caribbean federation - opposed the plans. But the AFC has now chosen to stand with their intercontinental counterparts, leaving Infantino's project - and potentially his FIFA presidency - facing a terminal threat. 136 FIFA members are now publicly opposed to the proposals, bringing the dissidents above the required 106 threshold to block the plans. In a statement, the AFC said: 'The AFC stands in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF in expressing serious concerns over FIFA's proposal to introduce private investment into FIFA's flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE. 'The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a FIFA World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game. Football should never have been placed in such a position. Gianni Infantino's controversial plan to sell off the World Cup appears to be dead in the water after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) joined UEFA and CONCACAF in opposing the plot Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro (right) has also now resigned in protest at the plans

Your browser does not support iframes.

'Against this backdrop, and in light of the clear positions expressed by UEFA and CONCACAF, as well as the unprecedented divisions that have emerged across the football world, the AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward. 'The FIFA World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world's leading football nations. 'Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered. 'While the immediate debate centres on FFE, the AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal. 'Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed. 'While the AFC notes FIFA's latest clarification on the proposal, the central concerns surrounding governance, institutional process and meaningful consultation remain unanswered. 'A proposal of such significance, with the potential to affect the commercial, sporting and strategic future of world football, must not emerge through processes that leave Confederations, Member Associations (MAs) and even FIFA's own governing bodies, including the FIFA Council, feeling sidelined. 'The primary objective for world football must be to ensure that decisions of such magnitude are being developed through processes that are anchored on transparency and command the confidence of the football community. 'This is not the first occasion where major stakeholders have been confronted with significant initiatives after the direction of travel appears to have already been determined. 'Such an approach undermines confidence in FIFA's governance framework and diminishes the authority of its statutory bodies. Join the discussion Should the World Cup ever be used as a tool for private profit, or does selling stakes betray the spirit of the game? FIFA issued a late-night response to furious backlash over the controversial plan to sell World Cup stakes to private investors by blaming the media for the uproar 'No subsequent consultation process, however well-intentioned, can replace early engagement with the appropriate FIFA bodies and the football family. 'The AFC believes this moment must become a catalyst for strengthening institutional reform. While every FIFA MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote. 'It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process. 'Accordingly, the AFC calls upon FIFA to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by FIFA's statutory bodies. 'The FIFA World Cup, and the game itself, belong to the entire global football family. Their future must always be shaped collectively, through institutions that reflect the voices of all Confederations and MAs.' The AFC's statement criticises FIFA's clarification of their proposals released on Friday morning, where they blamed the media for misconstruing their plans and made a dig at UEFA for holding FIFA to account. FIFA said: 'We have heard the feedback provided by the respective confederations in relation to the proposed establishment of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) and would like to address the issues that have surfaced since the initial media reporting on Tuesday. 'We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation. ⁠'Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA has the ability to express its vote based on facts. 'FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all FIFA Member Associations (MAs) have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of FIFA or football itself. Infantino has been widely criticised for his decision to put the World Cup 'up for sale' The core investor would be a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner (pictured earliere this month in California), the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner 'Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain. 'Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world. Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA.' They continued by outlining the plans, subject to consultation with member nations. There is frustration across the international football landscape, however, that such proposals have been unilaterally developed - with proposed investors already lined up - in complete secrecy despite an eventual 'consultation'. UEFA nations are boycotting all FIFA competitions so long as the proposals remain on the table. All 55 UEFA nations met virtually on Thursday, with more than 40 federations providing testimony. Daily Mail Sport were told associations expressed ‘outrage’ on the call with ‘total unanimity’ against the proposal, before deciding to abstain from FIFA competitions. Daily Mail Sport also understands there is growing opposition to Infantino's presidency, with CONCACAF nations losing - or having already lost - confidence in the Swiss football administrator. UEFA and their member associations are yet to be drawn on that matter. Infantino is seeking a fourth term as FIFA president next year. One international football insider told Daily Mail Sport: ‘UEFA’s response is at the nuclear button end of the spectrum, which is impressive. We thought Infantino would survive the Trump refereeing intervention - but he has overreached this time.' In a statement, UEFA said: 'UEFA and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA's proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors. 'The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale. 'It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football. 'National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football's greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a 'democratic decision', but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game. 'But our opposition goes far beyond process. 'The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure. From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders. 'This model has no place in world football. Football's future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return. Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain. 'Europe's position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation. 'As a result of today's discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership. 'Nobody should be in any doubt: UEFA and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination. 'There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments. 'Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.’ An FA spokeswoman added: 'We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose FIFA's plans - the FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will.’ Concacaf later added: 'Concacaf is a confederation united by the love of our game, where football comes first. Guided by this philosophy over the past ten years we have built, from the ground up, an organisation founded on service, transparent governance, and the long-term stewardship of football. 'History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values. 'With this in mind, Concacaf today convened a meeting of the presidents of its 41 Member Associations, together with its President, Council members, and its FIFA Council members, to discuss a proposal developed and presented by the FIFA President to establish 'FIFA Forward Enterprise' and sell interests in the FIFA World Cup to private investors. 'During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies. In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programs following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned. 'The discussion reinforced the need for greater transparency and proper governance. 'For these reasons, Concacaf and its 41 Member Associations have: Rejected the proposal; Tasked their FIFA Council Members with engaging FIFA to determine how existing FIFA reserves could be used to increase FIFA Forward funding for football development across our region; and Tasked their FIFA Council Members with instructing the FIFA President to ensure that any matter follows the proper governance processes via staff and FIFA Council, in accordance with the FIFA Statutes. 'Through these actions, Concacaf reaffirms that football's future - and its greatest asset - must remain in the hands of our football family.'

Sports.title: Inter Milan continue pursuit of £30m-rated Liverpool star, Bournemouth agree deal for Benfica defender - and West Ham step up chase for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

United keeping tabs on Hall

Manchester United remain appreciative of Newcastle left back Lewis Hall but acknowledge it would be a difficult transfer to pull off.

The club are still assessing market movements, checking who is available at the right price, before deciding on their next priority position. Another midfielder has been at the forefront of their thinking while another forward still hinges on Marcus Rashford departing. Despite interest from other clubs, as it stands, he remains likely to start the season at United.

Cover at left back is required as United are going into the new season with Luke Shaw, who has one year left on contract, as their only senior option in that position. Harry Amass can cover but has been told he would be better seeking first team opportunities elsewhere.

Manchester United are keen on Newcastle left back Lewis Hall

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise once Matthias Jaissle is in place.

Though midfielder Bruno Guimaraes may yet join Arsenal, if they make a formal offer over £80m, the club want to add players to ensure they are competitive.

Hamer heading back to Coventry

Coventry are closing on a deal to bring back midfielder Gustavo Hamer from Sheffield United. The 29-year-old Brazilian has one year left on his deal.

He spent three years at Coventry after joining from PEC Zwolle, before moving to Sheffield United in August 2023.

Inter continue Jones pursuit

Inter Milan are continuing to pursue Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones but have still to hit the Anfield club's valuation.

The 25-year-old has cut a frustrated figure in recent months and has wanted more regular game time.

He has one year left on contract and Liverpool say they are relaxed about his situation.

Liverpool value the academy graduate around £30million but Inter's last offer was just under £22m.

The Italian club were interested in January and proposed a loan with a view to a permanent move but that was also turned down by Liverpool.

Inter Milan are continuing to chase Curtis Jones but are yet to meet Liverpool's valuation

Piero Ausilio, Inter's sporting director, confirmed he was still on their radar earlier this summer, saying: 'Curtis Jones - we are paying attention to him. We didn't hide. We understand what the developments will be.'

Teammate Federico Chiesa, another who could depart, also told Italian media that Jones asked him what it is like to live in Italy.

The midfielder has been with Liverpool since he was nine and signed his first professional contract with them in 2018.

Inter yesterday confirmed the signing of England defender John Stones on a free transfer.

Cherries swoop for Silva

Bournemouth have agreed their £25m deal with Benfica to sign defender Antonio Silva.

The 22-year-old centre back captained and played 90 minutes for Benfica in their emphatic 5-0 Europa League qualifying win against St Gallen last night.

The transfer is worth £21.4million plus £4.3m in add-ons.

The Portugal international is due to travel over this weekend to have a medical and complete his move.

Antonio Silva is set to move to Bournemouth from Benfica

Leicester bring in Championship forward

Leicester City have signed Swansea City forward Liam Cullen for an undisclosed fee.

The Wales international, who has agreed a three year deal, can play as a centre-forward, attacking midfielder or right winger.

He previously worked under manager Russell Martin at Swansea.

Cullen, 27, said: 'When this opportunity came about and with the size of the club and the project they’re getting started with now, I thought it was the perfect fit for me.'

Welsh forward Liam Cullen has signed for Leicester, who will play in League One this season

Hammers trying to nail down Engels

West Ham are moving ahead on talks for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels.

The 22-year-old was the subject of bids up to £25million from Nottingham Forest in January which Celtic rejected.

West Ham have a long-held interest in the Belgium international and, after sounding out figures over a couple of conversations with the Scottish champions, are pressing to see if agreement can be reached on bringing Engels to London and making him the midfield replacement for Mateus Fernandes.

Forest, Sunderland and Fulham had also shown interest.

West Ham are pressing ahead in a move for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels

Sports.title: 'He'll be a handful': Why Alexander Isak is ready to fire in second Liverpool season - LEWIS STEELE reveals his new role under Andoni Iraola, new intensity in training and mentoring Reds' young stars
Sports.content:
One of many phrases to tick off during the weekly Friday morning game of Arne Slot Press Conference Bingo was ‘Alexander Isak has signed for six years, not six months’. The now-departed Liverpool boss would use it as a quip to those questioning why the £125million man had not even got close to repaying his British-record price tag, with just two goals in his first 15 games for the club as he struggled to gain fitness. Six years, remember, not six months. The problem was that one of those years has already been and gone. Given the mammoth outlay, that’s £20.8m of the fee gone already with just four goals to show for it. Just when he looked like he had finally cracked it, away at Tottenham in December with a first-half goal, he was crocked in the process of scoring by defender Micky van de Ven and broke his leg. That was pretty much that for the season and he was nowhere near full fitness until the World Cup. But 12 months on from his acrimonious exit from Newcastle, Isak is finally ready to put that nightmare year behind him and be the player Liverpool thought they were signing. On Sunday, he is expected to play his first pre-season match against Leeds United here in Chicago and Andoni Iraola, the man now sitting in Slot's chair, could do with Isak more than anyone. Alexander Isak, the £125million man had not even got close to repaying his British-record price tag, with just two goals in his first 15 games for the club as he struggled to gain fitness Just when he looked like he had finally cracked it, away at Tottenham in December with a first-half goal, he was crocked while scoring by defender Micky van de Ven and broke his leg

Your browser does not support iframes.

There were many reasons Slot failed – but one was the failure of his two big-money buys last summer, Isak and £116m Florian Wirtz, to step up. Isak was barely fit and Wirtz looked like a fish out of water at times. In both cases, one bad season can be forgiven and forgotten but serious questions will be asked if it continues into their sophomore years at Anfield. I understand that both have been enjoying the intensity of Iraola’s new regime and are ready to step up. Isak, it is easy to forget, is one of the best strikers in the Premier League. Since he joined Newcastle ahead of the 2022-23 season, only three forwards have more than his 57 goals: Erling Haaland, Mohamed Salah and Ollie Watkins. Iraola needs him to rediscover that form more than ever. With fellow No 9 Hugo Ekitike a long-term absentee with a ruptured achilles, Mohamed Salah gone and no new top winger yet signed, Liverpool need a goalscorer. Isak needs to show why he was worth £125m just a year ago, and rediscover the form that saw him score 62 goals in 109 games for Newcastle. ‘Alex is exciting,’ said Iraola when asked about Isak this week in Chicago. ‘He has come to pre-season in a good place, had a good World Cup, feeling comfortable. First training here, still early but I hope he can play against Leeds and have a proper pre-season. It is not long, but three or four weeks of quality training I hope and he is in a good place because he is going to be massive for us.’ There was emphasis on the word ‘massive’ and he is not wrong. Robbie Fowler, who proved 183 times he knows how to score goals for this club, sat down with Daily Mail Sport earlier this week in New York City and told us why he is such a big fan of Isak – backing him to pay back the club’s huge investment. ‘I am a massive fan,’ Fowler tells us. ‘He is proven in the Premier League. For whatever reason, he turned up not fit or whether it was that he struggled to step up to a big club. Robbie Fowler, who proved 183 times he knows how to score goals for this club, told us why he is such a big fan of Isak I understand that both Isak and Florian Wirtz have been enjoying the intensity of Andoni Iraola’s new regime and are ready to step up ‘But I have no qualms with him. He is exciting. He will score goals. He will be a handful. Hopefully this is the season he kicks on. He got injured at the wrong time but I want him to come back fit and firing. He did OK in the World Cup but I want him to be ready at the start of the season rather than waiting months and months like last season. ‘If it was me, the price tag would not bother me. The players are focused on doing well, it is left to others to talk about money. Price tags are only one thing the clubs put on a player. For me, it would not bother me, whether that’s my mentality, I don’t know… some players don’t have that. ‘Alexander is world-class and the price tag won’t bother him either. He has everything in the locker, exciting when he drives with the ball, he makes things happen. He excites the fans which is imperative for a club like Liverpool. ‘Not only can he beat players, he can bring others into the game and he can score goals which is massive. He has other areas in his game which are impressive.’ Isak has been working hard on bulking up after a positive World Cup, in which he enjoyed playing in tandem with Arsenal’s Viktor Gyokeres for Sweden, and scored an impressive solo goal against Tunisia in the group stage. Isak has rubbed shoulders with one of the best strikers of this generation, Robert Lewandowski, here in Chicago. The former Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Bayern Munich striker, now 37, recently moved to MLS club Chicago Fire having won eight Bundesligas, three La Ligas and a Champions League. He, like Isak, has been working hard in their gym here, which has personalised dumbbells. The Swede has also been helpful to young strikers out here, such as teenagers Will Wright and Josh Sonni-Lambie. Isak has been working hard on bulking up after a positive World Cup, in which he enjoyed playing in tandem with Arsenal’s Viktor Gyokeres (left) for Sweden The Swede has also been helpful to young strikers out here, such as teenagers Will Wright (pictured) and Josh Sonni-Lambie Six years, not six months – but now more than ever, it is time for Isak to step up Iraola is keen for Isak to play as an out-and-out No 9, with Florian Wirtz playing as a traditional No 10 – close to the striker, unlike last season when he would often be instructed to drift out to the left. At £241m, the duo – and Liverpool’s bank balance – cannot afford another year of adaptation. Neither can Iraola, who will be relying on the pair that ultimately let Slot down. The Basque has been impressive in his opening weeks but cannot deliver success if the big-money duo do not start to look like the mega-money players they are. Six years, not six months – but now more than ever, it is time for Isak to step up.

Sports.title: World Cup hero Jack Charlton's son hit with £200,000 Inheritance Tax bill after receiving legend's iconic 1966 medal
Sports.content:
Jack Charlton's son claims that he faces a £200,000 Inheritance Tax blow if he wants to keep hold of his father's precious World Cup winner's medal from 1966.

John Charlton was bequeathed the award in his father's will but he has to leave it with his mother Pat – or pay up if he wants it.

His father started at centre-back as England beat West Germany 4-2 in the World Cup final before dying aged 85 in 2020 after suffering from lymphoma and dementia.

Jack, the older brother of fellow England legend Bobby, also went on to manage Ireland and lead them to two World Cups, even reaching the quarter-finals in 1990.

Son John told talkSPORT: 'I think there's only him and my uncle Bobby who have kept their medals. Everybody else doesn't have them anymore.

'There's a bit of a problem with it, actually.

Jack Charlton (pictured) bequeathed his World Cup winner's medal to his son John - but he may face a huge tax bill to keep it

Jack seen playing for England in the 1996 World Cup final against West Germany at Wembley

Jack Charlton and his brother Bobby kept their medals - other players donated or sold them

'When I say I've got it, it was left to me in my dad's will, but the tax man wants £200,000 off me in Inheritance Tax.

'I've given it back to my mother because whilst she's got it, I don't have to pay that money.

'There's a journalist from the Daily Mirror who's been working on it and helping us to try and sort it, but the same applies to Olympic gymnasts and people like that.

'If they decide to sell their gold medals, they’re going to have to pay. Their family, sorry, pass it on, they’re going to have to pay Inheritance Tax on that. This is something that they’ve been trying to sort out.

'I’ve got his shirt. Well, we’ve got his shirt as well. His shirt and his medal are in a safe place, tucked away.

'And the England cap that he got because he only got one cap for the tournament and that’s the only cap that he left. He gave the rest away.'

The £200,000 figure is disputed, mostly due to a Daily Mirror article in 2024, when John told the publication that HMRC valued his father's medal and kit at a collective £100,000-£200,000, and wanted £80,000 in tax.

John has previously called for Labour to abolish Inheritance Tax, calling it 'scandalous'.

There are tax exemptions which can, for example, apply to medals from the armed forces, but not the heroes of 1966.

John told the Daily Mirror: 'I think it is only my dad and uncle Bobby who have not sold theirs. I wonder what would happen if I said that I could not afford the tax on it. Would the Government take my dad's medal from me?'

Born in the coal-mining village of Ashington, Northumberland, in 1935, Jack was the eldest of four brothers and his father was a miner. The siblings at one point shared the same bed because of the family's tight finances.

He went on to play for Leeds United with distinction for 21 years, winning the First Division and the FA Cup.

In July 2020, he passed away at his Northumberland home, leaving behind his wife Pat and children John, Debbie, and Peter.

Sports.title: 'I stayed up for England vs Mexico - then fell asleep at half-time!': Cole Palmer on World Cup heartache, feeling fresh after seven-week summer holiday and his bromance with new team-mate Morgan Rogers
Sports.content:
'I stayed up for England vs Mexico - then fell asleep at half-time!': Cole Palmer on World Cup heartache, feeling fresh after seven-week summer holiday and his bromance with new team-mate Morgan Rogers

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cole Palmer is talking his ‘cold’ celebration and whether he will allow his best friend in football and new team-mate, Morgan Rogers, to continue to use it after scoring at Chelsea.

It is technically his, after all, as per the register for the Intellectual Property Office.

‘I’ve trademarked it so if he tries to do anything, he’ll have the bailiffs at his door,’ Palmer tells us, prompting a fair few laughs from the journalists interviewing him in Sydney, Australia.

It is a classic Palmer line, delivered nonchalantly as we sit down with this 24-year-old at the training ground of local side Sydney FC, and he continues: ‘Nah, we’ll do it together, I think.

‘We've never actually spoke about it. He does it. I do it. I always speak to him but when I heard Chelsea were trying to sign him, I was texting him even more.

‘He was probably sick of me but at least he’s here now! Morgs told me straightaway when he was coming. It didn’t get leaked. Nobody knew. Just me and him and the higher people at the club.

Cole Palmer says he will share his 'cold' celebration with new team-mate Morgan Rogers

The Chelsea star is glad to have his boyhood friend alongside him going into the new season

‘So it was a difficult secret to keep, but I kept it! Everyone knows how good he is. Obviously he’s one of my best friends so I’m very happy about it.

‘We’re two different players. He’s more physical than me, on and off the ball. He likes to drive with it. I like to play passes. I think we can play well together, and we played together when we were young (in the academy of Manchester City).’

Palmer is speaking for the first time since Rogers signed from Aston Villa for £117million – he describes it as a ‘next-level’ buy by Chelsea – and since he missed out on making Thomas Tuchel’s England squad for the summer’s World Cup. Without him, his country reached the semi-finals, where they were beaten by Argentina.

‘If someone told you that you're essentially not good enough to get in the squad, then you’re going to think, like, alright, whatever then, try to go that extra bit harder,’ Palmer says when asked whether he is carrying some extra motivation into the next season.

‘I watched some of it (the World Cup). Obviously I was away and the times were a bit mad in America. It was a bit difficult. But I did watch.’

Did he manage to stay up to watch England v Mexico in the round of 16? ‘Yeah,’ he says of that 2am kick-off in the UK. ‘But then I fell asleep at half-time.’

A summer break was not the worst news for Chelsea, selfishly. It allowed Palmer a chance to rest, recover, and reset after having not had any off-season for a few years. In 2025, he had the Club World Cup. In 2024, he had the Euros. In 2023, he was at the Under 21 Euros.

Is he itching to return to the England fold after Tuchel’s snub, however?

He had seven weeks off and reveals that he fell asleep at half-time of England vs Mexico

Chelsea are on tour in Australia and face Tottenham in Sydney on Saturday

‘I’m not really thinking about that now, to be honest,’ Palmer adds. ‘I’m just looking forward to the season with Chelsea, and to be honest, I’m not too bothered about that.

‘My summer was great. I had like seven weeks off or summit. Which I’ve never really had. It was good. I went on holiday with my family and that. I feel fresh.

‘It was strange. I didn’t know where to go. I went on holiday and was thinking, “Where do I go next?” Checking when I was back in. To be fair, I got bored after like six weeks. I was sat in Marbella thinking, “I want to go back in”, and I never thought I’d think that!’

Palmer’s new manager at Chelsea, Xabi Alonso, spoke to him during his seven weeks of downtime in the summer. ‘When I got told I wasn’t going to the World Cup, I think he knew, so he messaged me,’ Palmer says. ‘I can't remember what he said. I think he said don't worry about it or whatever. Normal stuff. It was nice. Him and his staff have been good, a breath of fresh air with his ideas.’

Palmer’s 2025-26 campaign, in which Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League to miss out on any form of European football, was disrupted by a groin injury.

He is not used to being sidelined or unable to freely act like his ‘cold’ self, and that was hard.

‘I didn’t really know how to deal with it,’ Palmer explains. ‘The first few months, with me being injured, I just wanted to go out and play. Which I probably shouldn’t have done.

‘Obviously I couldn’t play how I wanted to play. It was a bad season personally with injuries and stuff but I feel good now. The seven weeks obviously helped. I’m ready to go again.’

Palmer also reveals for the first time how he considered turning to surgery at the time, as he sought expert advice in Scandinavia, saying: ‘Yeah, I went to Sweden or Denmark, one of those countries, to see a doctor. We did speak about it. But I didn't end up getting it.’

Now that he feels fit again, Alonso has told him what he wants from him. ‘We spoke,’ Palmer says. ‘He sees me in the No 10, in the pockets, close to the striker, so we’ll see. When you sign good players, obviously your team is going to be better. It should be a good season.’

Sports.title: Sandro Tonali reveals why he chose Tottenham over Man City in just 10 minutes, how he already has a 'mini connection' with Roberto De Zerbi and how he fought for the 'best deal for Newcastle' before £100m switch
Sports.content:
Sandro Tonali reveals why he chose Tottenham over Man City in just 10 minutes, how he already has a 'mini connection' with Roberto De Zerbi and how he fought for the 'best deal for Newcastle' before £100m switch

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Our interview with Sandro Tonali is over, but as we shake hands, we have a small correction to make with Tottenham Hotspur’s £100million summer signing.

Earlier on in the conversation, Tonali had explained how nice it was that he was now getting to speak in Italian – with his new manager Roberto De Zerbi and his assistants and team-mates such as Guglielmo Vicario and Destiny Udogie – after three years of only using English at Newcastle United.

Except, as those of us from the heart of the North East will tell you, we do not talk in English. We speak Geordie, and to Tonali’s credit, he appreciates the difference. He tells us how he grew to love the locals who supported him around St James’ Park, and explains how he wanted his old club to feel like they were getting their money’s worth once it became clear that he would be leaving this summer.

‘The first thing was to get the best deal for Newcastle,’ Tonali says when discussing his decision to leave his former side managed by Eddie Howe, whose exit from Newcastle was coincidentally revealed on the same day as we spoke in Sydney.

‘I met there some of the best people for football. They love football. They live for football. When I decided to move, I said to my agent and to Ross Wilson (Newcastle’s sporting director) that I wanted the best deal for Newcastle because they deserve everything. This is football. Sometimes you have to understand how everything can change in your life in five minutes.'

Newcastle are in bother this summer. Not only might Bruno Guimaraes follow Tonali and Anthony Gordon out of the door at St James' Park, they have lost Howe now also. Tonali can only speak for himself, and he explains it was simply time for a change after three seasons and speaking with his family.

Sandro Tonali needed only a few minutes to convince him that Tottenham was his ideal Premier League destination

While sitting inside a makeshift boardroom set up inside Tottenham’s team hotel near the Sydney Harbour Bridge, Tonali explains how it was an easy decision to choose Spurs over others interested.

The £100m asking price that Newcastle placed on him influenced his options as he and his family were initially interested in returning to Italy. But they soon realised those in Serie A could not afford his services.

‘We stayed three years in Newcastle and after three years, we spoke all together, me and my family,’ Tonali says. 'It was impossible for the money (to return to Italy). For the salary, you can speak all the time, but if you don’t find the money for the transfer, you don’t have the chance to move.

'England was our solution and we found the best solution in England for me, for my career, for my football, for my happiness, for my family. I spoke with two teams. I understood after 10, 15 minutes that Tottenham would be my next team.’

Manchester City were believed to be the other club in for Tonali, who has won 32 caps for the Italian national team at 26 years old. He is rather liking the Little Italy connection developing within Tottenham now as he tells us: ‘After the last season, I spoke with my wife. We wanted to change our life. Not just for the city. We wanted to change everything. We spoke with two clubs.

‘When we spoke with Tottenham, we decided to sign for this team. They spoke with 100 per cent passion, 100 per cent seriousness. For this city, for my life outside of football for my family, OK, it’s like 10 per cent. Roberto and the director made the difference to the deal.

'I spoke after two minutes with my wife and my family and I said, “Probably it will be one of my best decisions of my career”. She told me, “You have 100 per cent the control over this decision”. I wanted to speak with her because it’s our life.

‘Roberto said the project will be tough but will be perfect for me, for you, for the city, an we can do one of the best seasons because we have big players. We just have to put a lot of work in.’

Alongside Tonali, Spurs have also spent £85m on signing Mateus Fernandes on West Ham, to complete their midfield. On officially being a £100m footballer, Tonali says: ‘You have to understand that this is football. The price is different now to 10 years ago. I know I have a lot of pressure but I know I’m a football player, I know my responsibilities, I know this team, I know the people here. I have to play like I’m a normal player, a normal Tottenham player, with passion, putting my energy in every day. It’s not £1m, £10m, or £100m. You just have to be a passionate player for this gaffer.’

Tonali previously spent a decade in Italy with Brescia, De Zerbi’s hometown. He and the Spurs boss have this ‘mini connection’, as Tonali describes it, and they previously met up there. ‘We spoke about him, about his work, about the passion that he puts into every single moment with the team for this work and I think now, after two weeks, I know everything is real,’ Tonali adds. ‘All gaffers are different. I passed three years with Eddie and he was fantastic, especially for me. But now I’ve found a different gaffer who works a lot on the pitch, a lot with the tactics, a lot with the ball. We love to play with the ball because we are a big team with big players.’

Sports.title: Franco Baresi dead at 66: AC Milan legend passes away with club sharing heartbreaking tribute to one of football's best ever defenders
Sports.content:
AC Milan and Italy legend Franco Baresi has died at the age of 66, his former club confirmed on Friday.

The one-club man was synonymous with the red-and-black side of the San Siro, playing every minute of his 20-year career for il Rossoneri.

As such, there was no shortage of emotion in the club's statement shared in the early hours of Friday morning, as AC Milan extended support not just to Baresi's family, but to their entire community.

'The entire history of AC Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi,' the statement read. 'His example and integrity will be forever etched into the Club's DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is.

'The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi's family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own.'

The defender, long considered one of the best of all time, served as captain for 14 years, and helped Milan claim six Serie A titles and three European Cups among numerous other honours.

Italian football legend Franco Baresi has died at the age of 66, his former club confirmed

The heavily decorated defender dedicated the duration of his career to his boyhood club

In 1999, Baresi's feats in club colours won him AC Milan's Player of the Century award.

The player known as 'Piscinin' also won the World Cup with Italy in 1982, later coming heartbreakingly close to claiming a second when the Azzurri reached the final in 1994 before defeat to Brazil on penalties.

Just hours before sharing the tragic news, AC Milan were forced to deny rumours on Wednesday that Baresi had died, after the player was admitted to hospital in Milan.

Italian outlet Tuttosport had broken the 'news', which prompted tributes from football fans including Italy's deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini.

Baresi had previously undergone lung surgery in August 2025 to remove a pulmonary nodule, and later was treated with cancer-prevention immunotherapy.

His last public appearance came touchingly at the San Siro, as he and his great friend - and former Inter Milan rival - Beppe Bergomi walked into the iconic stadium bearing the Olympic flame during the Winter Olympics Opening Ceremony earlier this year.

Baresi had initially been rejected by Inter Milan's academy as a junior player, after being deemed too small and frail for the rigorous demands of 1970s football, with his eventual rivals instead taking on his elder brother Giuseppe.

That twist of fate brought Baresi to Milan's academy, and he would go on to make his debut for the senior team at the age of 17 - after being given his nickname by the club's masseur at the time, Paolo Mariconti, which means 'little one' in Milanese dialect.

Baresi donned the captain's armband for Italy's second tilt at the World Cup in 1994, after winning the trophy in 1982

His trophy haul with il Rossoneri contains three European Cups, six Serie A titles, and countless other honours

His last public appearance came poignantly at the San Siro where he acted as a torchbearer in the Winter Olympics Opening Ceremony

Beppe Baresi was later made Inter captain, with the pair regularly exchanging pennants during the Milan derbies of the 1980s.

Inter shared their own touching statement to one of their bitterest competitive rivals, writing: 'Farewell to Franco Baresi, protagonist of the great clashes in the Milan Derby and one of the figures who most defined the history of the rivalry.

'Captain, team man, and flag bearer of AC Milan, he lived every matchup with Inter between competition and respect, within a challenge that wrote unforgettable pages of Italian soccer.

'President Giuseppe Marotta and all of FC Internazionale Milano stand in solidarity with the Baresi family, brother Beppe, and AC Milan in this moment of grief.'

Baresi stuck with AC Milan throughout the match-fixing Totonero scandal which saw the club relegated in 1980, and a second relegation in 1982, before going on to see Milan through their heavily decorated glory years under legendary managers Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello.

His role as the bedrock in Milan's all-Italian defence saw him written into the club's legend, and in 1989, named Ballon d'Or runner-up.

His defensive partner Paolo Maldini shared his grief in a touching statement on Friday, calling Baresi 'the strongest player' he had ever 'had the honour' to play alongside.

'Ciao Franco,' his statement began. 'Today I feel the same feeling when, for whatever reason, you couldn't go on the field next to us: "what will we do without our Captain?"

'You taught me to fight until my last breath, what does sticking to the shirt mean and the value of being a true leader. You did it by example, every day: few words, but lots of facts.

'You protected me as a child, guided me as a boy and inspired me as a man. You were the strongest football player I have ever had the honor to play with.

'A loving hug to your whole family, especially to your wife and your children. We'll miss you, Captain. But the light of your star will continue to shine on us forever.'

Italy's greatest ever defender Paolo Maldini shared a heartbreaking tribute to his former team-mate (pictured at a Legends match in 2012)

In 2020, Baresi was named as the club's honorary vice-president, and he continued to be enmeshed in Milan's culture, attending matches at the San Siro when possible.

Baresi is also thought to have even hoped to visit Milan's pre-season training camp at Milanello earlier this month, but was unable to due to his ill health.

After retiring from football in 1997, Milan retired his No 6 shirt, and after a brief stint as director of Fulham, Baresi returned to the club to coach their youth ranks until 2006.

Tributes from other Serie A sides began to pour in shortly after the news broke, with Juventus honouring his 'class and leadership'.

'There are people who, with their talent, enter history. And others who, with their humanity, remain there forever. Franco Baresi was both,' the statement read. 'Class, style, leadership, and respect on and off the field.

'An example for generations of players and fans, loved and admired by all football enthusiasts. His memory will live on forever. Juventus Football Club stands in solidarity with the Baresi family and AC Milan in this moment of profound sorrow.'

The president of the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) Giovanni Malago added: 'Italian football has lost one of its legends, an extraordinary champion who wore only two jerseys throughout his career: AC Milan and the Azzurri.

'A romantic choice, which has rightfully won him a place in the hearts of fans and millions of Italians. We will remember him as he deserves during the national team's upcoming matches, the national team for which he has always demonstrated exceptional dedication, becoming one of its most glorious symbols.'

Jamie Carragher shared his own tribute, with the Liverpool defender singling out Baresi as one of the 'all time greats'.

'It’s always a sad day for football when one of the all time greats pass away, and that’s exactly what Franco Baresi was,' Carragher shared on X. 'I’ve always seen him as the greatest centre back I ever saw & the ultimate one club man. RIP Capitano'.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua told exactly how he can beat Tyson Fury
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua told exactly how he can beat Tyson Fury

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are finally set to fight later this year to settle their decade-long heavyweight feud

View Image Anthony Joshua knocked out Kristian Prenga (Image: Getty Images)

Anthony Joshua has been told the only way he can beat Tyson Fury is to knock him clean out.

‌



Joshua returned to the ring last weekend with a second-round stoppage of Kristian Prenga, but only after twice being knocked down himself in the opening session. Twenty four hours earlier, Fury stopped Mariusz Wach in his own warm-up fight to set up a clash with Joshua later this year.

‌



And former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew believes Joshua will have to flatten Fury to to win. "There’s never been a better time to beat Tyson Fury," Bellew told Fight Your Corner, in partnership with Midnite. "Eighteen months ago, Fury is an overwhelming favourite. He is the one who doesn't want to have a straight up fight with you, he's the one who wants to box you.

‌



"And the best way to beat a boxer is, well, it is to just get rid of them, and I think that's Anthony Joshua 's best chance. If this fight goes to points, Anthony Joshua loses. Anthony Joshua has to win by knockout to win this fight, in my opinion. Let's be brutally honest, he's not going to out-box Tyson Fury."

Anthony Joshua opponent finally addresses fight 'fix' claim READ MORE :

Fury's clash with Joshua as yet has no venue or date and could head to New York to satisfy Netflix's demand for a prime-time US audience. Bellew has been outspoken about the prospect of the showdown being moved from London, and added: "Listen, the top and bottom of it is, is I'd understand it if it was going to Saudi because they're paying for the fight.

Article continues below

"What I don't like and don't understand is why it's going to the US. Why take a British fight and put it in America because no one cares in America? And I know I went a bit far when I said American boxing's been dead since Evander Holyfield. I was talking about the heavyweight division.

"Terence Crawford's amazing. I'm a fan of Terence Crawford, a brilliant fella, an amazing fighter, but let's just be brutally honest here, you've had the WBC heavyweight champion of the world for nearly a decade. He could walk down the street and be unrecognised, no one cared. After the Klitschkos took rein and dominated an era, American heavyweight boxing is just forgotten about, and it is right now.

"Now the people who are bringing it to life is Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. American boxing public don't care about Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. This is me now putting in layman's terms for everyone to understand, they don't care. So why should the fight go there? No one's going to be paying to want to come and see Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. The American public aren't doing it."
