World.title: At least 19 die after breach of border between Morocco and Spanish territory of Ceuta
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Spain deployed troops to reinforce police after thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in North Africa. The scene was reminiscent of 2021, when about 10,000 migrants entered the territory.

Spain and Morocco reinforced the border fence of a Spanish enclave on Friday and appeared to have largely halted mass crossings after tens of thousands of people arrived by sea and land in a day, with ‌at least 19 dead bodies found in the water.

The Spanish Department of National Security said on its website that more than 49,000 people were estimated to have crossed illegally in 24 hours, citing the Interior Ministry. The statement was later deleted from the website with no immediate explanation.

The mass crossing into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish-held spit jutting into the Mediterranean from Morocco, caused shock and division in Europe. France said it was increasing checks on its border with Spain, and Italy threatened to suspend Spain from the European Union's internal ​open border scheme.

At the gates into Ceuta, Moroccan authorities had deployed water cannon trucks and pushed people ​back. The charred remains of a bus and seven cars could be seen nearby from clashes with the crowds.

Spanish authorities said they would try to expel those who had entered illegally as quickly as possible, despite a court ruling that put some restrictions on special "border rejection" rules that allow immediate expulsions from the enclave.

Prime ​Minister Pedro Sanchez was due to visit Ceuta on Friday with Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish autonomous city in northern Morocco, have the ⁠European Union's only land borders with Africa. The two ⁠cities, each home to around 85,000 people, both periodically experience surges in attempted crossings by migrants seeking ‌to reach Europe, but the scale of Thursday's rush had little precedent.

Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres said on Friday that among factors contributing to the surge may have been a ruling by Spain's Supreme Court earlier this month that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned under special rules.

A migrant from Morocco arrives at the Spanish border, in Ceuta, Spain on Friday. (Fabian Bimmer/Reuters)

To reach Ceuta, located on the northern African coast, migrants often swim from the Moroccan town of Fnideq, covering about five kilometres to reach Spanish territory. Others attempt the crossing from the nearby town of Belyounech, where the distance is shorter.

On the Moroccan side of the border, thousands of migrants streamed into the town of Fnideq overnight despite a reinforced deployment of security that foiled most attempts to cross.

Although the crossing appeared blocked, groups moved along the coast seeking routes around the fence. Some prepared to swim.

"I was late," said Brahim, 32, who gave only one name. He said he had arrived from ‌Tangier hoping to cross through the gate but found it effectively shut. Among those hoping to cross were women and children, from both Morocco and sub-Saharan African countries further south.

In a post on X, Spain's Guardia Civil police association AUGC said there had been too few police in place to monitor the fence during the surge on Thursday, making them unable to stop it.

Migration is a sensitive issue across Europe, where right-wing parties have surged in the decade since a 2015 crisis when more than a million people crossed the ​continent mainly on foot and sought asylum, most fleeing war in Syria.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said he had already issued instructions "to immediately step up checks at the Spanish border."

Nunez's statement did not spell out what that meant in practice and there was no immediate response ⁠to a request from the ministry for further comment. There are normally no checks at borders between members of the EU's internal Schengen Area, though they can be introduced for a limited time ⁠in exceptional circumstances.

Migrants in the water attempting to cross the border between Ceuta and Morocco on Friday. (Marcos Moreno/Europa Press/Getty Images)

Italy's right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said her country was prepared "to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area ⁠with Spain."

Finland's ⁠interior minister, also from a right-wing party, praised Meloni's proposal and said the ​EU should follow Italy's lead.

While Spain's Socialist government says it remains firm over illegal crossings, it says immigrants help strengthen the economy and has offered a mass amnesty that saw hundreds of thousands of people ​seek citizenship over the past year.

"The images coming from ⁠Ceuta show how the Madrid Government's decision to grant Spanish, and therefore European, citizenship to over 500,000 irregular immigrants is profoundly wrong and encourages human trafficking," Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani wrote.

Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares replied that Tajani's message was "inappropriate," and said Spain expected "solidarity and not partisan demagoguery" from its partner. He added he would summon the Italian ambassador to protest.

World.title: Man linked to Toronto police corruption probe has global drug-trafficking ties, court documents say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto man investigated for potential involvement in a murder plot targeting a senior jail officer — and facing extradition to the U.S. on drug conspiracy charges linked to alleged cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding — has far-reaching criminal ties and is believed to have killed people, according to the RCMP.

Newly unsealed court documents provide fresh insight into the purported underworld connections of Gurpreet Singh, an accused cocaine smuggler whose name also appears in files stemming from a high-profile Toronto police corruption probe.

The documents contain unproven allegations submitted to a Quebec judge in 2024 as the RCMP sought authorizations for wiretaps and to surreptitiously record a meeting in February of that year involving Singh, his uncle, Hardeep Ratte, and a Montreal-born FBI informant who was later shot dead in Colombia .

Signed by RCMP Corp. Jonathan Hachey, the application alleges Singh is involved in “numerous” criminal activities, “knows all the major drug traffickers/transporters in Ontario and works with many groups,” including an unnamed “U.K. person … who is a very big player in the drug-smuggling business.”

Singh is also believed to have carried out killings himself, Hachey added.

Singh’s lawyer, Brian Greenspan, said in an email to CBC News on Thursday that his client is not facing criminal charges in Canada, despite untested allegations made public in search warrant documents.

“Mr. Singh has not been charged with any offence arising from the search, months after the execution of the warrants.”

Singh, left, and his uncle, Hardeep Ratte, right, were charged in a U.S. federal indictment alongside alleged cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding in 2024. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California)

Singh, 32, and Ratte were both arrested in the Toronto area in October 2024 as the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed an indictment in California targeting Wedding��’s purported transnational criminal network. Singh and his uncle were both charged with a drug-trafficking conspiracy.

Both men remain detained in a Toronto jail as U.S. prosecutors demand they be sent to Los Angeles to stand trial.

An Ontario Superior Court justice ordered the unsealing this month of the partially redacted documents, following a request from Singh and Ratte’s legal teams for further disclosure in an effort to fight their extradition case.

Wedding, a former Team Canada Olympic snowboarder, is accused of leading a murderous criminal enterprise that smuggled 60 tonnes of cocaine per year across North America.

The indictment alleges Singh and Ratte co-ordinated drug shipments to Canada for a “flat rate” of $220,000 Cdn per transport truck load.

According to the newly unsealed documents from early 2024, investigators hadn’t yet identified Ratte and only referred to him as Singh’s associate known as “uncle.”

Canadian Ryan Wedding, 44, was arrested in Mexico City and is now in custody in the U.S (FBI)

The planned February 2024 meeting with the FBI informant — Jonathan Acebedo-Garcia — was ultimately held at a Brampton, Ont., auto body shop, according to U.S. prosecutors.

Unbeknownst to Singh and Ratte, the Canadian Colombian drug trafficker was wearing a recording device provided by the Mounties, as he discussed with them plans to move truck loads of cocaine on behalf of Wedding’s network.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Edward Morgan said in his decision this month that Singh and Ratte’s defence teams should be given a copy of the video recording, but he declined to release the file publicly.

Jonathan Acebedo-Garcia, a Canadian Colombian drug trafficker who turned FBI witness in the Wedding case, was shot dead in January 2025. (Submitted by name withheld)

Connections from Mexico to Dubai

The list of accusations surrounding the Brampton-born Singh previously reported by CBC News — as laid out by U.S. and Canadian authorities after his arrest — read like a crime novel, tying together a violent Mexican drug cartel, a European crime syndicate and York Regional Police's sweeping Project South investigation into corruption and organized crime.

Search warrant documents from the Toronto-area corruption probe recently revealed how investigators looked into whether Singh and a personal acquaintance — a jail guard — were involved in an apparent assassination plot targeting a senior official at the jail where Singh is being held. The alleged murder attempt last year set off the sweeping investigation.

Neither the female acquaintance nor Singh have been charged in connection with Project South.

Two days after CBC News first reported on Singh's apparent ties to a central figure in the Project South case, Singh was moved to a special handling unit of the facility, the Toronto South Detention Centre.

The special handling unit at the Toronto South Detention Centre is seen in a 2018 provincial report. (Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General)

Singh, who went by the aliases Popey and Farmer, was previously held under much different circumstances.

According to Ontario Superior Court records, Singh reported being kidnapped "and tied up" by Mexican cartel members while on a visit to Sinaloa state in August 2024 — purportedly over a $600,000 drug debt. Wedding claimed he had to personally intervene to ensure Singh's release.

The newly unsealed court documents say earlier that year, a confidential informant for the FBI said Singh was under “a lot of pressure 'from Mexicans' to pay off his outstanding debts for cocaine loads they gave him in 2023.”

When Singh asked to be released on bail early last year, U.S. prosecutors warned in a letter filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice that he “presents a substantial risk of flight.”

He was involved in a scheme to ship stolen high-end cars through the Port of Montreal to Dubai, the L.A.-based prosecutors said. They alleged Singh has “extensive organized crime connection within Dubai,” including with members of the Kinahan organized crime group.

A 2025 grand jury indictment includes images of colourfully packaged cocaine bricks, allegedly linked to Wedding's network. (U.S. District Court, Central District of California)

Founded in Ireland, the prominent criminal syndicate has been linked to drug-trafficking across Europe, arms sales, money laundering and murders.

“Singh’s criminal conduct,” assistant U.S. attorneys Maria Jhai and Lyndsi Allsop wrote, “makes him a danger to the community.”

World.title: Hamas will hand over weapons under Gaza peace deal only if Israel withdraws forces, ends attacks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Implementation of the deal to bring peace to Gaza announced by U.S. President Donald Trump will depend on Israel first meeting its commitments under an agreement reached last year, a senior Hamas official told Reuters on Friday.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday, Trump announced a "major milestone" toward ending the war in Gaza, saying his Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups.

Ghazi Hamad, a Hamas official involved in the negotiations, said the agreement was a "comprehensive framework" that went beyond the issue of disarmament and would depend on Israel implementing the first phase of an agreement hammered out last year in the Egyptian resort of Sharm el-Sheikh.

Under that agreement, he said Israel was obliged to end its attacks in Gaza and withdraw its forces to where they stood in October, as well as increase the flow of goods and aid coming into the enclave.

Only then would Hamas agree to hand over its weapons to the new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body set up to run the enclave.

"We insisted to the mediators that Israel must abide by the agreement," he said.

Hours after Trump ann ounced the Hamas deal on Thursday, several Palestinians were wounded in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza, medics said.

An Israeli official said on Thursday that Israel would not agree to withdraw behind the so-called Yellow Line before Hamas is disarmed and the Gaza Strip is demilitarized.

World.title: 'It was hell': French communities are on the front lines of Europe's new wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The flames came quick and strong.

Pushed by westerly winds, they'd already devastated Saumos, France, 14 kilometres away, and in the early morning hours of last Friday, were heading, like a match to gunpowder, through an exceptionally dry forest of pines, in an exceptionally hot summer, toward Le Porge.

When Stéphanie Dhont looked outside her window, sparks were raining down.

"Everything was orange and since it was all so dry, even the smallest bush would instantly burst into flames," said Dhont, whose husband had left only hours before, around 1 a.m. local time, to rescue the couple's 15-year-old daughter from an evacuation order at her summer camp in Biscarosse, south down the coast, where another wildfire had broken out.

Only Dhont and her 18-year-old son, Timothée Collin, a lifeguard and surfer, were left to defend the family's home near the centre of the town in southwestern France against the encroaching wildfire.

Dhont's family is one of many in Le Porge who says they felt abandoned in dealing with a new climate disaster reality.

"So we did what we could to save our house," the 45-year-old mother said of the wood home they built 13 years ago.

The mother and son pulled out the garden hose and started spraying the outside walls, the hedges, the roof, "everything."

Within an hour, Dhont says, the village was surrounded by flames.

Stéphanie Dhont, centre, in white, fought the fire off her home with her 18-year-old son on July 24. Dhont, 45, has been volunteering in her town of Le Porge, France, where the Gironde wildfire destroyed 183 homes. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

There had been no phone alerts, no text messages, "nothing — not even a siren." Instead, neighbours drove by honking, yelling at everyone to leave, she said.

"It was total panic, it was hell."

One hundred and eighty three homes burned in Le Porge in the hours that followed.

"A field of ruins," the town’s mayor, Martial Zaninetti, called it.

The wildfires that have burned in the area near the city of Bordeaux may be smaller than those Canada and the U.S. are used to — totalling over 100,000 hectares — but French authorities and wildfire experts say they are unprecedented in Europe in terms of size, scale and impact.

The small communities that pepper the pine forests around Bordeaux have been left reeling. Many residents stayed behind to help fight the fires, which only began to let up Thursday morning as a light rain fell.

A drone view shows burnt buildings in an area affected by a wildfire in Le Porge, Gironde, amid drought conditions following a heat wave and water shortages across much of France, on Tuesday. (Yves Herman/Reuters)

'We've had to fend for ourselves'

On Wednesday, they'd scrambled, along with firefighters from across the country, in punishing 40-degree heat to tamp out spontaneous re-burns — when heat and dryness cause the smouldering ground to ignite.

But with the emergency out of the way Thursday, and 84,000 out of over 220,000 people allowed to regain in their homes in nine communities — but not Le Porge — resident volunteers there were starting to absorb the extent of their town's destruction and the sense that they’d been left to their own devices.

"We've had to fend for ourselves," said Didier Deyres, 65, a farmer and the vice-president of the local forest fire defence department.

Standing outside Le Porge's party hall, which had been converted into a bustling volunteer and firefighter hub, Deyres decried a lack of resources from the French government he said his town has received since its residents had to flee nearly a week ago.

"We're starting to lose heart," said Deyres. "We need help. We are going to start seeing traumatic shocks, but there's also going to be [health] problems because of the smoke."

Didier Deyres, the vice-president of the forest fire defence department in Le Porge, says his town has been 'abandoned.' (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

A sign at the hall warned of high rates of carbon monoxide in the air and said masks were "mandatory." Few people wore them.

Deyres says he believes that if the French government had been better prepared and had more ressources, including more water bombers, his community would have shouldered far less destruction.

France owns 12 Canadair water bombers, but it can only use five at the moment due to maintenance issues — a fact most people affected by fires in France will mention.

In the back of the party hall, ad hoc health care is underway. Young volunteer health and body workers sit on cots they’d arranged in a corner to treat members of their community.

Emma Jambert, a 25-year-old osteopath from Le Porge, said the solidarity of the town has been motivating, but she, too, wondered aloud when more help would come.

"There’s a lot of fatigue," Jambert said. "The aftermath is going to be complicated."

WATCH | A frontline look a France's fight against wildfires near Bordeaux: Inside France's battle to save Bordeaux from unprecedented wildfires | Duration 2:58 CBC News gets a frontline look at France's pitched fight against unprecedented wildfires in the historic Bordeaux region, where another heatwave is expected to fuel flames that have forced at least 250,000 people from their homes.

'Solidarity,' but questions remain

A group of residents are planning a class action against French authorities who ordered firefighters to leave Le Porge as the fire raged Friday and direct their efforts to Lège-Cap-Ferret, where a wealthy community sits on a nearby peninsula.

The government has justified its actions, saying there is only one route out of Cap-Ferret, making a rapid evacuation nearly impossible.

Dhont and Deyres said the town had been "abandoned" and "sacrificed."

Zaninetti, the mayor, says he "understands their pain."

He prefers to focus on the future, noting he has started gathering local associations and collaborating with nearby communities on a reconstruction plan in an effort he says resembles the response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

"What keeps us going is this solidarity … without it, I think we would have collapsed."

Along with the solidarity, there has been a sense of guilt.

Dhont served meals to a lineup of other volunteers and firefighters at the hall. She, her husband, daughter and son have been working late into the night every day over the past week.

"I’ve been asking myself: why them and not me?"

Timothé Collin, 18, has been volunteering in Le Porge, where he and his family live. It's one of the hardest hit communities by wildfires in southwestern France. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

She hopes all the media attention will result in more help for Le Porge, where she says everyone knows each other cares for each other.

Her home is in the centre of town, where most were spared, but down the road, along the Avenue du Bassin d'Arcachon is a kilometre-long stretch of ashes where homes used to stand.

Blackened trunks reach out of a carpet of cinders. Cars are carcasses and stone walls stand like ancient ruins without roofs without their interiors, their couches, their beds, their curtains. Without shoes in the entryway or homework on the kitchen counter.

'No turning back now'

Timothé Collin, Dhont's 18-year-old, used to drive through down the Bassin every day to get to high school.

Now, it's unrecognizable. Every once in a while, a house, a tree, a shed, or a car is left unscathed.

"It's a lottery," Collin said, while driving through the devastation. "A gust of wind can make the difference."

Collin, fought the wildfire in Le Porge overnight last Friday with his mother. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

In the months and years to come, the residents of Le Porge say they want accountabily — for the warning signs that were missed, the air water bombers that weren't ordered or delivered, the help that didn't come or left, the water the firefighters didn't get enough of to keep flames at bay.

Europe is the fastest warming continent. France has had four heat waves this season alone. These fires were only a matter of time, Collin said.

"There’s no turning back now and it's our fault, humans' fault," he said.

"I try to keep things in perspective; I tell myself that things will change and that all the little things I do — all my small efforts to bring about change — matter. I tell myself that with all these catastrophes, people's mindsets are shifting. I believe in it, I do. We have to, because if we don't, nothing will ever change."

World.title: Debate over trans athletes overtakes WNBA
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The WNBA has been on a meteoric rise the last few years. It's so popular it just signed media rights deals worth $3.1 billion US.

But with that explosion in popularity and cultural cache has come the projection of larger culture war issues onto the league.

The latest? The debate over trans athletes in sports.

It started earlier this month, when Indiana Fever sharpshooter Sophie Cunningham ignited an online firestorm after an ESPN profile quoted her voicing support for barring transgender girls and women from women's sports.

"I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think, with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men," Cunningham said.

The issue — which has been a major point of contention in the U.S. for more than a year now after President Donald Trump signed an executive order preventing trans people from participating in women's or girls' sporting events — remained a focal point during Tuesday's matchup between the Fever and Seattle Storm.

Rally outside game renews controversy

Outside the arena, there was a small rally in support of Cunningham's comments and pushing for a proposal currently on the ballot in the state of Washington that would bar transgender students from competing in girls' athletics at school ( the Supreme Court upheld similar laws in Idaho and West Virginia last month ).

Inside the arena, a Storm player wore a trans rights shirt ahead of playing. Cunningham was booed throughout the game, according to ESPN . And the co-owner of the Storm, Celeste Keaton, got suspended for five home games for allegedly cursing out two fans wearing t-shirts with XX and XY chromosomes in support of Cunningham.

The Storm apologized for Keaton's comments and said in a statement: "Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome, and we remain committed to creating an inclusive environment where every fan is treated with respect."

People rally to support Cunningham and her comments outside Tuesday's game. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Cunningham weighed in as well, posting on social media: "Truly embarrassing of the co-owner. Unfortunately shows the type of leader she is."

She also wrote, "I truly believe there is a safe space and love for EVERYBODY. Biological girls, biological boys, trans women, and trans men. Everyone is welcome at my table! You can disagree and still be kind."

The events at the Tuesday game and Cunningham's initial comments have been fodder on Fox News. White House spokesperson Karoline Leavitt also weighed in, saying it was "astonishing" to see the backlash Cunningham was receiving from "Democrats and left-wing figures across the country."

"Men should not be playing in women's sports. It's completely ludicrous that anyone could support that."

More people gathered in support of Cunningham outside the game Tuesday. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Politics 'a lightning rod'

Trans rights has been a longtime pet issue for the Trump White House. In the lead up to the 2024 election Trump ran an ad attacking Kamala Harris's support for gender-affirming care for trans people. The campaign focused on NFL and college football.

"I think anything political from an athlete right now, particularly around race, around transgender issues, it's going to become a lightning rod right now," said Molly Yanity, the director of the sports media and communication program at the University of Rhode Island. She said Cunningham is particularly high profile and on social media, including Reddit, has earned the nickname "MAGA Barbie" — fair or not.

"[Cunningham] hasn't really come out with any, let's say, progressive, kind of politics. So I think that the absence of her saying anything opens the door to assumptions that she is on the other side of that."

While the Indiana Fever came out saying neither the organization nor Cunningham had any knowledge of the demonstration at the arena Tuesday, Alejandra Caraballo, a clinical instructor at the Harvard Law Cyberlaw Clinic who frequently speaks about trans rights, sees the WNBA's suspension of the Storm's co-owner as a kind of green light for protesters to keep bringing politics to the sport.

"They're saying they're there to support Sophie, but what they're really there to do is support a transphobic message," she said. "They're intentionally trying to go to these events to get reactions to film and create content and further this controversy and bring attention."

Not WNBA's first brush with controversy

This isn't the first time the WNBA has found itself at the nexus of American culture wars.

Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas said she had received death threats and been called racial slurs for making contact with star player Caitlin Clark's throat during a game in June . Republican lawmakers have recently fuelled the controversy by writing a letter in early July saying they were concerned by reports that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated."

Attendees at Tuesday's game hold a sign referencing Cunningham's comments. (Steve Bisig/Imagin Images/Reuters)

Yanity thinks a lot of the controversy is being drummed up by fans, not the players. And then are being discussed ad nauseum on social media.

"It has become a very, very toxic place where threats of violence have been made against specifically the Black players."

The league has faced criticism that they are not doing enough to protect players from the online onslaught. Last week, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert called the online abuse "unacceptable," saying "The racism, the misogyny, the homophobia, the harassment, and threats directed to our players, has no place in sport or anywhere else."

The WNBA did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CBC.

WATCH | Supreme Court upholds U.S. laws banning trans athletes: SCOTUS upholds laws banning trans athletes from women's school sports | Duration 1:16 The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favour of overturning the decisions of lower courts that found laws in Idaho and West Virginia banning transgender athletes from competing in women's sports at the school level violated the U.S. Constitution and a federal anti-discrimination law. The 6-3 ruling to uphold the laws in Idaho and West Virginia opens the pathway for as many as 29 other states to pursue laws that limit the participation of trans athletes in women’s sports.

Ultimately, said Yanity, this is a league that has seen explosive growth over the last several years. "It used to be that you'd have to search high and low to find the games. [Now] they are all readily available and at your fingertips. … These social aspects of the game are also being analyzed."

To add to that, she said politics are inherent to women's sport, pointing to the fact that it took an act of Congress in the U.S. and a president's signature for women to even get on the court and have a somewhat even playing field.

"Everything about a woman's existence, and particularly a Black woman's existence, is political."

World.title: What you need to know about FIFA's private investment plan — and the backlash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Less than two weeks since the conclusion of the 2026 World Cup, soccer is once again front-page news thanks to a new proposal by FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Not one to shy away from big announcements, Infantino caught many in the soccer world unaware with a plan to sell off part of FIFA's commercial interests to private investors.

It's caused significant backlash in the soccer world, including the prospect of European nations boycotting future editions of the World Cup.

Here's what you need to know.

WATCH | FIFA's World Cup profits soar: How FIFA got even richer this World Cup | Duration 2:24 CBC’s Jonathon Gatehouse breaks down how Gianni Infantino doubled profits for the 2026 World Cup, and how much of that money ends up in the hands of organizations like Soccer Canada.

What are FIFA, UEFA and the other soccer confederations?

The Fédération Internationale de Football Association is the international governing body of association football, also known as soccer. Founded in 1904 and headquartered in Switzerland, FIFA today has many stated objectives , including overseeing the development and innovation in the sport, conducting disciplinary matters and organizing international tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cup.

FIFA's membership is currently comprised of 211 national soccer federations (such as Canada Soccer), which are the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law.

Each national federation is also a member of six continental confederations that oversee the sport in their respective regions:

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol (CONMEBOL).

Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF).

Oceania Football Confederation (OFC).

Union of European Football Associations (UEFA).

UEFA is arguably the most powerful of the six, as it counts many of the sport's most successful countries among its 55 members — including France, Germany, Italy and current world champion Spain — as well as the four "home nations" of the United Kingdom, where the sport was formalized.

Infantino, left, stands with Spanish Football Association president Rafael Louzán after the trophy ceremony for the World Cup final on July 19. Spain would be one of the nations involved in a UEFA boycott. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

What is the FIFA plan causing the latest furor?

On Tuesday, FIFA president Gianni Infantino announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup.

Under FIFA's plan, which was pitched as a way to boost the development of soccer around the world, 20 per cent of FFE would be sold off to private investors, including a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, brother of U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

National federations that approve FFE would see their promised $8 million US development funds from FIFA more than doubled to $20 million US for the next four years. It would then increase to $22 million US and $24 million US in the following cycles through 2038, FIFA said.

What was UEFA's reaction?

The continental confederations appear to have been blindsided by Infantino's announcement.

Almost immediately, UEFA called an emergency meeting of its member federations. On Thursday, it released a strongly worded statement saying its members would boycott all the global soccer body's competitions as long as the FEE proposal remains on the table.

UEFA delivered a stinging rebuke of Infantino's plan, saying "the World Cup is not for sale."

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors."

It added that FIFA's plan, under which "commercial return becomes a permanent obligation" and "investor expectations become a daily pressure," would upend the way soccer is governed.

"You're giving undue influence to people that are not going to necessarily be motivated by what's best for soccer but what's best for their bank accounts," said Moshe Lander, a sports economist at Concordia University in Montreal.

Spanish players celebrate after winning the 2023 Women's World Cup at the final in Sydney, Australia. The next Women's World Cup is scheduled to be hosted in Brazil in summer 2027. (Hannah Mckay/Reuters)

Which competitions would be affected by a boycott?

Three FIFA World Cup tournaments are still to be played this year:

The U-20 Women's World Cup in Poland is set to kick off on Sept. 5.

The U-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco is due to get underway on Oct. 17.

The U-17 Men's World Cup in Qatar gets underway in mid-November.

The next senior World Cup, the women's tournament, is scheduled for next summer in Brazil.

UEFA has sent a "powerful message" in threatening to boycott future FIFA events, said Graham Scott, a former English Premier League referee and now a correspondent with The Athletic.

"The withdrawal of UEFA countries from any FIFA tournament effectively renders it worthless," he said.

What about the other confederations?

UEFA's statement blasts FIFA for its lack of consultation with member federations about the FFE plan, a sentiment echoed by both the confederations covering Asia, and North and Central America and the Caribbean.

On Wednesday, a statement by the AFC voiced disappointment "that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it."

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa went further in a letter to member federations, saying "FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football" and warned of risks to their own competitions.

Several hours after UEFA's statement was released Thursday, CONCACAF said its member federations had rejected the proposal to create FFE.

While it didn't go as far as threatening a boycott, a CONCACAF statement called for "greater transparency and proper governance" and raised concerns about "the lack of due process surrounding the proposal."

It also questioned why FIFA deemed that private equity was necessary after what was the most profitable World Cup in history.

The CAF says it will discuss the proposal at a meeting next week, while the OFC said it had begun a consultation process with its members about the proposal. As of late Thursday, CONMEBOL, which covers South America, had not released a statement about the proposal.

The combined votes of the AFC, CONCACAF and UEFA would be enough to defeat the proposal, which requires a majority from member federations to pass.

U.S. President Donald Trump, left, and Infantino stand together during the trophy presentation after the final of the FIFA World Cup 2026, the most lucrative in the tournament's history. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Has Infantino put his position in jeopardy?

Prior to the FFE announcement, it looked as if Infantino would easily win re-election for a fourth term as FIFA president when a vote of member federations is held next March.

That's perhaps less of a certainty now, especially considering the comments from AFC president Sheikh Salman, who has been a staunch ally of Infantino.

It also follows concern over some aspects of the recent World Cup hosted by Canada, Mexico and the U.S., including the high price of tickets, controversies over the video assistant referee, the introduction of hydration breaks during games, and a red card for an American player that was rescinded after the intervention of U.S. President Donald Trump.

FIFA has set a Nov. 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in the vote for the association's next president.

World.title: A concert to remember: Metal band rocks out at Ottawa hospital, granting patient's wish
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hospitals aren't the usual venue for a high-energy hard rock concert, but that's exactly what took place at Ottawa's Bruyère Health last week, helping one longtime patient live out his dream of attending a heavy metal show.

With a colourful light show, hair-blowing fans and aggressive headbanging, a board room at the hospital was transformed into a rock club last Tuesday after 27-year-old Tim Berry expressed his wish to rock out there.

Roshene Lawson, a clinical chaplain at Bruyère Health, said she was visiting Berry after he'd received some bad health news and was dwelling on the things he'd missed out on.

"I said, 'Well, we can talk about all the stuff you've lost, or we can talk about how you want to live for however much longer you're around," Lawson said.

The Scepter performs for patients at Bruyère Health on July 21. (Bruyère Health)

What Berry wanted was to attend a heavy metal show. Lawson called Scott McClinton, owner of hard rock venue the Dominion Tavern in the ByWard Market, who in turn recruited local band The Scepter.

"It was a quick yes, and then he reached out to The Scepter, and they gave a quick yes," Lawson told CBC’s All In A Day. "All of a sudden, people in heavy metal outfits with guitars and stuff are asking where the chaplain is."

Berry's condition was deemed too fragile to leave the hospital, so the crew decided to bring the show to him. With Berry’s approval, it turned into a full-blown event for patients at Bruyère Health on July 21, coming together within a week.

Heavy metal band The Scepter quickly accepted the invitation to put on a show at Bruyère Health. (Bruyère Health)

"He had tears and I joked with him, I said, 'Are the tears because it's so bloody loud?'" Lawson said. "And he laughed and he said, ‘No, I'm happy'"

Lawson said even the "tough heavy metal guys" had tears in their eyes, too.

"It was absolutely emotional," McClinton recalled. "I never thought I'd cry during a metal show, but that definitely happened."

11:36 A heavy metal concert in a hospital? When a patient shared with staff at Bruyère Health that it was his dream to see a heavy metal concert, they made it happen. Dominion Tavern and local metal band The Scepter came through to deliver an electric performance for patients at Bruyère.

The Scepter pulled out all the stops, making the most of the unconventional venue by using the space between each patient as a catwalk to show off their guitar-shredding skills.

"We had enough space with all the lights and stuff to still move around and go up to the patients and give them a little taste of our heavy metal might," said guitarist Josh Collins.

After the show, Berry met with the band and got some merch including a T-shirt and CD.

Chaplain Roshene Lawson says it is important to think outside the box when it comes to patient care. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

Lawson said it was much more than a fun musical experience: It was about providing the best quality of life for a patient she helps navigate the ups and downs of hospital life.

"I listened to what it was that would bring him meaning and value. It's not my role to judge that," she said. "It's my role to support and listen."

She said while a strong focus on medical care is crucial, the clinical team at Bruyère Health also prioritizes spiritual wellness.

"Sometimes we've got to think outside the box, and in this case I went to a heavy metal concert."

World.title: Premiers tell Ottawa they 'urgently' want negotiations to begin on future of the RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's premiers are calling for more clarity from the federal government around the future of the RCMP and to start negotiations as soon as possible with those who plan on keeping the Mounties as their boots-on-the-ground police force.

According to a joint communiqué, the provincial and territorial leaders discussed what's next in their relationships with the RCMP when they gathered last week in Charlottetown.

"They highlighted policing challenges, such as staffing shortages, vacancies, rising costs and governance concerns," said the communiqué.

"The federal government must provide a clear decision on the future of RCMP contract policing and to urgently begin negotiations regarding new police service agreements for those who want them."

It alludes to years of uncertainty and debate about whether Ottawa should keep the RCMP in front-line policing across the country, or shift to solely focus on what's known as federal policing — which includes espionage, violent extremism and terrorism, money laundering, cybercrime and organized crime.

Earlier this year, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told CBC News the government is committed to keeping Mounties in the business of day-to-day policing, while signalling that improving the federal crimes wing is his government's priority.

Alberta still considering if it will keep RCMP

Eight of the provinces, the three territories and some 150 municipalities across Canada have contracts with Ottawa to use the RCMP as their local police. The current agreements — which see the provinces and territories pay for 70 per cent of the contract and the federal government cover the rest — are set to expire in 2032.

While still six years away, multiple provinces are pushing for those talks to start soon. They say they need more details to plan ahead.

Regional support for the RCMP has wavered in parts of the country. After a heated fight, Surrey, B.C., transitioned away from the Red Serge in 2024 and stood up its own police force.

Canada's premiers discussed their future contracts with the RCMP as they gathered in Charlottetown last week. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

Late last year the Alberta Next Panel, aimed at finding ways the province can strengthen its autonomy, suggested Premier Danielle Smith's government continue its work in establishing an Alberta Police Service "and transition community policing services from the RCMP to the APS and municipal policing services."

In a statement this week, a spokesperson for Alberta's Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services said the province is "continuing to explore options to strengthen public safety."

"While the federal government has signalled a willingness to negotiate police service agreements beyond 2032, provinces and territories continue to seek formal certainty and an accelerated negotiation process given the long lead times required for policing, recruitment, infrastructure, budgeting and governance decisions," said the spokesperson, Sheena Campbell.

WATCH | Minister responds to AG report on RCMP staffing: RCMP application process being shortened to 6 months after report finds dire shortage: minister | Duration 1:52 Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree was asked Monday if the auditor general's report on the RCMP — which indicated the Mounties took an average of 330 days to process recruitment applications — suggests that more reform is needed. 'We are condensing the recruitment process down to six months,' Anandasangaree said.

British Columbia, the largest RCMP contract policing jurisdiction in Canada, said "given the complexity of contract policing, all parties require the necessary time to plan, engage and fully participate in meaningful negotiations.

"It is critical that contract negotiations be initiated to ensure the long-term strategic response to public safety," said a spokesperson for the province's Ministry of Public Safety and Solicitor General.

Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson said he's looking for a renewed agreement "that reflects the unique realities of policing in the North."

"We support greater transparency and engagement with provinces and territories throughout the negotiations, continued federal investment to maintain strong RCMP services and measures that strengthen recruitment, retention and staffing stability in remote communities," he said in a statement to CBC News.

He said he's also looking for sustained support for complementary community safety initiatives like programs looking at prevention and wellness alongside policing.

"Ultimately, improving public safety in the North requires both effective policing and continued collaboration to address the underlying social factors that drive crime," he said.

Both the governments in Newfoundland and Labrador and New Brunswick said they are looking for negotiations to start "as soon as possible."

Staff shortages, recruitment ongoing issues

Staff shortages have been flagged by premiers in the past as an area of concern in their contracts. Multiple reports have concluded the RCMP's multiple mandates are straining the institution.

Earlier this year the federal auditor general found the RCMP didn't recruit enough new officers or effectively assign its members to meet its operational needs.

"As a result of chronic shortages of front-line police officers, the RCMP faces a higher risk of police officer absences and burnout, which could make it more challenging for the force to prevent and investigate crime, maintain peace and order and contribute to national security," said the report.

The Mass Casualty Commission, which investigated the April 2020 massacre in Nova Scotia that killed 22 people, put out a report in 2023 calling on government to review and restructure the RCMP.

As part of its response to the tragedy, the Nova Scotia government announced this week that it's making changes to how it funds and bills for RCMP services.

The federal Public Safety Department didn't answer when negotiations will begin, but said it's been "actively engaging with jurisdictions to identify their policing needs beyond 2032."

The RCMP deferred to Public Safety when reached for comment.

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Universidad de Chile Eliminated by Curicó Unido in Copa Chile Upset

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.
