A Sculpture Born from a Historic Moment

Fernando Botero (1932-2023) donated the bronze sculpture to the nation on September 24, 2016, just hours before the Colombian government signed a landmark peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).

The accord formally ended more than five decades of internal armed conflict that had killed over 260,000 people and displaced millions.

Botero, Colombia’s most internationally celebrated artist, was known for his signature ‘Boterismo’ style, which exaggerated the volume and roundness of figures to create a sense of monumental sensuality and political weight.

His works, instantly recognizable for their plump, oversized forms, hang in major museums from New York to Tokyo and command millions of dollars at auction.

The dove itself is a classic Botero interpretation: a plump, voluminous bird whose swollen chest and compact wings convey a heavy, almost burdened peace rather than a fragile one.

Botero also created a separate, widely exhibited painting of the same name, reinforcing the dove as a personal motif for reconciliation.

The Botero Dove of Peace and the 2016 Accord

The sculpture became an immediate symbol of the peace process, representing the fragile hope that followed the end of hostilities with the FARC, a Marxist guerrilla group founded in 1964.

President Juan Manuel Santos, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his role in the negotiations, placed the dove in a prominent position to highlight the government’s commitment to the accord.

For international observers, the dove stood as a visual shorthand for Colombia’s long and painful journey toward ending the hemisphere’s last major armed conflict.

The 2016 agreement was deeply polarizing domestically, narrowly losing a public referendum before a revised version was ratified by Congress.

Botero’s donation was seen as a personal endorsement of peace from a figure who had transcended Colombia’s political divisions through his global artistic stature.

His death in 2023 at age 91 in Monaco prompted a national outpouring of grief and renewed attention to his public works.

A Routine Protocol During Presidential Transitions

Removing symbolic artwork from the Casa de Nariño, the presidential palace in Bogotá, is standard protocol during a change of government.

The same procedure was followed when President Santos left office in 2018, with pieces on loan from museums returned to their original collections.

Presidential officials and conservation experts jointly carried out the transfer to ensure the bronze sculpture was handled without damage.

The incoming administration of president-elect Abelardo De La Espriella will decide which artworks will decorate the palace during its term.

Outgoing President Gustavo Petro had moved the dove to the palace at the start of his term roughly four years ago, placing it in a visible location that connected his administration to the peace process.

The transition on August 7, 2026, will mark the latest chapter in Colombia’s democratic history, with the dove’s return to the museum signaling the formal end of Petro’s tenure.

The National Museum: Custodian of Colombia’s Story

The National Museum of Colombia (Museo Nacional) in Bogotá is the country’s oldest and most important museum, housed in a former prison built in the 19th century.

It holds the nation’s most significant collections of art, archaeology, and history, serving as the primary custodian of objects that define Colombian identity.

The museum previously displayed the dove before Petro’s government requested it on loan, and it will now reintegrate the piece into its collection.

For foreign visitors and expats, the museum is a central cultural reference point in Bogotá, located in the city’s international district and easily accessible.

The return ensures the sculpture remains publicly viewable in a controlled conservation environment, rather than in the working seat of government.

Museum officials have not yet announced whether the dove will be placed in a special exhibition or returned to its previous gallery.

What the Move Signals for International Observers

For expats, investors, and diplomats following Colombia, the orderly transfer of symbolic art reinforces the country’s institutional stability.

Colombia has a long tradition of peaceful democratic transitions, even amid deep political polarization and ongoing security challenges.

The dove’s removal is not a political statement but a procedural step, though its symbolism inevitably resonates in a nation still grappling with the implementation of the 2016 accord.

Sporadic violence involving dissident FARC factions and other armed groups continues in some rural areas, making the peace process an unfinished project.

International readers should understand that the movement of such a charged artwork is both a bureaucratic act and a quiet reminder of the peace that remains elusive for many Colombians.

The incoming De La Espriella administration will face immediate decisions on security policy and peace implementation that will shape how the dove’s legacy is perceived in the years ahead.

Botero’s Enduring Legacy in Colombia and Beyond

Fernando Botero remains Colombia’s most universal cultural ambassador, with his voluminous figures recognized on every continent.

Born in Medellín in 1932, he developed his distinctive style by the 1950s and went on to exhibit in the world’s most prestigious museums, including the Louvre and the Hermitage.

His public sculptures dot the streets of Medellín’s Plaza Botero, a major tourist attraction that houses 23 of his monumental bronze works donated to his hometown.

Botero also addressed Colombia’s violence directly, creating a powerful series of paintings depicting the drug war’s brutality in the 1990s and 2000s.

His donation of the Dove of Peace in 2016 was one of his final major public gestures toward his homeland, cementing his role as an artist deeply engaged with Colombia’s fate.

The sculpture’s return to the National Museum ensures that Botero’s vision of peace remains accessible to all Colombians and international visitors, regardless of who occupies the presidential palace.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the Botero Dove of Peace removed from the presidential palace?

The sculpture was removed as part of the routine protocol during Colombia’s presidential transition. Artworks on loan from museums are typically returned before a new president takes office on August 7.

What does the Botero Dove of Peace symbolize?

Fernando Botero donated the bronze dove on September 24, 2016, just before the Colombian government signed the historic peace accord with the FARC guerrillas. It symbolizes the hope for reconciliation after more than five decades of armed conflict.

Where can I see the Botero Dove of Peace now?

The sculpture has been returned to the National Museum (Museo Nacional) in Bogotá, where it was housed before being loaned to the presidential palace. It will remain in the museum’s public collection.

Expats & Nomads · Colombia

Key Facts —Artist Katie James is a Colombian-Irish singer-songwriter who blends Colombian and Irish folk influences, singing in Spanish and English. —Album Her new album ‘Bajo mi Corteza’ was released in March 2026 and features 10 original songs across Latin American styles like bolero, cumbia, and vallenato. —Cali Concert She performs at the Sala Antonio María Valencia, part of the Bellas Artes complex in Cali, on July 31, 2026, in a full-band format. —Tour The ‘Bajo mi Corteza Tour’ includes dates in other Colombian cities, such as Bucaramanga, bringing her acoustic sound to a national audience. —Style The album maintains an acoustic, sensitive sound while exploring traditional rhythms including tonadas llaneras and Argentine zamba.

Katie James, the Colombian-Irish singer-songwriter, is bringing her new album ‘Bajo mi Corteza’ to stages across Colombia this year, offering expats and nomads a rare chance to hear a truly bilingual folk voice in an intimate setting.

Cali, Colombia, on Katie James’s Bajo mi Corteza tour. (Photo: internal archive)

Who Is Katie James?

For foreigners who have not yet discovered her, Katie James occupies a unique space in Colombia’s music scene.

Born to an Irish father and a Colombian mother, she moves fluidly between English and Spanish in her lyrics, weaving together the folk traditions of both countries.

Her sound is acoustic and sensitive, built around guitar and voice, but it draws deeply from Colombian rhythms like cumbia and vallenato as well as Irish melodic sensibilities.

This cultural duality makes her work immediately accessible to English-speaking audiences while remaining authentically rooted in Latin American soil.

The ‘Bajo mi Corteza’ Album

Released in March 2026, ‘Bajo mi Corteza’ translates to ‘Under My Bark’ and marks a mature chapter in her career.

The album contains 10 original compositions that travel across a map of Latin American styles.

Listeners will encounter bolero, cumbia, vallenato, tonadas llaneras from the eastern plains, and even Argentine zamba, all filtered through her signature acoustic approach.

The title suggests a journey inward, peeling back layers to reveal something raw and personal.

For digital nomads working from Colombia, this album provides a beautiful soundtrack that bridges the familiar and the new.

A singer on stage; Katie James tours her new album across Colombia. (Photo: internal archive)

The Cali Concert: An Intimate Night at Bellas Artes

The most anticipated date on the tour for many is her Cali show on July 31, 2026.

She will perform at the Sala Antonio María Valencia, a well-known concert hall within the Bellas Artes complex, a cultural landmark in the city dedicated to arts education and performance.

This venue, whose full name is the Instituto Departamental de Bellas Artes, sits in the heart of Cali and is easily reachable by taxi or ride-hailing apps.

The concert promises a full-band format, meaning Katie James will be accompanied by musicians who bring the album’s diverse rhythms to life.

Organizers describe the evening as an intimate concert featuring new songs alongside highlights from her career.

For expats based in Cali or nomads passing through, this is a chance to experience a high-quality live performance in a respectful, seated venue rather than a crowded bar.

National Tour Dates and Other Cities

The ‘Bajo mi Corteza Tour’ is not limited to Cali.

Katie James is taking the album to other Colombian cities, with confirmed dates including Bucaramanga, the capital of Santander department known for its parks and modern vibe.

While the full itinerary is still being rolled out, expats in Medellín, Bogotá, and Pereira should watch her official social channels for potential additions.

Tickets for the Cali date are available through Tuboleta, one of Colombia’s primary ticketing platforms, which foreigners can access online with an international credit card.

If you are new to buying tickets locally, Tuboleta allows you to purchase digitally and present a QR code at the door, avoiding the need for physical pickup.

Practical Tips for Expats and Nomads Attending

Attending a concert in a Colombian city like Cali requires a bit of local know-how.

The Bellas Artes venue is located in a central area, but it is wise to arrange your return transport in advance, as hailing a taxi on the street late at night is not recommended for safety reasons.

Use apps like Didi or Uber, which operate widely in Cali, and expect a short wait after the event.

Ticket prices in Colombian pesos have not been officially confirmed for this show, but similar cultural events at Bellas Artes typically range from COP$60,000 (~US$15) to COP$120,000 (~US$30).

Doors usually open an hour before the listed showtime, and seating is often assigned, so check your ticket for a specific chair number.

The concert will be conducted primarily in Spanish, but Katie James often addresses her bilingual audience in English as well, making the experience welcoming for non-Spanish speakers.

Consider dining before the show in the Granada or San Antonio neighborhoods, both popular with expats and offering a range of international and local cuisine.

Why This Tour Matters for the Expat Community

Live music is one of Colombia’s greatest gifts, but language barriers can sometimes make local concerts feel inaccessible to foreigners.

Katie James bridges that gap naturally, offering a cultural experience that does not require fluent Spanish to appreciate.

Her music also serves as an entry point into Colombian folk traditions, from the accordion-led vallenato to the hypnotic gaita flutes of cumbia.

For digital nomads seeking authentic experiences beyond coworking spaces and expat bars, this tour represents a genuine connection to Colombia’s creative soul.

It is a reminder that the country’s cultural calendar is rich and varied, and that some of its most compelling artists speak directly to an international audience.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where can I buy tickets for Katie James in Cali?

Tickets for the July 31 concert at Sala Antonio María Valencia are available through Tuboleta, Colombia’s major online ticketing platform. You can purchase them with an international credit card and receive a digital QR code for entry.

What musical styles does Katie James perform?

She performs a blend of Colombian and Irish folk music. Her new album ‘Bajo mi Corteza’ includes bolero, cumbia, vallenato, tonadas llaneras, and Argentine zamba, all delivered with an acoustic, sensitive sound.

Is the concert suitable for non-Spanish speakers?

Yes. Katie James is bilingual and often speaks to the audience in both Spanish and English. Her music’s emotional delivery and diverse rhythms make it highly accessible even if you do not understand all the lyrics.

World.title: Costa Rica Pilgrimage: A Guide to the 2026 Romería
World.content:
Expats & Nomads · Costa Rica

Key Facts —Dates Official activities run July 23 to August 3, 2026. The main walk happens overnight from August 1 into August 2. —Route Pilgrims walk roughly 22 km from San José, often starting near La Sabana park, to the Basílica de los Ángeles in Cartago. —Purpose The pilgrimage honors the Virgen de los Ángeles, known as La Negrita, the patroness of Costa Rica. —Safety Authorities deploy 500 police officers and the social-security fund runs 25 medical posts along the route. —Traffic Major road closures and heavy traffic are expected on the San José-Cartago corridor on August 1 and 2.

The Costa Rica pilgrimage, known locally as the Romería, will bring hundreds of thousands of people to the streets on August 1 and 2, 2026. This annual walk to the Basílica de los Ángeles in Cartago is the country’s largest religious tradition and a profound cultural moment.

San José, Costa Rica, where the Romería pilgrimage to Cartago begins. (Photo: internal archive)

What Is the Romería?

The Romería is a massive walking pilgrimage honoring the Virgen de los Ángeles, Costa Rica’s patroness. The diminutive dark-stone statue, affectionately called La Negrita, is housed in the Basílica de los Ángeles in the city of Cartago.

This year’s events carry extra significance as they fall within the centennial of the Virgin’s pontifical coronation. Official activities are scheduled from July 23 through August 3, 2026.

Planning Around the Costa Rica Pilgrimage

The central act of devotion occurs overnight from Saturday, August 1, into Sunday, August 2. Pilgrims walk roughly 22 kilometers from the capital, San José, to the basilica in Cartago.

Many participants start their journey near La Sabana Metropolitan Park, around Calle 42 on the western edge of downtown San José. The flow of walkers continues through the night, arriving in Cartago by morning.

A traditional procession carrying the image to the Nuestra Señora del Carmen cathedral is scheduled for 9:00 a.m. on August 2. The atmosphere is peaceful, communal, and deeply reflective.

Costa Rica; the country honours its patron saint, the Virgen de los Ángeles, each August. (Photo: internal archive)

Road Closures and Traffic Impacts

For expats and digital nomads, the most immediate practical impact will be on transportation. The main San José-Cartago corridor will see major road closures and extremely heavy traffic from August 1 through August 2.

Driving between the capital and Cartago during this window is strongly discouraged. Public bus schedules on this route will also face significant delays and detours.

If you live in Cartago or the eastern suburbs, plan to stay put or move around locally on foot. If you need to reach the airport or western suburbs from Cartago, consider traveling before July 31 or after August 3.

Safety and Medical Support

Authorities treat this as a major public safety operation. The government deploys 500 police officers along the entire walking route to manage crowds and traffic.

The Costa Rican Social Security Fund, known as the CCSS, activates a special medical plan for the event. It operates 25 health posts along the route from July 18 through August 2.

These posts provide first aid, hydration, and rest areas for pilgrims. The event is overwhelmingly safe, but the sheer volume of people means walking with the crowd requires patience and sturdy footwear.

How Foreigners Can Observe Respectfully

The Romería is a religious act, not a tourist parade. Foreigners are welcome to observe and even walk, but the focus must remain on the pilgrims’ spiritual purpose.

Dress modestly and avoid turning the walk into a photo opportunity that intrudes on prayer. Many pilgrims walk in silence, recite rosaries, or carry small tokens of gratitude.

If you choose to walk a portion of the route, stay to the side and let faster groups pass. Bringing your own water and snacks is wise, though vendors and volunteers often offer free refreshments along the way.

Speaking Spanish is not required, but a quiet, respectful demeanor is. A simple “buenos días” or a nod of acknowledgment goes a long way in sharing this communal experience.

Practical Tips for Digital Nomads

If you work remotely from the San José metro area, treat August 1 as a no-travel day. Internet and power services remain stable, but moving between neighborhoods will be slow.

Coworking spaces in Escazu, Santa Ana, or San Pedro will operate normally, but reaching them from Cartago or Curridabat could be impossible. Plan your work schedule to avoid any need for cross-valley trips.

For those curious about the culture, watching the walkers pass through San José on the evening of August 1 is a moving experience. The crowd moves with a quiet intensity rarely seen in daily life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can foreigners participate in the Costa Rica pilgrimage?

Yes, respectful observers are welcome. The walk is a religious act, so maintain a quiet demeanor, dress modestly, and avoid intrusive photography.

What roads are closed during the Romería?

The main San José-Cartago corridor faces major closures and heavy traffic on August 1 and 2. Avoid driving between the capital and Cartago during this period.

Is the Romería safe for expats?

Yes, it is a peaceful mass event. Authorities deploy 500 police officers and the CCSS runs 25 medical posts along the route to ensure safety.

World.title: SushiFest Colombia 2026: A US$6 Sushi Crawl for Expats

Expats & Nomads · Colombia

Key Facts —Dates July 30 to August 9, 2026 —Cities Bogotá, Sabana Centro municipalities, and Cali —Participating restaurants More than 25 across the three zones —Signature dish price COP$23,900 (~US$6.05) per author roll —Official information hub sushifestoficial.com

SushiFest Colombia 2026 turns the country’s capital, its northern suburbs, and the salsa capital of Cali into a budget-friendly sushi crawl from July 30 to August 9. More than 25 restaurants will serve exclusive author rolls at a fixed price of COP$23,900 (~US$6.05) each, giving expats and digital nomads an affordable way to explore Colombia’s fast-evolving Japanese-fusion scene.

Sushi. Colombia’s SushiFest runs July 30-August 9 across Bogotá and Cali. (Photo: internal archive)

What Exactly Is SushiFest Colombia?

Now in its sixth edition, SushiFest Colombia is an annual gastronomic circuit that invites Japanese and fusion restaurants to design a single, never-before-seen creation called an author roll. Each roll is offered only during the 11-day festival window and priced identically across all participating venues.

An author roll is a chef’s signature festival dish, typically blending classic Japanese sushi techniques with Colombian ingredients and global flavors. Think lulo-infused rice, crispy patacón (fried green plantain) toppings, or ají amarillo-spiked mayonnaise wrapped around fresh tuna or tempura shrimp.

The festival is organized by a Bogotá-based culinary events team and has grown steadily since its launch. In 2026, the footprint expands firmly into Cali, while the Sabana Centro zone brings suburban restaurants north of Bogotá into the fold for the first time as a named cluster.

The Bogotá Scene: Where the Festival Lives

Bogotá anchors the festival with the largest concentration of participating restaurants. The city’s dining landscape has absorbed a strong Japanese influence over the past decade, visible in the sheer number of ramen bars, izakayas, and high-end Nikkei counters scattered across Chapinero, Usaquén, and Zona G.

For foreigners, Bogotá’s SushiFest stops are easy to reach using ride-hailing apps like Uber or DiDi. Most venues cluster in the north-central neighborhoods where many expats and nomads already live or co-work, making lunchtime sushi runs a realistic weekday plan.

The festival’s fixed COP$23,900 (~US$6.05) price point feels especially sharp in Bogotá, where a standard specialty roll at a mid-range restaurant often runs between COP$35,000 and COP$55,000 (~US$8.85-US$13.90). That gap makes the author roll an unusually good value for a chef-driven dish.

Bogotá, one of SushiFest’s host cities. (Photo: internal archive)

Sabana Centro: Suburban Sushi Worth the Short Trip

Sabana Centro is a collection of municipalities just north of Bogotá, including Chía, Cajicá, Zipaquirá, and Sopó. These towns have seen a wave of new restaurants open as more Colombian families and foreign residents move to the area for its quieter, greener lifestyle.

For a digital nomad based in Bogotá, a SushiFest outing to Sabana Centro doubles as a half-day escape. You can pair a sushi lunch in Chía with a visit to the famous Salt Cathedral in Zipaquirá, or simply enjoy a slower-paced meal in a suburban plaza.

Restaurants in this zone often have more outdoor seating and easier parking than their Bogotá counterparts. If you are craving fresh air and a festival roll, the northern suburbs deliver both without requiring a full weekend commitment.

Cali’s Sushi Boom and the Festival’s Expansion

Cali joins SushiFest Colombia 2026 as a full participant, reflecting the city’s growing appetite for Japanese and Nikkei cuisine. Over the last five years, Cali has quietly built a reputation for creative sushi spots that mix Pacific-coast seafood with local fruit and chili heat.

The city’s warm climate and relaxed pace give the Cali leg of the festival a different rhythm. Expect open-air restaurant settings, tropical-fruit-forward rolls, and a dining culture that starts later in the evening than in Bogotá.

For expats living in or visiting Cali, the festival offers a structured way to explore neighborhoods like Granada, San Antonio, and Ciudad Jardín. These areas are already popular with foreigners for their cafes and nightlife, and several are likely to host participating restaurants.

How to Find Restaurants and Order Like a Local

The official website, sushifestoficial.com, publishes the full list of restaurants, their author roll descriptions, addresses, and delivery options. Most venues offer on-site dining, takeaway, and delivery through platforms like Rappi, which is widely used across Colombia.

To order, simply ask for the “roll de autor” or “roll del SushiFest” when you arrive or place your delivery. Because the festival roll is a limited-time item, it is usually featured prominently on a separate menu card or the first page of the digital menu.

English-speaking staff are not guaranteed outside of Bogotá’s most international zones, so knowing a few Spanish phrases helps. A friendly “¿Tienen el roll del SushiFest?” (Do you have the SushiFest roll?) is usually all you need to get started.

Payment is straightforward. All restaurants accept Colombian pesos in cash or by card, and contactless payment is common. At COP$23,900 (~US$6.05) per roll, two people can share three or four rolls and still keep the total bill under COP$100,000 (~US$25.30) before drinks.

Practical Tips for Expats and Digital Nomads

Plan your sushi crawl around Colombia’s typical meal times. Lunch service runs from roughly 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., while dinner starts around 7:00 p.m. and can stretch past 10:00 p.m., especially in Cali.

Tipping is not mandatory in Colombia, but a 10% voluntary propina is common and appreciated. Some restaurants include it on the bill as a suggested amount, but you can always decline or adjust it.

If you are working remotely, many Bogotá and Cali restaurants have reliable Wi-Fi and are laptop-friendly during off-peak hours. A late lunch at 2:00 p.m. on a weekday often means a quieter dining room and a table you can keep for an extra hour.

Transportation between festival zones is manageable. Bogotá to Chía takes about 45 minutes by car, while a domestic flight from Bogotá to Cali runs just over an hour and costs roughly COP$150,000-COP$250,000 (~US$38-US$63) one way when booked in advance.

Keep an eye on the festival’s Instagram account, linked from the official site, for real-time updates, pop-up events, and chef takeovers. These unannounced additions often become the most memorable meals of the festival.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a ticket to participate in SushiFest Colombia 2026?

No. There is no entry fee or festival pass. You simply visit any participating restaurant, order the author roll for COP$23,900 (~US$6.05), and pay only for what you consume.

Can I order SushiFest rolls for delivery?

Yes. Most restaurants offer delivery through Rappi or their own channels. Check the official site at sushifestoficial.com for each restaurant’s delivery options and coverage zones.

Is SushiFest Colombia suitable for vegetarians or people with dietary restrictions?

It depends on the restaurant. The festival does not require a vegetarian author roll, but some chefs create plant-based or cooked options. Review the roll descriptions on the official website before choosing a venue.

The legendary musician brings his ‘Fearless: Anthology 1965-2025’ show to the Movistar Arena with Irish singer Imelda May as a special guest.

Ronnie Wood Buenos Aires: The Historic Solo Debut

For the first time, Ronnie Wood steps out from the massive shadow of the Rolling Stones to headline his own show in Argentina. The concert at the Movistar Arena in the Villa Crespo neighborhood marks a rare intimate encounter with a rock legend.

The show is billed as ‘Ronnie Wood & His Band’ and traces a wild musical journey from 1965 to 2025. Irish vocalist Imelda May joins him, adding a rockabilly and blues edge that complements Wood’s raw guitar style.

Securing Your Tickets Safely

Tickets went on general sale on Wednesday, July 29, 2026, exclusively through the official website movistararena.com.ar. Prices start at AR$95,000 (~US$72) plus a service fee, making it a premium but accessible experience for a living legend.

Expats and nomads should avoid third-party resellers or social media offers to prevent scams. The Movistar Arena uses digital tickets linked to a DNI or passport number, so have your identification ready when purchasing.

If the show appears sold out, keep checking the official site as production holds are often released closer to the date. The venue’s system is foreigner-friendly, accepting international credit cards with a straightforward online checkout.

Buenos Aires, host city for Ronnie Wood’s Movistar Arena concert. (Photo: internal archive)

Getting to Movistar Arena

The Movistar Arena sits on Avenida Corrientes, one of Buenos Aires’ main cultural arteries, in the Villa Crespo neighborhood. It is a modern, circular indoor stadium with a capacity of around 15,000, known for superb sightlines and acoustics.

For digital nomads based in Palermo, the venue is a short ride away. The B Line subway drops you at the Dorrego station, just a few blocks from the entrance, making it the most efficient route to avoid the city’s notorious traffic.

Ride-hailing apps like Uber and Cabify operate widely in Buenos Aires, though you must have a local SIM or data plan to use them. If you take a traditional black-and-yellow taxi, agree on the fare or ensure the meter is running before you depart.

Pre-Show Dining and Drinks

Villa Crespo has quietly become a foodie hub, offering everything from traditional parrillas to trendy plant-based cafés. Arrive early to enjoy a classic Argentine steak at a spot like Lo de Charly, just a short walk from the arena.

For a quicker bite, the streets around Avenida Corrientes are lined with pizzerías serving thick, cheesy slices of pizza al molde. Cash is still king in smaller eateries, so carry some pesos for a smooth transaction.

The arena itself has multiple concession stands inside, but lines can be long. A beer inside typically costs around AR$6,000 (~US$4.50), so a pre-show drink at a nearby bar is both cheaper and more atmospheric.

What to Expect Inside the Show

Doors usually open two hours before the announced showtime, giving you plenty of time to find your seat and soak in the atmosphere. The ‘Fearless’ anthology promises deep cuts and solo hits spanning six decades, not just Rolling Stones classics.

Imelda May’s powerful voice and stage presence make her more than just an opening act. She and Wood share a genuine musical chemistry, often duetting on blues standards that highlight their mutual love for raw, unfiltered rock and roll.

Phone signal inside the dense concrete structure can be patchy, so download your digital ticket before arriving. The venue has a clear bag policy, and professional cameras are strictly prohibited, so leave your bulky gear at your accommodation.

Making a Night of It in Buenos Aires

After the final encore, you will spill out onto Avenida Corrientes, which buzzes late into the night. The neighborhood is generally safe, but keep your phone tucked away and be aware of your surroundings, just as you would in any major global city.

Many expats and nomads use the concert as a chance to explore Buenos Aires’ legendary nightlife. From Villa Crespo, you are a short ride to the speakeasy bars of Palermo Hollywood or the traditional milongas where locals dance tango until dawn.

November weather in Buenos Aires is late spring, with warm days and pleasant evenings perfect for walking. A light jacket is advisable after midnight, especially if you plan to wait for a ride on the street.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I buy Ronnie Wood Buenos Aires tickets at the door on November 6?

Official sales are online only through movistararena.com.ar. The box office may open on show day only if tickets remain, but a sellout is likely for this historic debut.

Is the Movistar Arena safe for a solo foreign traveler?

Yes, the Villa Crespo area is busy and well-lit during events. Use official taxis or ride-hailing apps for departure, and keep valuables out of sight while walking on Avenida Corrientes.

Will Ronnie Wood play Rolling Stones songs at the solo show?

The ‘Fearless’ anthology covers his entire career from 1965 to 2025. While the setlist focuses on his solo work and collaborations, a few Stones numbers are a strong possibility given his deep connection to the material.
