World.title: Football and politics, brought to you by Big Business (and energy drinks)
World.content:
In “United Passions” — which really should have been called “Balls” — Blatter is played by Tim Roth, a fine actor who admitted he took the role to pay for his kids to go to college. If the movie was, heaven help us, ever updated to include Infantino’s tenure, surely the role would go to either Stanley Tucci or the ghost of late Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin.

Infantino has, you will doubtless be aware, decided to sell football off to the highest bidder, with FIFA publishing a proposal that would privatize the World Cup’s commercial operations. A venture capital firm headed by Josh Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is lined up as the lead investor in the proposed deal. Of course it is. The scheme is known as FIFA Forward Enterprise or FFE — although FFS seems rather more appropriate.

I, for one, am looking forward to the Raytheon World Cup of 2038 in South Sudan, where the 18-karat gold trophy depicting two human figures holding up the Earth is replaced by a cheap plastic bobblehead of Trump with his pants around his ankles.

But not everyone is so keen on Infantino’s plan. Glenn Micallef, the EU’s sports commissioner, pointed out that football “isn’t baseball,” which is very perceptive of him. It’s also not cross-country skiing, knitting or a cauliflower.

Micallef’s point is, of course, that football hasn’t — and shouldn’t — reach the level of commercialization of American sports, although it had a damn good go during this summer’s World Cup with the introduction of hydration breaks sponsored by Powerade.

But the further monetization of sports feels inevitable; it is entertainment, after all. Will politics go the same way? When, for example, will we see EU summits sponsored by Red Bull, the European Commission midday briefing brought to you by Xanax, or Germany sponsored by sausages in a glass jar?

World.title: Houthis vow 'full escalation' as Saudi Arabia launches Red Sea coalition
World.content:
Yemen's Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi threatened Saudi Arabia with "full escalation," hours before Riyadh announced a new maritime defence coalition designed to counter the Iran-backed group's expanding campaign against Red Sea shipping.

 

"The indicators show that the Saudi side is heading towards full escalation, and we will respond to its full escalation with full escalation," al-Houthi said in a lengthy televised address on Thursday.

The Houthi leader also warned that aircraft Turkey sold to Saudi Arabia would "turn into unsellable stock once they are shot down in Yemen," saying Riyadh had already lost American MQ-9 drones and Chinese-supplied aircraft in the conflict.

Al-Houthi accused Saudi Arabia of keeping Yemen in a deliberate cycle of economic and political crisis, saying what he described as "US-Saudi aggression" had been under way since the Saudi-led coalition intervened in the war in 2015.

The de-escalation period had come only after "a clear Saudi-American failure" to break Yemeni resistance, according to al-Houthi.

He denied the movement — formally known as Ansar Allah — was a proxy for Iran or any other power, saying it acted solely in defence of Yemeni sovereignty and resources.

"Our people are not disputing the Saudi regime over anything that belongs to it, but over our land, our resources, our freedom and our dignity," he said.

The Houthis, who came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile, are part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance.

The Axis is a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

Saudi maritime coalition

Saudi Arabia's response to the Houthi maritime campaign took institutional form on Thursday, when Riyadh hosted representatives from 43 countries — out of 51 invited — and the EU to discuss the creation of a new Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition.

Fourteen countries signed a founding statement, including Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt, Jordan and Djibouti.

The coalition is designed to protect freedom of navigation and energy supply routes through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

Saudi Arabia will serve as the founding and leading state and will host the coalition's permanent headquarters, joint command and operational centre.

The Saudi defence ministry said the door remained open for additional countries to join after completing their national procedures.

The EU, which already runs the Aspides naval protection mission in the Red Sea, sent a delegation but did not sign the deal. It was not immediately clear how the new Saudi-led coalition would interact with the existing EU mission.

Blockade and tanker attack

The Houthis announced last week a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia on 20 July. In the meantime, the movement claimed responsibility for an attack on a Saudi oil tanker off the port of Jazan on the kingdom's southern Red Sea coast.

Riyadh has since launched air strikes on Houthi military positions and infrastructure in Hodeidah, Yemen's main Red Sea port.

On the drone attack on the US-owned LNG terminal at Egypt's Damietta port on Wednesday, the Houthis issued a flat denial.

The group's Saba news agency quoted an official saying reports of the attack were "incorrect" and that the movement's operations were "limited to targeting Saudi Arabia in response to the siege and ongoing aggression against the Yemeni people."

Egypt's Cabinet confirmed on Thursday morning that preliminary investigations had found a drone caused the fire. No group has claimed responsibility.

The Bab al-Mandeb Strait, linking the southern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, carries roughly 12% of global maritime trade.

The Houthis disrupted it severely with their campaign against Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was in a show of support for Palestinians.

The Bab el-Mandeb campaign comes at a time when the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's other critical chokepoint, remained under blockade after the US-Iran war continued following the collapse of the interim deal between the two sides.

World.title: 'This is our wake-up call': EU crisis chief slams climate deniers after French fires
World.content:
European Commissioner for crisis management Hadja Lahbib has dismissed claims by climate sceptics that Europe's increasingly destructive wildfire seasons are simply the result of hot summers, describing the blazes sweeping southern Europe as "the biggest wake-up call" in years.

 

"Climate change is not knocking at our door. It is here," Lahbib told Euronews in an exclusive interview from France.

"They (climate deniers) should come here and see the situation, open their eyes."

Her comments echo those of EU competition chief Teresa Ribera, who told Euronews that climate deniers are "giving alcohol to alcoholics and telling them it's okay to drive." In a separate interview with Euronews, she described it as "dangerous and stupid."

The Belgian Commissioner spoke after touring the fire-ravaged Gironde region by helicopter, where more than 42,000 hectares have been destroyed in what French authorities describe as one of the country's worst wildfire disasters in decades.

Her comments come as wildfires continue to burn across southern Europe, with France, Greece, Turkey and Tunisia all requesting European emergency assistance in recent weeks.

The growing number of cross-border requests reflects what Brussels increasingly views as a continent-wide climate security challenge rather than a series of isolated national emergencies.

Lahbib argued that Europe must focus not only on expanding its firefighting capacity but also on investing more heavily in prevention and preparedness.

She defended the European Commission's proposal to allocate €10.7 billion for preparedness measures under the EU's next long-term budget, arguing that Europe must become better at anticipating disasters instead of simply responding to them.

Greater focus on forest management

Lahbib noted that this year's wildfire season began unusually early, with the Netherlands — not typically considered a wildfire hotspot — becoming the first country to activate the EU Civil Protection Mechanism on 30 April.

"The season started on 30 April," she said. "We don't know yet how it will end."

Piotr Borkowski, Executive Director of the European State Forest Association, said the outlook for the Mediterranean, particularly the Iberian Peninsula, remains "very negative".

"Early summer heatwaves have caused extreme moisture loss in vegetation, making it much more susceptible to ignition and allowing fires to spread rapidly and intensely," Borkowski told Euronews.

"This points to a high likelihood of extreme wildfires developing, at least until the end of the summer season."

Borkowski said the current wildfire season is not being driven by any single new factor, but by long-term structural problems.

"The issue is structural and territorial," he said.

"The problem lies in the abandonment of traditional landscape management and primary land uses such as forestry, agriculture and livestock farming, alongside the evolving climate conditions."

World.title: Solar eclipse accommodation demand surges in Spain and Iceland. Is it too late to book?
World.content:
On 12 August 2026 a total solar eclipse will cross the North Atlantic before passing over Iceland and Spain.

 

It will be the first total eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999 – and travellers are excited.

Booking data shows that it could become one of the biggest demand events of the year.

Where to see the solar eclipse in Europe?

Unlike most travel trends, eclipse demand is remarkably concentrated. Travellers don't spread evenly across a country. They “flock to the narrow corridor where the eclipse can be seen in full, creating a sharp but short-lived spike in bookings”, explains rental industry data site AirDNA.

In Spain, the path of totality crosses a broad swathe of the north and east, including Zaragoza, Valencia, Bilbao, and Palma de Mallorca, while Madrid and Barcelona sit just outside it.

In Iceland, the path crosses the country's west and south, giving much of its tourism infrastructure a front-row seat to the event.

Bookings spike in Spain and Iceland for solar eclipse

In Iceland, around 5,000 of the country's 8,300 available rental listings, or 60.6%, sit inside the path of totality. Because the eclipse crosses Iceland's busiest western and southern regions, it covers the majority of the country's active short-term rental inventory.

In contrast, of Spain’s 382,400 available listings, 86,300 (22.6%) fall within the path of totality. While that share is much smaller than Iceland's, the absolute volume is enormous.

Spain's in-path supply alone is more than 16 times the size of Iceland's entire short-term rental market.

In Spain, demand within the path is pacing 7.4% ahead of last year for the booking period of 11-12 August, while demand across the rest of the country is down 5.4%. The contrast suggests the uplift is being driven by the eclipse rather than a broader improvement in Spanish travel demand.

Zaragoza leads with demand pacing 123% ahead of last year, followed by Logroño (109%), Burgos (65%), Valladolid (64%), and León (63%).

The pattern is even stronger in Iceland. Demand within the path is pacing 56.9% ahead of last year, compared with 19.2% across the rest of the country. In other words, demand inside the path is growing almost three times faster than elsewhere. Kópavogur is pacing 48% ahead of last year, while Reykjavík is up 44%.

There's a behavioural split too: Spain draws short one-to-three-night eclipse trips from nearby Europe, while long-haul Iceland sees travellers build four-to-six-night vacations around the event.

Data from AirDNA is backed up by Hotels.com, which shows lodging searches are rising sharply for destinations along the path of the eclipse, with year-on-year demand up by as much as 250%.

As astro-tourists race to secure accommodation, the site found the most popular European eclipse-viewing destinations are Reykjavík (+250%), Valencia (+140%) and Mallorca (+15%).

Is it too late to book accommodation for the solar eclipse?

Big events can mean limited hotel availability and rising room rates, especially as travel dates get closer.

Consider staying in lesser-known neighbourhoods or alternative destinations within the eclipse viewing zone to find better availability and rates. In Spain, you could try A Coruña, while in Iceland look for rural accommodation just outside popular spots like Reykjavík.

As for types of lodging, expand your search beyond hotels and rental properties to rural guesthouses and campsites.

Don’t forget about cruises. The path of totality will pass over large areas of the ocean, and ships can reposition themselves for prime viewing.

Remember that as the event approaches, free cancellation deadlines will expire, so you may find accommodation reappearing on booking sites at the last minute as other travellers change plans.

World.title: Summer 2026: Ferragosto brings 17.5m tourists to Italy and €9bn in direct spend
World.content:
Alongside the extreme heatwaves, Italy is also approaching the height of its summer: Ferragosto. According to CNA Turismo e Commercio's estimates, between 1 and 23 August a total of 17.4 million tourists will be travelling in Italy, including 8.4 million Italians and nine million visitors from abroad.

 

Average stays will be around 4.5 nights and direct tourist spending will exceed €9 billion.

Taking into account the effects on other sectors, including accommodation, food services, retail, crafts, as well as culture and services, the overall economic impact over the coming month could surpass €15 billion.

These estimates form part of a summer which, according to forecasts, could top 224 million overnight stays in total in the July-September quarter, generating spending of around €27 billion.

August, and particularly the week of Ferragosto, thus confirms itself as one of the most promising periods for tourism, but data from an EMG survey show that travellers' habits are changing. Less than 40% of those going on holiday will depart in August, choosing instead to travel in June, July or September.

So what are the preferences of tourists, Italian and foreign, who will come to the country for their 2026 holidays?

Italian holiday habits: where they are going and when

According to the EMG survey, almost 12.3 million Italians have already travelled in June and July, while another 8.2 million will do so in September, confirming a trend seen in recent years towards a more even spread of holidays across the summer months.

Most of the Italians interviewed continue to choose domestic destinations, while 6.2 million will travel elsewhere in Europe, favouring Spain, Greece and France.

The study also shows that for transport and accommodation travellers will spend an average of €939 each. As for how they travel, more than half of respondents (55.5%) prefer trips in their own car, while the second most popular option is flying.

Holiday homes are the preferred choice for 7.6 million Italians, equal to 28.9% of holidaymakers, while traditional tourism, combining hotels, farm stays and B&Bs, is chosen by 38.2% of the sample, around 11 million people.

The most popular destinations for travellers in Italy

According to CNA Turismo e Commercio, the most popular destinations remain seaside resorts, followed by cities and historic villages, mountain areas, lakes and spa towns. However, demand is growing for holidays that offer different experiences, such as hiking, cycle tourism or attending concerts, festivals, food fairs and shows.

The role of Italy's food and wine excellence, its crafts and cultural heritage also remains decisive in choosing a destination.

For all these reasons, Rome will continue to exert a strong international pull, together with the coasts and villages of Lazio, the Conero Riviera, the Costa dei Trabocchi, the Gran Sasso area and the Molise coastline.

In the Mezzogiorno, some of the most sought-after destinations remain the Amalfi Coast, Salento, Tropea and the Costa degli Dei, Matera and the Lucanian Dolomites, while for seaside resorts the main draws are Sardinia and Liguria, with the Riviera dei Fiori.

Where foreign tourists come from and how much they spend

To gain a clearer picture of foreign travellers' preferences, spending and consumption provide important indicators. According to data from the Bank of Italy, total spending in 2025 was almost €57 billion, up 4.8% on the previous year.

This positive balance is reflected in the volume of people recorded, with 477 million overnight stays – in tourism, the total number of nights spent in a place – and 185 million arrivals, corresponding to the number of people who checked in to accommodation facilities.

Figures for the first half of 2026 are also encouraging: the Interior Ministry reports a 4.43% increase in arrivals compared with the same period last year. In particular, the foreign component has risen by 6.45%, while domestic tourism is up by 1.97%.

Looking at the same period, spending by foreign travellers in Italy (€4.5 billion) has increased by 2.1%, while spending by Italian travellers abroad (€2.7 billion) has fallen by 1.6% compared with April 2025.

Forecasts for summer 2026 therefore confirm Italy's competitive position in the European landscape. Some 54% of European travellers name Italy as their preferred destination for their summer 2026 holidays, putting it ahead of Spain (51%), Greece (46%) and France (41%).

According to the Tourism Ministry, demand for accommodation is being driven by seaside destinations, with an occupancy rate (the percentage of beds taken compared with those available) of 82%, while among cities the highest rates are seen in Rome, Naples and Venice.

The main flows, according to the ministry, come chiefly from the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany.

World.title: Exclusive: MEPs demand Infantino appear before European Parliament over FIFA's private investment plan
World.content:
The European Parliament is set to call FIFA President Gianni Infantino for a hearing over his controversial plan to allow private investment in its competitions, which has met with furious backlash in the football world and led European football associations to threaten a boycott of the next World Cup.

 

A draft letter obtained by Euronews and now circulating among MEPs from all political groups is inviting Infantino to answer lawmakers' questions directly, in the spirit of "transparency and democratic accountability that FIFA has itself publicly endorsed".

The plan involves setting up a new company to run FIFA's competitions and selling stakes of up to ​20 percent to external investors, among them Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared is US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

FIFA claims that all the national associations should have a chance to consider the plan in an "open and democratic" consultation, and is currently resisting calls to suspend the project coming from the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) and the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF).

The European Parliament’s political groups are concerned about FIFA’s project.

“The global good that is the World Cup is not anyone’s to sell," Irish MEP Barry Andrews told Euronews. "We are extremely concerned by FIFA’s recent announcement.”

The draft letter, which was circulated by Polish conservative MEP Bogdan Zdrojewski, has been sent to the leading MEPs of the Parliament’s Culture and Education committee for their approval. It directly blames Infantino for FIFA’s leadership and calling on him to appear before them to explain himself.

“We wish to express our grave concerns at FIFA’s current leadership, governance and direction,” the MEPs wrote, adding that it is “a betrayal of your duty to football stakeholders – most notably fans – across the world”.

EU lawmakers are concerned by the lack of consultation over the plan, and by the fact that it has been announced ahead of FIFA’s presidential election year in 2027. Infantino has already declared he will stand for re-election.

“Let us be very clear: the European Parliament will not stand by if FIFA is treated as a personal asset, campaign fund and political career ladder,” the MEPs wrote.

“These developments come against a wider backdrop of public outrage regarding FIFA’s – and your own specifically – political relationships, commercial practices and decision-making.”

If the letter is approved by a majority of the committee's lawmakers, the invitation to Infantino will be formally sent in September.

World.title: Spanish PM Sánchez: Ceuta migrant crisis 'a violation of territorial integrity'
World.content:
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez sent a message of support to the people of Ceuta in the wake of the migration crisis, saying that "the whole of Spain stands with them" and acknowledging the "anguish" the population is going through. "We understand the emotional strain the people of Ceuta are under," he said.

 

Sánchez described what had happened as a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity", an action which, he said, "deserves our reproach and our condemnation at the strongest possible level".

The prime minister also recalled that Melilla had experienced a similar in 2021, and stressed that both autonomous territories require the government's utmost attention.

In this context, he gave assurances that the government will mobilise all the resources needed to preserve security in Ceuta. "The Spanish government will deploy all the resources of the state to guarantee security in Ceuta," he said.

As for the origins of the crisis, Sánchez argued that, according to the talks held with the Moroccan authorities, the increase in irregular entries is due to "a self-interested reading by criminal gangs" of a court ruling on the repatriation of people who enter by swimming, as they consider there is no physical border in such cases.

Finally, the prime minister defended the government's migration policy and pointed out that Spain has managed to steadily reduce irregular migration flows. "We have seen a systematic reduction of more than 30% in irregular arrivals," he concluded.

World.title: Ceuta migrant surge reignites Europe's right-wing assault on Spain's migration policy
World.content:
European right-wing figures blame the escalation in the Ceuta enclave on Spain's naturalisation policy, in what left-wing parties call opportunistic attacks.

 

On Thursday, thousands of migrants stormed the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, prompting Spain's Interior Ministry to declare a national emergency and mobilise troops to restore order in the autonomous city.

Leading right-to-centre figures across Europe have seized on the escalation, accusing Madrid of losing control of its border and blaming the mass illegal crossings on Spain's extraordinary regularisation of hundreds of thousands of migrants.

"Appalling situation at the Spanish border. The devastating images are the direct consequence of the pull factor of massive regularisation doubled with instrumentalisation of illegal migration," Manfred Weber, leader of the centre-right European People's Party (EPP), wrote on X.

Right-wing attacks

The "pull effect" is the idea that generous reception conditions and other migration policies make a destination country more attractive, encouraging more arrivals. Here, the suggestion is that Spain raised expectations of future regularisations.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, of the hard-right Brothers of Italy party, went as far as proposing the suspension of the Schengen area with Spain, and announced extraordinary measures to defend Italy's border.

"On illegal immigration, we will not yield an inch: defending the borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriations will continue to be the line of this Government," Meloni wrote on X.

The pull factor is not a scientifically proven phenomenon. Academic consensus holds that migration is driven primarily by "push" factors, such as war and political repression, while pull factors tend to stem from labour and welfare prospects.

Yet with most EU countries veering to the right, Spain has bucked the trend with a massive regularisation programme that drew over 1 million applicants — and the ire of right-wing politicians.

"The images coming from Ceuta show how the Madrid Government's decision to grant Spanish, and therefore European, citizenship to over 500,000 irregular immigrants is profoundly wrong and encourages human trafficking," Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani wrote on X.

Right-wing politicians in other member states argue that Spain has a responsibility to defend Europe's external borders, since the resulting migratory inflows ultimately spill over into destination countries.

"Spanish authorities have recorded 50,000 illegal border crossings in Ceuta so far, with Germany likely the destination for most of these migrants," Alice Weidel, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany, wrote on X. "Germany must prepare itself: borders must be secured and rejections rigorously enforced."

Jordan Bardella, France’s radical right leader who is the president of the Patriots for Europe Group in the European Parliament, sent a letter on Friday, seen by Euronews, asking President Roberta Metsola “to hold an urgent debate on the developments in Ceuta and on the failure of the European Union's migration policies.”

Left-wing pushback

For left-wing politicians in Spain and abroad, these attacks are opportunistic. The Ceuta crisis, they say, has simply given critics an excuse to target the only alternative to right-wing migration policy left standing in Europe.

"In Europe, right-wing attitudes have prevailed in picturing migrants as a threat," said MEP Juan Fernando López Aguilar (Spain/S&D), a former justice minister under the Zapatero government.

"Meaning that the humanitarian approach, which is the characteristic response of left-wing-led governments, as is the case of the Spanish government led by Pedro Sánchez, is not only being marginalised, it's increasingly isolated," López Aguilar said.

Experts such as Haizam Amirah Fernández, director of the Centre for Contemporary Arab Studies, point out that the current influx of irregular migrants into Ceuta could hardly have happened without the tacit approval of Moroccan authorities.

Another explanation points to human traffickers exploiting a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that pushbacks cannot be applied to migrants intercepted at sea while swimming into Ceuta or Melilla, as opposed to those climbing the border fence.

Spanish authorities say the recent regularisation applied only to people already on Spanish territory six months before applications opened, meaning new arrivals would not benefit from the measure.

For MEP Cecilia Strada (Italy/S&D), the attacks from the centre to the far-right reflect a clear intent to target Spain, since the Sánchez government has shown it is possible to have a credible progressive leader capable of managing migration flows by tackling its causes rather than its effects.

"This is right-wing propaganda at its worst. Before a humanitarian emergency with tens of deaths and an unknown number of missing people, one would expect European solidarity rather than instrumental attacks aimed at political profiteering," Strada told Euronews.

Vincenzo Genovese contributed to the reporting.

World.title: Solitude standing: Stonehenge opens lottery for unique solo experience at English Heritage site
World.content:
Millions of people have walked around Stonehenge over the past century, but almost none have experienced Britain's most iconic prehistoric monument in complete silence. That is about to change.

 

Throughout August, English Heritage is giving one visitors each day the opportunity to step inside the UNESCO World Heritage site's famous stone circle before opening hours, with exclusive access reserved solely for the winners and their group.

The unique experience comes at no additional cost. Anyone who books a Stonehenge ticket through the English Heritage website at least 72 hours before their visit will automatically be entered into the daily prize draw.

FILE: A summer solstice reveler enjoys a moment within the iconic ancient circle at Stonehenge, 20 June, 2026, England AP Photo/Alberto Pezzali

Each winner will be left alone at the monument to spend 20 minutes inside the 5,000-year-old stone circle between 9:10am and 9:30am, before the site opens to the public.

Although a member of the Stonehenge team will accompany the lucky recipient to answer questions about the site's history and conservation, no other visitors will be present during the exclusive access period.

Stonehenge has welcomed millions of visitors since becoming a ticketed attraction around 125 years ago but, according to English Heritage, the honour of having the monument entirely to oneself has traditionally been reserved for heads of state, celebrities and participants in premium private tours.

This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to stand within the ancient stones with no one else around, soaking up the atmosphere and spirituality of this remarkable place Georgia Butters Head of Operations for Stonehenge at English Heritage

The private visit offers a rare chance to appreciate details often missed during a standard visit, from the sheer scale of the megaliths to ancient carvings that cannot be seen from the public pathways. Winners will also have the chance to take photographs and videos without the usual crowds in the background.

And if that's not enough to tempt you into trying your luck, each member of the winning party will receive a complimentary breakfast roll and a hot drink.

What you need to do

Stonehenge attracts around 1.3 million people every year, making it one of England's most popular heritage attractions.

While visitors can already book premium Stone Circle Experience tours that are shared with groups of up to 52 people, the August prize draw is the first initiative to offer complete privacy inside the ancient monument at no extra cost.

Book your Stonehenge ticket through the English Heritage website at least 72 hours before your visit in August, and you'll automatically be entered into the daily prize draw.

World.title: FIFA plans: Infantino under pressure as senior advisor quits
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino was under increasing pressure on Friday as global opposition grew to his controversial private investment plans and one of his senior advisors resigned in protest.

The football world was rocked earlier this week when it was reported that FIFA, the sport's global governing body, was planning to sell a stake in a new commercial subsidiary to private equity investors close to US President Donald Trump, prompting widespread outrage.

European football's governing body, UEFA, quickly condemned the plans with its 55 member associations voting unanimously to boycott future FIFA competitions — including the next men's World Cup in 2030 but potentially starting with the under-20 Women's World Cup on September 5 — were the plans to be implemented.

The Europeans soon received backing from CONCACAF, the regional body representing 41 North American and Caribbean football federations, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) with its 47 members, technically robbing Infantino of majority support among FIFA's 211 member associations (MAs).

FIFA advisor Cordeiro steps down

On Friday, the pressure on FIFA grew even more when Carlos Cordeiro, former head of the United States Soccer Federation (USSF) and more recently a senior advisor to both Infantino and President Trump during this year's men's World Cup, resigned in protest at the plans, which he described as a "bad deal for football."

Carlos Cordeiro (center left) was a senior advisor to US President Trump (left) and FIFA President Infantino (second from right) Image: Daniel Torok/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

In statement, Cordeiro, 69-year-old former partner at Goldman Sachs, questioned why FIFA needed to seek private equity investment at all given its unprecedented World Cup profits, and criticized a lack of transparancy, oversight and due process surrounding the plans.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources," he said. "The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt. The FIFA president himself has highlighted the $15 billion in revenue generated [during FIFA's last four-year World Cup cycle] between 2022 and 2026.

"If member associations believe additional investment is needed to develop the game, FIFA already has the financial capacity to provide that support from its existing resources. Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification."

FIFA: 'Nobody is selling football'

Despite the opposition voiced by UEFA, CONCACAF, AFC and individual national associations including the German Football Federation (DFB), FIFA had earlier doubled down on its plans to establish "FIFA Forward Enterprise" (FFE).

The subsidiary, valued by FIFA at around $20 billion (€17.5 billion), would be responsible for FIFA's commercial rights like broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing contracts for its competitions, including the World Cup, but would sell a non-controling minority stake worth $4.2 billion to private equity investors.

The proposed investor consortium is expected to be led by "Thrive Eternal," a fund run by "Thrive Capital," in turn founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US ​President Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

"Nobody is selling football. ‌This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA said in statement earlier on Friday, slamming "incorrect media reports" without issuing clarification and what precisely was wrongly reported, and insisting that it would proceed with its "consultation process" — with member associations obliged to make a decision by September 19.

"FIFA [member associations are] now being asked to believe that outside investors are needed to unlock greater value. I do not accept that proposition," said Cordeiro.

"Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions: Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?"

UEFA lead FIFA criticism, threaten World Cup boycott

UEFA and its president Aleksander Ceferin have been at loggerheads with FIFA for some time Image: Mike Egerton/PA/picture alliance

European football's governing body UEFA, which has been at loggerheads with FIFA and Infantino for years and criticized the global body throughout the recent World Cup over expensive ticket prices and the Folarin Balogun red card affair, had come out publicly in opposition to the plan within an hour of it first being reported by the Financial Times and Times on Tuesday.

"No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership," UEFA said in a statement after a unanimous vote by its 55 member associations at a hastily convened emergency meeting on Thursday.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product ... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale," the statement added.

CONCACAF and AFC join opposition

Shortly after, North America's soccer body CONCACAF also unanimously rejected the FIFA plan, though it stopped short of threatening a boycott by its 41 members.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) also issued a scathing letter to its 47 member associations and warned the FIFA proposal would never succeed without the support of all six regional blocs.

"While the immediate debate centres on FFE, the AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal. Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed," read an AFC statement.

"This is not the first occasion where major stakeholders have been confronted with significant initiatives after the direction of travel appears to have already been determined. Such an approach undermines confidence in FIFA's governance framework and diminishes the authority of its statutory bodies."

African body CAF said it would convene an executive committee meeting next week to look into the proposal, saying in a statement:

"CAF is committed to continue consulting and working together with its Member Associations, FIFA, other Football Confederations and stakeholders in support of increasing financial and other resources for the development and growth of football in Africa and worldwide," it said.

South America's CONMEBOL has yet to comment, but its president, Alejandro Dominguez, recently spoke out in favor of a further expansion of the men's World Cup to 64 teams in 2030 — which would effectively result in all but one South American nations qualifying automatically.

Amid the outrage over the investment plans, the Press Association reported on Friday that FIFA was indeed pursuing precisely such an expansion, with a decision expected by August 14.

Germany: What has the DFB said?

German DFB President Bernd Neuendorf can't see the FIFA plan going forward without UEFA on board Image: Ulrich Wagner/picture alliance

Germany's mass-circulation Bild paper reported that key UEFA officials including German Football Federation (DFB) President Bernd Neuendorf had already discussed the FIFA plans via a video call on Wednesday.

"We must not lose the fans' support, but we are well on the way to squandering that," Neuendorf told public broadcaster ZDF, adding:

"I consider this to be extremely problematic and unacceptable. If UEFA rejects this request [for approval of the plan], then it is dead, because I believe that you won't be able to find any investor who would be willing to go ahead with this project if UEFA is out."

It's not the first time that the DFB has crossed swords with FIFA. At the Qatar World Cup in 2022, Germany's men's team covered their mouths before a game in protest at not being allowed to wear a "One Love" rainbow armband to support LGBT+ rights.

German football also has recent experience of similar private equity investment proposals.

In 2024, the Bundesliga was forced to abandon plans to sell a share of its TV rights to foreign investors due to fan protests that included tennis balls and remote control cars with smoke bombs being thrown onto pitch during matches.

Such actions are commonplace in German football, where the so-called 50+1 ownership model bars single investors owning a majority stake in a club and ensures fans retain more power than elsewhere in the world.

Read more on Germany's response to the FIFA plans here.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Ceuta: Spain scrambles after thousands breach exclave border
World.content:
07/31/2026 July 31, 2026 Ceuta government head estimates that 60,000 people have entered

The head of the regional government in the autonomous city, Juan Jesus Vivas, has told reporters that crowds equivalent to well over half of Ceuta's population have entered the city.

"Estimates indicated that around 60,000 people have entered our city as a result of this event," he said. "This figure shows that it is impossible to absorb such pressure. It is absolutely impossible."

Vivas had on Thursday called on Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to declare a national emergency and to deploy military troops to assist with securing the border, issuing this appeal at roughly the same time as much larger crowds started to circumvent the border checks.

World.title: German court rules that AI music firm Suno violated copyrights
World.content:
Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, says the verdict has "global significance," as Suno is also directed to pay yet-to-be-quantified damages.

The Munich Regional Court ruled on Friday that Suno AI, a US-based company, which generates songs from text prompts. has violated copyrights and has to disclose illicit revenues.

The lawsuit initiated in January 2025 by GEMA, Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, argued that Suno trained its AI models on copyrighted music without obtaining licences or compensating its rights holders.

According to the ‌verdict, Suno will have to pay damages that have yet to be quantified. Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options, including an appeal.

"This is a verdict of global significance," Gema CEO Tobias Holzmueller told Reuters.

A closely watched case

The lawsuit has been closely watched, as it is one of the first major cases anywhere in the world to test how traditional copyright law applies to AI music training and AI-generated music outputs. Among Suno's arguments was the fact that the German court does not have proper jurisdiction to rule on AI model training activities that occurred exclusively inside the United States.

Paul McCartney & Rosalia: Strategies for surviving AI music To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The proceedings could help determine whether AI music companies must obtain licenses before training their models on copyrighted songs, and whether AI-generated music that closely resembles existing songs constitutes copyright infringement.

"Our goal is not to clear Suno from the face of the earth, but obviously to get into licensing negotiations on an eye-to-eye level, which was not possible with Suno so far," explains GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmüller, who describes the company as "by far the largest and commercially most successful of all AI music models." He believes Suno pursues a much more aggressive business strategy than its competitors.

Tobias Holzmüller, CEO of GEMA Image: Sebastian Linder

The outcome of this case is also linked to another central question: How should creators be compensated when their music is used to train generative AI systems?

At the forefront of the battle to protect artists' rights

Last year, GEMA won a related case against OpenAI before the same court. It found that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI models on copyrighted song lyrics and reproduced them via ChatGPT without authorization.

OpenAI was ordered to cease and desist from reproducing the works in the model, to disclose information and pay damages. But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.

In contrast to that decision, the current lawsuit does not focus on song lyrics, but on entire music pieces.

One of the aspects that makes this lawsuit important is that it has not been initiated by a private company or record label, but rather by a music collecting society, notes Martin Senftleben, professor of intellectual property law at the Amsterdam Law School.

Such initiatives "are particularly important because, by definition, you could say that they're more inclusive," Senftleben tells DW. "You can become a GEMA member even if you're not a very well-known high-profile artist or composer. And that means there's a chance of bringing remuneration for AI users to a much broader group of rights holders."

GEMA represents more than 95,000 composers, songwriters and music publishers in Germany, along with over 2 million rights holders worldwide.

How did GEMA present its case?

GEMA claims that Suno trained its AI on copyrighted music without permission or payment to songwriters, composers and publishers represented by the German music collecting society. GEMA also says that the US-based company is commercially benefiting from those works without compensating the artists.

Suno's music creation platform generates songs through simple text prompts. Users can describe the mood, style or genre they desire and the system synthesizes a structured track — complete with lyrics, vocals and instrumentation — in under a minute.

The songs that are produced by the AI system can be very similar to copyrighted songs.

During the court proceedings, GEMA demonstrated this by prompting Suno AI to create tracks with the original lyrics of different popular songs in its repertoire, including "Forever Young" by Alphaville, "Mambo No. 5" by Lou Bega, "Daddy Cool" by Boney M., "Cheri Cheri Lady" by Modern Talking and "Atemlos durch die Nacht," written by Kristina Bach and popularized by Helene Fischer.

Along with the lyrics, the plaintiffs prompted the desired musical style and the title of the work, without specifying any melody, rhythm, harmony or arrangement.

Yet the resulting AI songs are very similar to the original works.

German music: From 'Schlager' to 'Deutschrap' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Suno admits that the original songs at the center of GEMA's lawsuit are among the numerous pieces that were used to train the AI model.

AI companies such as Suno claim that the ingestion of data for AI training can be done freely on the basis of what is known as "fair use" in the US and the "text and data mining exception" rule in the EU.

But whether such licence-free AI training is allowed under copyright law remains heavily contested globally. In different lawsuits around the world, courts are now examining whether such uses harm the economic market of the original creators through unfair competition.

"The novelty in the lawsuit is that GEMA does not focus on the AI training stage," explains Senftleben. By basing their claim on tests that demonstrate that these AI systems generate songs that have similarities with copyright-protected works from their repertoire, "they bridge this gap between relevant use now taking place in AI training, and the market harm done at AI output level," he adds.

Why AI shouldn't be compared to human brains

Anyone who wants to become a good musician needs to listen to and learn from existing music.

Similarly, the AI industry claims this analogy applies to how their models are trained — by absorbing countless creative works in order to generate new ones.

But from the rights holders' perspective, AI models are rather copying and commercially exploiting their works.

This argument that an AI learns from music and is inspired by it like a human being is "completely ridiculous," notes Tobias Holzmüller. "These are concepts that come from the human brain and have been designed for the human brain, and not for a machine that is able to digest millions of sound files in split seconds. I mean, just the amount of sheer data — they say it's data; for us, it's music — that these machines have swallowed up and then digested and are now spitting out, this is completely incomparable to what's happening in a human brain.

"To humanize these machines by using these concepts is not logical — and it's certainly not moral."

Suno users generate around 7 million tracks every day Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Across Suno's platform globally, users collectively generate roughly 7 million songs per day. Around 75,000 of them end up on streaming services daily, adds Holzmüller. "This is definitely where it's not sustainable anymore, but really toxic for the music ecosystem."

"If you want to create a sustainable model where you accept that AI music is here to stay, but at the same time, that it shouldn't push human-created music out of the market, the only way to tackle this is to put a price tag on the output," says the CEO of GEMA. "Because otherwise you will have free-of-charge AI sounds that will outcompete human music in a lot of circumstances."

For example, music in movie scores or social media has until recently allowed various songwriters to make a living. For Holzmüller, if licences lead to an increase in costs in AI-created sounds to a point that they are as expensive as human-created songs, it could provide a level playing field. "Then — it's my firm belief — people will continue to use human music, because it has this additional element."

This article was originally published on July 30, 2026 and was updated on July 31, 2026 to reflect the court's ruling.

Edited by: Brenda Haas

World.title: Military flare-up between Houthis and Saudi Arabia challenges relative calm in Yemen
World.content:
Riyadh and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are on the brink of renewed conflict. Could war-ravaged Yemen be drawn into a wider Middle East war?

Military strikes between Yemen's ruling Houthi militia and Saudi Arabia have flared for the first time since the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Houthis agreed to a truce in 2022.

Tensions rose earlier in July when the Iran-backed Houthi group claimed that Saudi Arabia had struck the airport in Sanaa to prevent Houthi leaders from returning after the funeral of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. Saudi Arabia, for its part, has denied the attack and claimed that the Houthis were spreading false claims.

Since then, the Houthis have struck facilities owned by Saudi Arabia's national oil company, Aramco, forcing the Jazan production site to shut down. The blow hit Saudi Arabia particularly hard as Jazan has been serving as an export hub to circumvent Iran's ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis also announced that they would block Saudi-linked commercial vessels from passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden — prompting several ships to turn back this week. The narrow strait has become more significant for Saudi oil exports due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis said they fired missiles at the oil tanker NCC Ghazal.



Riyadh, meanwhile, confirmed it had struck Houthi targets in response to the threats to Red Sea shipping. On Thursday, Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry announced that it was establishing a multinational defense maritime coalition to protect key shipping routes. According to the statement on X, 14 countries had already confirmed participation.

Will Yemen be dragged into the wider US-Israel war in Iran?

"The current escalation appears to be driven primarily by the Houthis," Elham Manea, a political scientist and adjunct professor at the University of Zurich specializing in Middle East and Gulf studies, told DW.

For her, it is increasingly obvious that the Houthis, who are part of Tehran's "Axis of Resistance" — Iran's paramilitary proxy groups including Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and Shiite militias in Iraq who all call for the elimination of the United States and Israel — have abandoned their strategy to refrain from joining the wider US-Iran war.

The conflict, which began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, has since engulfed much of the Middle East. This week, Saudi Arabia also joined US forces in striking infrastructure used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

"The Houthis are now using the wider US–Iran confrontation to revive unresolved issues with Saudi Arabia," Manea said, noting that "the Houthi strategy is to raise costs for Riyadh and strengthen their own bargaining position."

She added that Houthi leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi's recent speeches are quite revealing in this respect. "While they express solidarity with Iran, they increasingly justify escalation through specifically Yemeni demands directed at Riyadh."

Above all, the Houthis want Saudi Arabia to end its air and sea blockades on Houthi-held territory which have not been fully lifted despite the truce in 2022.

Yemen's Houthi group declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia, and reportedly attacked vessels Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Some hesitation to return to a full-scale war

Despite the current escalation, it is still too early to conclude that Saudi Arabia has abandoned its policy of restraint in Yemen, Manea cautioned. "Since the 2022 truce, Riyadh's priority has been to extricate itself from the Yemen war and create the regional stability needed for its broader economic transformation 'Vision 2030'," Manea said.

Sherwan Hindreen Ali, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict monitoring watchdog ACLED, also still sees some leverage before a return to a full-scale war. "The Houthis have left some room for de-escalation," he noted in a recent analysis . Two ships bound for China carrying Saudi crude passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait without incident on 23 July, suggesting that at least some ships are exempt from the Houthi blockade, he wrote.

Michael Stephens, senior Middle East security advisor at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, points to previous experiences between the factions. "If Saudi Arabia and the Houthis go back to war in Yemen, I suspect the ending will be the same: A lot of money spent, many lives lost, and eventually the realization that both sides will have to talk," he told DW. In his view, the Houthis are unlikely to be defeated without a costly invasion.

The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and Saudi Arabia escalated in 2015 when Saudi Arabia joined the war in Yemen in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Since the truce in 2022, the Houthis have largely consolidated their position as the de facto rulers of Yemen. However, the country remains divided: The Houthis control the capital Sanaa, most of northern Yemen and parts of the center. The UN-recognized government, now based primarily in Aden and exiled in Saudi Arabia, controls parts of the south and east, while the separatist Southern Transitional Council dominates much of the south. Tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

Yemen's population still suffers from the consequences of the war in Yemen between 2014 and 2022 Image: Essa Ahmed/AFP

Fighting exacerbates Yemen's dire humanitarian situation

Human rights organizations point out that the population is yet to recover from those years of devastating war. According to the United Nations, Yemen is still suffering from one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

"Since 2014, the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis have destroyed food and water infrastructure across Yemen and they have also blocked food, fuel, and humanitarian aid from reaching segments of the population," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "The impact on the population has been clear," she said.

The conflict has left more than half of the population without adequate access to basic food needs and many people are already on the brink of starvation, Jafarnia told DW. Her worry is that "as warring parties escalate the conflict again, there is a real risk that they will also again weaponize civilians' basic needs."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

World.title: Spain's PM heads to Ceuta after thousands breached border
World.content:
Thousands of people continued pouring into Ceuta from Morocco during the night, after Spanish police lost control of the border. Unofficial estimates from security forces suggested more than 40,000 gained entry in a day.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, his interior minister and military personnel were bound for the North African enclave of Ceuta on Friday, a day after thousands of people gained irregular entry to the Spanish territory.

At least 18 people died as tens of thousands of people rushed into the small coastal city, many of them drowning but some also perishing in a stampede to cross the breakwater fence.

Authorities are still puzzling over what prompted such large crowds to suddenly seek entry.

Spanish authorities were overwhelmed by the latest influx Image: Atlas/REUTERS

People 'still entering' Ceuta despite reinforcements

Preliminary estimates suggest that tens of thousands gained entry on Thursday alone as the Guardia Civil lost control of the border to Morocco.

Spanish news agency EFE cited security force estimates as saying around 49,000 people had entered Ceuta irregularly from Morocco in recent days. Around 24 hours earlier, prior to the mass breach, estimates had stood at between 1,500 and 2,000.

Government sources have yet to release an no official figure as yet. Reuters attributed the same figure of 49,000 to the interior ministry, while AFP cited a police source as saying more than 40,000 were thought to have entered.

Ceuta's population is roughly 85,000 people.

"People are still entering. The reinforcements that have arrived are only helping the injured and other humanitarian efforts," Rachid

Both EFE and AP said correspondents observed some people seeking to return to Morocco on Friday, with the city's small migrant reception center completely overwhelmed.

Border police said they had to switch their focus to trying to keep people safe, with at least 18 people killed in the chaos Image: Atlas/REUTERS

Prime miniser and interior minister expected in the city

Spain's government said on Friday that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez would accompany Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska on an impromptu visit to the city.

The Interior Ministry also said on Thursday that it was deploying millitary personnel to assist at the border.

Spain has two enclaves, Ceuta and Mellila, on the North African coast bordering Morocco.

Local authorities had already noted an uptick, but on a much smaller scale, of people seeking to swim around Ceuta's border checks prior in the days prior to Thursday's rush.

A similar crisis hit Ceuta in 2021, when more than 8,000 people are thought to have entered irregularly in a matter of days.

Italy, Finnish minister question Spain's Schengen status

Italy and France both announced they would temporarily boost border checks with Spain.

"In response to the situation observed in the Ceuta enclave, I gave instructions as of last night to immediately strengthen the controls at the Spanish border. Furthermore, I am activating the Rapid Intervention Border Force for in-depth checks," French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez wrote online early on Friday.

Italian right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had on Thursday called for the "suspension" of Spain's Schengen membership. On Friday, Finland's Interior Minister, a member of the right-wing populist Finns party that's the second-largest in Helsinki's coalition government, said she supported the proposal.

"Spain has completely failed to protect the Schengen Area's external border from infiltration. This cannot continue. All European countries must support Meloni's proposal," Mari Rantanen wrote on Friday.

World.title: Dozens of miners killed in coal mine explosion in Pakistan
World.content:
Several miners remain unaccounted for following the Balochistan coal mine blast, with authorities saying the explosion was likely due to the build up of methane gas.

An explosion in a coal mine southwestern Pakistan has killed 34 miners, according to Pakistani authorities.

Thursday's deadly explosion, which likely occurred due to a build-up of methane gas, took place in a mine near Quetta, the capital of Pakistan's Balochistan province. Around 40 miners were on site at the time of the blast.

What are officials saying?

Balochistan's senior government mining official Ghani Baloch said that rescue operations would continue until all miners were found, but added that "the chances of finding anyone alive diminish" due to methane explosions rapidly consuming oxygen.

Rescue efforts were taking place at a depth of 4,000 feet (1,219 meters), the chief inspector ​of mines said.

Expressing his condolences for the victims, Balochistan's Minister for Mines and Minerals Shoaib Nosherwani said there would be compensation of 500,000 Pakistani rupees (roughly $1,800, €1,570) for each victim's family. He promised an investigation into the cause of the explosion, as well as a safety review of coal mines across Balochistan.

Coal miners and relatives were waiting for the news of at the site Image: Banaras Khan/AFP

Why do accidents keep occurring in Pakistan's coal mines?

Deadly accidents are common in Pakistan's coal mining industry, and especially so in Balochistan. In 2024, a methane gas coal mine explosion killed 12 in the province.

Balochistan is Pakistan's largest, but poorest province. It is rich in raw materials — such as coal, gold and copper — but its mines are often hazardous, lacking proper ventilation, systems for gas-monitoring and other safety measures.

Despite the risk, thousands continue to work in the mines, driven by high unemployment and a lack of other opportunities in Balochistan.

Labor associations have repeatedly called for improved safety standards and stricter enforcement in the mining sector.
