"I can think of no better word to put at the very centre of education, because a future that leaves a single child behind is not a future that benefits anyone in this country," National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter said on Friday morning.

The commissioner promised that she would come back to Garma every year for as long she held her role and "tell the truth about how this nation is treating our children".

Sue-Anne Hunter told the crowd Indigenous children "learn to walk in in two worlds, yet they walk in many". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"Our children learn in two worlds, yet they walk in many," she told those gathered in Arnhem Land for the nation's largest Indigenous meeting.

"They carry language, kinship, ceremony, country in one hand and the classroom and the curriculum and the exam in the other.

"We ask a great deal of them."

On Friday young people from local schools played AFL and took part in workshops as part of the festival's education fair.

Education was the focus on Friday. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Opposition makes the most of PM's absence

Shadow Education Minister Julian Leeser said the "single best thing" to improve outcomes across the board in Indigenous affairs was to get kids to attend and complete school.

Leeser says Albanese has 'lost his direction' on Indigenous affairs Shadow Indigenous Australians Minister Julian Leeser has accused the federal government of being "adrift" on Indigenous affairs during his speech at the Garma Festival.

"In Australia an Aboriginal boy is more likely to go to jail than university," he said.

"But, as I have said before, on graduation, an Indigenous graduate will earn at least on par with a non-Indigenous graduate."

Mr Leeser took advantage of Anthony Albanese's absence from the event, telling the audience that the prime minister had "lost his direction on Indigenous affairs" since the Voice referendum failed.

"We all know where the prime minister stood on the Voice," he said.

"I stood there too. But since the defeat of the Voice he just hasn't gotten off the mat."

Albanese's absence looms large over Garma The theme of this year's Garma Festival is "bukmak", a Yolŋu word meaning "everyone", but the prime minister's decision not to attend may indicate how high on the government's priority list Indigenous affairs sit.

Mr Albanese's absence from Garma this year has not gone unnoticed.

"Mob want to hear directly from our prime minister, showing leadership and the ability to come and listen," Kerrupmara and Gunditjmara man Travis Lovett told the ABC's Tahnee Jash.

"Our people — as First Peoples, but also Australians — have expectations that when politicians say they will do something, that they deliver on that."

Lia Finocchiaro announces a major Aboriginal land tenure agreement to help save the remote town of Nhulunbuy ahead of its Rio Tinto mine winding up. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro used her first keynote address at the festival to announce a major Aboriginal land agreement to help the remote town of Nhulunbuy ahead of the winding up of the Rio Tinto mine there.

As ABC Darwin's Matt Garrick reported, the announcement comes as long-term businesses prepare to sell up and leave the region, including Woolworths.

It also coincided with the 50th anniversary of the NT Aboriginal Land Rights Act.

Penny Wong and Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy are set to address the festival on Saturday. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy have arrived at the festival and will be giving a keynote speech on Saturday.

The most popular guest at Garma on Friday was not a politician. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Bluey steals the show

The most popular guest at Garma on Friday was not a politician, but a beloved Australian dog.

One boy brought his puppy to meet Bluey. (ABC News: Dana Morse)

Bluey was welcomed onto country with a ceremonial dog dance and posed with kids and adults, including ABC Chair Kim Williams, throughout the day.

One child even brought his puppy, Rio, to meet the cartoon blue heeler.

Later tonight people will gather to watch Bluey episodes translated into Yolŋu Matha. They were produced at Yolŋu Radio's studio in north-east Arnhem Land.

Garma attendees will gather to watch episodes of Bluey that have been translated into Yolŋu Matha. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Bluey's dad, Bandit, is voiced by Dimathaya Burarrwanga, a founding member of Yolŋu surf rock band King Stingray, and her mum, Chilli, is voiced by Yolŋu educator Rosie Mununggurr.

"It was really fun to be able to put the oldest language into an actual Bluey scene," Burarrwanga told the ABC.

"I think it's really important for the Yolŋu kids to be able to understand what Bluey means."

Loading Instagram content

ARDS Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Julia Wormer said the communities across north-east Arnhem land were thrilled about the translated episodes.

"Absolutely, the kids have been so excited to watch it," she said.

"There's been so much excitement across all of the communities in north-east Arnhem Land and it's created a real sense of pride in these children.

"I have already heard from other language groups that they would love more translations in their own languages."

World.title: It's easy to see why Australia brought a psychiatrist to Glasgow
World.content:
When Kiana Elliott finished fourth for the second straight Commonwealth Games, to say the Australian weightlifter was crestfallen would be an understatement.

Over the Birmingham and Glasgow Games, a combined 11 kilograms of weight on the bar kept the gymnast from back-to-back bronze medals.

After faltering on the 118-kilogram clean and jerk that could have secured her third place on the podium, Elliott sat on the Armadillo stage and dropped her head to a depth only permitted by her background as an elite gymnast.

Australian weightlifter Kiana Rose Elliott after missing her last lift at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old was distraught to have missed the medals just as she did four years ago in Birmingham, graciously speaking to the media in barely a whisper as she tried to maintain her composure.

For a woman who embodies strength and power, her vulnerability was incredibly affecting.

"It's just a moment in time, and you're just hoping that everything will be there," she said.

"Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't."

Competition weightlifting is a tricky beast, with athletes having to walk a fine line between lifting the most they can, while also ensuring they can fall into the optimum weight class.

Kiana started weightlifting after an injury. Now, she's a Comm Games athlete Kiana Elliott thought gymnastics would be her pathway to the podium, but turned to weightlifting after an injury forced her to retire.

Elliott was in the 71kg weight class in Birmingham four years ago. At last year's Commonwealth Championships, she won as a 58kg competitor. In Glasgow, she lifted as a 63kg athlete.

She said it was a "really tough decision" to go up to the higher weights where the lifts need to be bigger, but she did it for her mental health.

"In Australia we do sport and we do life, and I needed my brain and my mind for the rest of my life," she said.

"Pushing my body fat down that low was not a sustainable thing for me, so I chose the competitive option.

"Weightlifting is about lifting weights, it's about lifting more weights, it's not about being a smaller person, and I'm proud that I chose the difficult option and fought my hardest.

"This isn't the end of my story. I'm not done yet."

Kiana Elliott is a study in determination while lifting. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

But for this one moment it was. As painful as the result was, she could drop her shoulders and unclench her jaw in an enormous release of emotion.

"So much has gone into this and while I was hoping for a podium result, I think it's just all a culmination of all that's gone into this starting to come out," she said of her reaction after the competition.

"There's so much to process as part of this; there's more stuff to do when I get home. I think I just need to breathe a sigh of relief and move on."

It was five minutes of wholly self-aware introspection, spoken like a woman who has done and will continue to do a lot of work on her brain.

That reflects an emphasis for the entire Australian team, so much so that, for the first time, they have an in-house psychiatrist travelling with the team.

Australian team psychiatrist Adam Deacon. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Adam Deacon is part of a varied team of experts embedded within the team, with one of the floors of the Team Aus HQ effectively transformed into a mini hospital ward.

"We'd be very surprised if any other country has matched the standards that have been established here in the headquarters," Dr Deacon told ABC Sport.

"There's an extraordinary range of talented, experienced people who are able to cater to the broad needs of the athletes.

"It's really just a pop-up sports medicine clinic where all aspects are covered as it would be in a regular clinic."

The margins are fine and tension is high at meets like the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

And while massage therapists, physios, nutritionists and dietitians have been working to keep Australia's 255 Commonwealth Games athletes physically fit over 10 days of intense competition, Dr Deacon is focusing on their minds.

"I think most athletes would argue when they're in a good mental space they're more likely to perform at a high level," he said.

"And you could argue they can't compete at a high level unless their mental health is well. So I think that's a necessary focus."

The team has travelled with sports psychologists before but, after consultation with the athletes, feedback was received that many of them, with their own dedicated psychologists, would like to stick with those programs.

Dr Deacon provides a different, more clinical than therapeutic, service.

"The athletes are people before they're athletes and they can experience everyday issues and concerns and mental health challenges as we all do," he said.

"There are particular things that arise in this environment, in terms of performance or lack of performance or perceived failure, and that can be really, really challenging for the athletes and also the staff.

Failure is a part of sport, but it's still hard to swallow. (Supplied)

"Injuries, illness, these sort of interruptions are not necessarily expected or anticipated, and that can be enormously stressful, and that's where an acute level of crisis response is sometimes necessary."

Unlike footy players who get to take it "one week at a time", for many the Commonwealth Games is the culmination of four or more years of tireless, single-minded work.

Elliott's teammates Chloe Perkins, who missed her 48kg weight, did not even get a chance to compete, and Brenna Kean and Ridge Barredo, both suffered nasty injuries while on stage at the Armadillo.

Dr Deacon, of course, did not reveal any of the people he had spoken to in the team, but the weightlifters like Elliott, Perkins, Kean and Barredo perhaps best exemplify the risky prospect of this high-stakes quadrennial cycle.

Some athletes seek him out, some are referred to him, and for some he attends their competition for a little extra care.

Whatever form it takes, the Australian team is lucky to have him here.

World.title: Drug driver who killed 20yo in stolen car to have sentence reduced
World.content:
The speeding drug-driver who received the maximum penalty for killing Matthew McLuckie in a head-on crash in Canberra's south four years ago will have her sentence reduced.



Warning: This story contains a confronting image of a car crash.

Shakira Adams, 24, was sentenced to 14 years' jail, with a nine-year non-parole period after pleading guilty to culpable driving causing the death of the 20-year-old in May 2022.

The ACT Court of Appeal is set to re-sentence Adams after the Director of Public Prosecutions conceded the offending did not fall within the "worst category" of culpable driving.

While both parties agreed Adams should be re-sentenced, they disagreed over how much weight should be given to her disadvantaged background, traumatic brain injury, guilty plea and new evidence about her conditions in custody.

Shakira Adams (far right) pleaded guilty to culpable driving causing death and driving a stolen car. ( ABC News: Ethan French )

Driver was unlicensed, affected by drugs

Adams was 19 when she drove a stolen car almost 20 kilometres across Canberra before crashing head-on into Mr McLuckie's vehicle on Hindmarsh Drive as he drove home from work in 2022.

The ACT Supreme Court found she was unlicensed, affected by methamphetamine and travelling at up to 186 kilometres per hour and on the wrong side of the road immediately before the crash.

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum sentenced Adams to the rare maximum penalty for culpable driving causing death, describing the offending as "one of the utmost seriousness".

She found Adams's driving had placed other road users at risk "almost every second" during the journey.

While Adams suffered a severe traumatic brain injury in the crash she caused, the court heard she continued using methamphetamine afterwards, which the chief justice said made her a "significant danger to society" and "more dangerous" than she had been at the time of the crash.

"I cannot be confident that Ms Adams would not attempt to drive if she were at liberty in the community. That is a risk that cannot be taken, and will not be taken through me," she said.

Shakira Adams was travelling at a speed of up to 186km/h, on the wrong side of the road, when the two cars collided. (ABC News)

Sentence 'excessive': defence lawyer

Adams's barrister, Kristin Edwards SC, argued the original 14-year sentence was "manifestly excessive" and said greater weight should be given to Adams's disadvantaged upbringing, youth, traumatic brain injury and prospects of rehabilitation.

She relied on new evidence, including an ACT Corrective Services report that found Adams's placement in the Alexander Maconochie Centre's management unit breached her human rights and risked exacerbating her brain injury.

She told the court her client remained housed in segregation in the management unit because she could not safely be accommodated in the general prison population, leaving her in a "punitive environment", "lonely and isolated" from other prisoners.

Ms Edwards said the unit was not designed for female inmates or long-term accommodation and was usually used as a form of punishment or protection.

Matthew McLuckie was killed in a car crash while driving home from work on May 19, 2022. (Supplied)

She argued Adams's traumatic brain injury and complex medical needs, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychiatric care, could not be adequately managed there.

The court heard Adams had experienced panic attacks and engaged in self-harm because "she hoped she'd die".

Ms Edwards argued the risks identified at Adams's original sentencing had "now crystallised".

She said hopes Adams could be transferred to a more suitable interstate facility had not materialised, and a transfer also did not guarantee she would receive better care.

Ms Edwards also challenged Chief Justice McCallum's finding that Adams remained a danger to the community, describing it as "particularly puzzling" and urged the sentencing judges to consider her adverse childhood.





Matthew McLuckie (centre) with his brother Joe and parents Amanda and Tom. (Supplied) "She's a 19-year-old who was from a disadvantaged background. She's at a very early stage to be considered someone who is beyond hope, who is beyond redemption," she said.

Reduced sentence to be handed down

Counsel for the Director of Public Prosecutions Elizabeth Ruddle SC accepted Adams's disadvantaged background and cognitive impairment reduced her moral culpability and agreed the case did not fall within the worst category of culpable driving.

However, she argued those factors did not diminish the objective seriousness of the offending.

In the nine minutes before the crash, Adams was seen travelling at extreme speeds, ran a red light, drove on the wrong side of the road and overtook other vehicles.

"Due to the appellant's extreme recklessness, a young law-abiding citizen is dead," she said.

"The driving conducted in this case was at the extreme end of culpable driving.

"Given the nature of the driving, it's surprising it took nine minutes for a fatal collision to occur."

The prosecution did not dispute the ACT Corrective Services report that found Adams's placement in the Alexander Maconochie Centre's management unit breached her human rights, but argued it was a "technical breach" that arose from her placement.

Ms Ruddle said authorities continued to pursue a transfer to New South Wales, where specialist treatment remained available, and argued Adams's rehabilitation prospects remained uncertain because of her cognitive impairment and history of dangerous driving.

Justices David Mossop, Darryl Rangiah and Andrew Muller reserved their decision, with a new sentence to be handed down at a later date.

Australian Paul Trainor has lost his 80kg semifinal against England's Dimeji Shittu.

He lost the first two rounds on all cards so was hunting a third-round knockout.

Shittu was dancing away dropping his hands and hyping up the crowd and Trainor couldn't find the knockout.

"I probably go ta little reckless in the last round just swinging for his head but that's what needed to happen.

"You kind have to throw defence to the wind and look to take one or two to give one and just hope you're hitting him harder than he's hitting you.

"I've been on the other end when you've won two rounds and you just go for a walk he doesn't wanna take the risk and lose his chance at a gold medal.

(ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I understand it, it's part of the sport. You can't take anything in the ring personally, it's all just business."

Trainor is a medallist at his debut Games, but it's a bittersweet moment right now.

"The mission was win gold. I'm obvs grateful to join the small list of Aussie boxers that have won a Comm Games medal, but if you're not first you're last in my eyes.

"Not to be ungrateful, I'll definitely take my medal home and relish the moments I had at this competition."

World.title: Coles Bay arson accused granted bail in Launceston court
World.content:
One of three men accused of attacking a 76-year-old man in a violent robbery on Tasmania's east coast three weeks ago has been granted bail.

Charlie Hills, 29, was granted bail at the Launceston Magistrates Court by Justice Robert Pearce today, with strict conditions and a $10,000 surety imposed.

Coles Bay man Grant Whelan was allegedly tied up with cable ties at his home at 5am on Saturday, July 11, his 15 firearms stolen, ute stolen and his house burnt to the ground.

Mr Hills was arrested in the week after the incident alongside two other men from the Launceston area; Jason Burns, 33, and Hayden Morrison, 31.

Mr Hills's bail was unopposed by the state.

His charges include attempted aggravated burglary, aggravated burglary, aggravated armed robbery, aggravated assault, arson and motor vehicle stealing.

Mr Hills's lawyer previously indicated he would plead not guilty.

Mr Burns and Mr Morrison face the same charges, alongside an additional charge of a breach of family violence order.

Report crime Call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000

Report anonymously via the Crime Stoppers website

There has been an outpouring in support from the Tasmanian community for Mr Whelan since the incident, with more than $100,000 raised in an online fundraiser and volunteers working to help clean up the burnt remains of his home.

Mr Whelan was released from the Royal Hobart Hospital on July 16 after six days.

The missing firearms remain missing, with Tasmanian Police calling for information.

"Illegal firearms in the community pose a serious threat to public safety, and we remain determined, not just as part of this investigation … to locate and seize unlawful firearms," Detective Inspector David Gill said.

Today is the second time Mr Hills has applied for bail. He was previously denied bail in the Launceston Magistrates Court.

He will next appear at court on September 8.

The name Orazio is synonymous with blistered Neapolitan-style pizza in Sydney. So it’s a surprise to find chef-restaurateur Orazio d’Elia’s new trattoria in Rushcutters Bay doesn’t serve a single slice.

Instead, the menu draws on regional specialities from across Italy, from tortelli Milanese bundled with braised osso buco ragu to cannelloncini alla Fiorentina, pasta tubes filled with spinach and ricotta and baked in bechamel. World.title: Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again
World.content:
St George Illawarra 22 Dolphins 28 SportNRLNRL 2026 Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again Christian Nicolussi Updated July 31, 2026 — 8:54pm ,first published 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

You have to give St George Illawarra a bit of credit for refusing to throw in the towel, despite knowing they have already won the wooden spoon this season. The Dragons lost 28-22 against the Dolphins on Friday evening, but they were pushing for a try inside the final two minutes in the hope of sending the game in Wollongong to golden point. Loading Kyle Flanagan put up the kick at the end of an ordinary set, the Dragons kept the ball alive, then lodged a captain’s challenge when they thought the Dolphins had got a hand to the ball during the frantic play. But the bunker spotted Hamish Stewart in an offside position as he chased through Flanagan’s kick, and the Dolphins received the ball.



The Dragons have not had much luck for a lot of the year when it comes to close calls, which was pointed out by the club’s own CEO Tim Watsford last week after the club officially announced Dean Young would be the head coach. There was a moment late in the game when Isaiya Katoa knocked down a Valentine Holmes pass, and there was a suggestion the ball went forward. Katoa himself laid there and looked at debutant referee Kieren Irons to make a call. Selwyn Cobbo scores for the Dolphins. Getty Images But Katoa played on, and the Dolphins scored a minute later through Tom Flegler to give them a decent lead. Dragons coach Dean Young was not too bothered by the call, especially given Irons was overseeing his first game, and was disappointed his side squandered their chances.



“There are moments we’re not icing,” Young said. “We’ll make a couple of line breaks, but not turn them into points, while the Dolphins made a few line breaks, score tries and nail them – we need to nail our opportunities when we get them.” Lyhkan King-Togia was brought into the starting halves at the expense of Daniel Atkinson, grew in confidence the longer the game went – and Young confirmed he would retain the starting role next Sunday when they host Cronulla. The Dragons celebrate Tyrell Sloan’s try. Getty Images King-Togia started to ask plenty of questions down the left edge, and came up with a ripper of a cutout ball for Tyrell Sloan that sent him down field before the play finished with Clint Gutherson getting across the line. King-Togia was also the one who went down the short side before Holmes’ pass was touched by Katoa.



“I thought he was great, I thought he defended great, he saved a tackle down on the tryline against Kuli [Finefeuiaki] who is a handful,” Young said. “He’ll only get better from here on in. Lyhkan will be five-eighth next week because of tonight’s performance.” Young added Atkinson would feature in reserve grade on Saturday, while another playmaker, Kade Reed, was a chance to return from a broken hand via NSW Cup next weekend. The Dragons trailed at half-time, but three of the Dolphins tries had come from nowhere, and inside their own half. Connelly Lemuelu’s flick pass hit the chest of Kodi Nikorima who stormed down field before he threw the final pass back in for Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to score the opening try.



Related Article Live

NRL 2026 NRL LIVE updates: Bulldogs into top eight as Crichton try caps win in Melbourne Jack Bostock’s pass for Selwyn Cobbo was even better, while Kurt Kurt Donoghoe brushed past some soft defence to gallop down field before the Dolphins scored the next play through Ray Stone. When young referred to his side not cashing in on their chances, there were none bigger than just after half-time when Holmes intercepted a Katoa pass, sprinted 40m, then threw a bludger of a ball for Setu Tu that dribbled another 10m forward. Tu scored a try in the first half and came up with the shot of the night on future Dragons’ teammate and Dolphins’ playmaker Kodi Nikorima. The Dragons, who have already collected the unwanted wooden gong, host the Sharks, while the Dolphins try to keep their top-four hopes alive when they host the Broncos next Saturday.

World.title: Families of men killed in ADF helicopter crash launch class action
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAir accident Families of men killed in ADF helicopter crash launch class action Courtney Kruk July 31, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The families of four Australian Defence Force members killed in a helicopter crash in North Queensland during a training exercise have launched a class action against the Commonwealth and aerospace manufacturer Airbus, alleging failings led to their death. Captain Danniel Lyon, Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent, Warrant Officer Class 2 Joseph “Phillip” Laycock and Corporal Alexander Naggs died when a MRH-90 Taipan helicopter crashed at 259km/h into the water off Queensland’s Whitsunday Islands in July 2023. The crew were flying in a nighttime training exercise, and were killed instantly. Warrant Officer Class 2 Joseph “Phil” Laycock (left), Corporal Alexander Naggs, Troop Commander Captain Danniel Lyon and Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent were all killed in the crash. In October 2023, the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force launched an independent inquiry into the incident to understand the causes of deaths and determine whether actions or inactions by ADF personnel were contributing factors.



The 15-month inquiry heard evidence from dozens of witnesses, including the men’s families and ADF personnel, and raised issues around fatigue and operational equipment, namely the software upgrade of “TopOwl” night vision goggles. Related Article Exclusive

ADF ‘Cover-up’: Families, pilot demand justice for dead Australian soldiers Lyon and Nugent were both wearing TopOwl helmets at the time of the crash. Retired test pilot Major Ian Wilson told this masthead he had warned the army in 2020 that it risked “industrial manslaughter” by putting TopOwl 5.1 into service after discovering serious faults in the software. He also found the helmet’s night vision to be deficient, with 50 per cent less visibility compared with other systems.



A draft report of the 15-month inquiry has been shared with the families of the men but has not been released publicly. Four other investigations have been launched in the three years since the tragedy, including a Senate inquiry and a probe by the Defence Flight Safety Bureau. The latter, released in May last year and described as “one of the most complex conducted by defence in recent history”, found the accident was primarily caused by “an unrecognised loss of spatial orientation” or spatial disorientation. Loading It found it was “very unlikely” the known hazards relating to the TopOwl helmet contributed to the loss of spatial orientation.

World.title: Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again
World.content:
St George Illawarra 22 Dolphins 28 SportNRLNRL 2026 Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again Christian Nicolussi Updated July 31, 2026 — 8:54pm ,first published 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

You have to give St George Illawarra a bit of credit for refusing to throw in the towel, despite knowing they have already won the wooden spoon this season. The Dragons lost 28-22 against the Dolphins on Friday evening, but they were pushing for a try inside the final two minutes in the hope of sending the game in Wollongong to golden point. Loading Kyle Flanagan put up the kick at the end of an ordinary set, the Dragons kept the ball alive, then lodged a captain’s challenge when they thought the Dolphins had got a hand to the ball during the frantic play. But the bunker spotted Hamish Stewart in an offside position as he chased through Flanagan’s kick, and the Dolphins received the ball.



The Dragons have not had much luck for a lot of the year when it comes to close calls, which was pointed out by the club’s own CEO Tim Watsford last week after the club officially announced Dean Young would be the head coach. There was a moment late in the game when Isaiya Katoa knocked down a Valentine Holmes pass, and there was a suggestion the ball went forward. Katoa himself laid there and looked at debutant referee Kieren Irons to make a call. Selwyn Cobbo scores for the Dolphins. Getty Images But Katoa played on, and the Dolphins scored a minute later through Tom Flegler to give them a decent lead. Dragons coach Dean Young was not too bothered by the call, especially given Irons was overseeing his first game, and was disappointed his side squandered their chances.



“There are moments we’re not icing,” Young said. “We’ll make a couple of line breaks, but not turn them into points, while the Dolphins made a few line breaks, score tries and nail them – we need to nail our opportunities when we get them.” Lyhkan King-Togia was brought into the starting halves at the expense of Daniel Atkinson, grew in confidence the longer the game went – and Young confirmed he would retain the starting role next Sunday when they host Cronulla. The Dragons celebrate Tyrell Sloan’s try. Getty Images King-Togia started to ask plenty of questions down the left edge, and came up with a ripper of a cutout ball for Tyrell Sloan that sent him down field before the play finished with Clint Gutherson getting across the line. King-Togia was also the one who went down the short side before Holmes’ pass was touched by Katoa.



“I thought he was great, I thought he defended great, he saved a tackle down on the tryline against Kuli [Finefeuiaki] who is a handful,” Young said. “He’ll only get better from here on in. Lyhkan will be five-eighth next week because of tonight’s performance.” Young added Atkinson would feature in reserve grade on Saturday, while another playmaker, Kade Reed, was a chance to return from a broken hand via NSW Cup next weekend. The Dragons trailed at half-time, but three of the Dolphins tries had come from nowhere, and inside their own half. Connelly Lemuelu’s flick pass hit the chest of Kodi Nikorima who stormed down field before he threw the final pass back in for Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to score the opening try.



Related Article Live

NRL 2026 NRL LIVE updates: Bulldogs into top eight as Crichton try caps win in Melbourne Jack Bostock’s pass for Selwyn Cobbo was even better, while Kurt Kurt Donoghoe brushed past some soft defence to gallop down field before the Dolphins scored the next play through Ray Stone. When young referred to his side not cashing in on their chances, there were none bigger than just after half-time when Holmes intercepted a Katoa pass, sprinted 40m, then threw a bludger of a ball for Setu Tu that dribbled another 10m forward. Tu scored a try in the first half and came up with the shot of the night on future Dragons’ teammate and Dolphins’ playmaker Kodi Nikorima. The Dragons, who have already collected the unwanted wooden gong, host the Sharks, while the Dolphins try to keep their top-four hopes alive when they host the Broncos next Saturday.

World.title: AI v the benefits of doing the hard grind yourself
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters AI v the benefits of doing the hard grind yourself July 31, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hot topic. To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Kylie Moore-Gilbert (Comment, 30/7) gives us a timely warning about the dangers of AI producing a ″⁣dunce army″⁣, especially among young people who might over-rely on it in their studies. We certainly don’t want to make medical students dumber as Moore-Gilbert speculates. At the risk of giving my version of ″⁣the old days″⁣, and even before dial-up modems, university work in my humanities course involved lots of reading, writing and analysis. Much as I grumbled about it at the time, the hard grind of hours in the library, reading and taking notes, gave me a good educational foundation.

David Fry, Windsor Strengthen our critical thinking

Kylie Moore-Gilbert is right to highlight a worry that students may offload logical and critical thinking to Claude or ChatGPT. AI is cheaper but I’d rather we strengthen our thought processes. Fortunately, some schools are beginning to address this particular matter. We do need our human teachers to teach. As Moore-Gilbert suggests, it’s use it or lose it.

Vivienne Daniels, Mornington Where are we heading in this race?

Kylie Moore-Gilbert’s article should wake up all of us, especially our governments, federal and states, regarding the AI rush risking ″⁣making a dunce army”. It is interesting to note that Silicon Valley tech billionaires send their kids to tech-free Waldorf schools. A telling statement that they want their children’s brains to be developed without AI influence. She outlines so many consequences once this technology takes hold in our society. Social media has already conditioned our children to be homogenised in their thinking. Where are we heading when there is such a race to introduce this technology into Australian society and for what purpose?

Christine Baker, Rosanna



The rise in job insecurity

With the arrival of artificial intelligence, white-collar employees will soon be changing their jobs with the same frequency most of us change our underwear. Job security will become next to non-existent in so many professional and office roles, in the relatively near future.

Michael Gamble, Belmont An encyclopaedic answer

Re Google search as a first line of inquiry (Letters, 31/7), World Book Encyclopaedias still publish an annual print edition if you have a metre of available shelving to house it. You’ll get quick answers and serendipitous cross-references without the ads.

Sue McKenzie, Belmont THE FORUM The right direction

What a good idea from your correspondent (Letters, 31/7). If it is feasible to move works to SRL West using existing contractors it could reduce compensation fees by amending contracts instead of cancelling them. And the billions of dollars would be spent where the need is most urgent.

Jan Lacey, North Melbourne Have to move forward

Most of Melbourne’s rail network was built in the latter part of the 19th century and the earliest part of the 20th century. It was always going to cost billions to bring up to 21st century standard. Your correspondent (Letters, 31/7) believes the Liberals wouldn’t be reckless to spend taxpayers’ money on such a project, but if so Melbourne’s population of more than 5 million, and growing, would now and in the future be relying on an antiquated train network that was built to cater for a population that was around 2 million.

Phil Alexander, Eltham



Study economics

Shane Wright’s article “Most of us don’t understand the RBA. That’s a problem” (30/7), could just as easily read “Most of us don’t understand economics and that’s an even bigger problem”. As an economics teacher and university teaching associate I have always advocated that all students should study this subject. Economics provides relevant, real-world learning that no student I know has ever regretted studying.

The knowledge and skills gained by studying economics are drivers of success in everyday life and empower people to engage intelligently in public debate about current economic issues and policies.

Those who do understand the role of the RBA and monetary policy are year 12 economics students.

This is sophisticated knowledge for young people. So, while RBA surveys of the public’s knowledge of economics is poor, it’s good to know that students studying the subject have a solid understanding of the economy.

In my view, the study of economics should be compulsory.

Margaret Wilson, Brighton We don’t have to take it

Waleed Aly’s anger is not irrational (Comment, 31/7). It has a name: “Enshittification”. The eponymous book by Cory Doctorow describes in detail the strategies and intentions of the creators of this dystopian online universe. It should be required reading for everybody, because we don’t have to just suck it up.

John Laurie, Riddells Creek Great balls of ire

I totally agree with Waleed Aly’s comments concerning digital chaos.

On Thursday, I spent the entire afternoon trying to navigate the labyrinthine world of a company’s website. Finally, I simply gave up. The wonderful cyber world has simply created colossal balls of technological spaghetti.

Oriana Collins, Hawthorn Celebrating legacy

Thank you Tony Wright (″⁣Back Hanson? Hawke would turn in his grave″⁣, 31/7) Unlike the deputy director of the IPA, I, like most in this country think the Welcome to Country ceremony has nothing at all to do with racial discrimination.

Rather it recognises and celebrates the wonderful rich legacy that our Indigenous ancestors have given us. What Pauline Hanson and Daniel Wild don’t get is the idea that we like and appreciate our rich history and cultural heritage.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson Apartment living

Having rented apartments in inner Melbourne and the CBD over the past 20 years, I’m for living in low-density buildings. Lifts cannot be used when fire alarms are activated – bushfire smoke a summer contributor – and they break down. I often wonder if residents higher up decide to sit it out while others exit the building on shaky legs long after those of us from lower floors.

More worrying is a childcare centre on the ninth floor of a CBD office building where I left my small grandson one morning. The few staff present for the number of babies and toddlers in their care would have challenged their capacity to evacuate all safely down the fire escape if needed.

COVID also exposed limitations when signs ordered only one person per lift. Would our adventurous three-year-old exit on the ninth floor or reach other buttons once inside?

Janet Barr, Toorak



Turning a blind eye

David Crowe’s report from Bordeaux puts the spotlight on a conundrum (″⁣It’s not just the flames Bordeaux residents fear″⁣, 31/7). Do we downplay damage and risk from climate change so that businesses, including tourism, can operate as usual, (or limp from one disaster to the next)?

Or do we acknowledge the fact that these disasters are increasingly frequent, and that unless urgent reduction of fossil fuels burning occurs, the cycle will keep repeating? The concerted emissions-reduction course would be cheaper.

As Crowe reports, the economic damage from the fires in France “will be measured in billions of euros from the destruction of properties, the suspension of 13,000 companies during the evacuations and the collapse of tourism”.

The major parties in Australia have answered. They want more coal, more gas and even more oil. Some even say they want nuclear.

All are delaying any genuine reduction in emissions.

Fiona Colin, Malvern East Lament for a tree

How my heart resonated with Melissa Hoyer’s article (Comment, 30/7). I am a tree person. I come from Canada, the land of trees, trees and more trees. I formerly lived in Elwood with a magnificent Norfolk fir tree half a dozen houses away. It towered into the sky and was a landmark for our area. It marked our home. Whenever I returned home from work travelling down Nepean Highway I could see our home from a kilometre or two away. The towering tree would welcome me home. Then one day on my return, I found people cutting it down. The tree, my homecoming tree, was gone. I was upset and unsettled.

I then did something I never do, I wrote a poem about the tree. I never write poems. I am not particularly good at it. But I felt something was needed to mark the passing of the old giant tree that had been on that street for years watching us all come and go welcoming us home.

Jane Cheong, Aspendale Gardens Paved paradise

I, too, mourn the loss of suburban trees; in my case an ancient golden ash growing in our front garden. Like Melissa Hoyer, our tree with its thick broad trunk and leafy canopy provided summer shade, autumn glory as well as a natural climbing feature for our three sons.

Alas, when we moved house after 27 years, the new owners cut it down to make way for a concrete driveway and frontage. Separate to identified sick or unsafe trees as in Hoyer’s situation, destruction of healthy trees contributes to urban heat intensification, loss of habitat for our native fauna and aesthetic beauty of our neighbourhoods.

Sandra Fordyce-Voorham, Black Rock No-brainer loop

When I was a student attending Monash University many decades ago, my public transport route from the south-eastern suburbs took about an hour, if you were lucky enough to actually have your train and bus seamlessly connect – which it mostly didn’t. Monash University Clayton is now the biggest university campus in Australia, surrounded by research institutions, the Heart Hospital and other large employers.

It still takes an hour on public transport to get there. The SRL will take 10 minutes from Cheltenham to Monash University. Thousands of cars off the roads and a seamless 10-minute trip – it’s a no-brainer.

Shelley Durance, Beaumaris Frame of mind

Alzheimer’s is a totally cruel disease but sorry, I don’t want to know 20 years early that I have it (″⁣Blood test to give Australians valuable gift of time″⁣, 31/7). Why waste valuable living time in a medicalised approach to life?

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

If Ben Carroll can get Labor back on track then we’ll call him Big Ben.

Robin Jensen, Castlemaine If you were told you owed $15 billion, you would demand that the amount be properly audited and proven. Bring on the Big Build royal commission, ASAP.

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood How will Victorians celebrate Christmas? By singing Carrolls of praise, or by trying to digest a democratic sausage comprising Liberals, Nationals and One Nation?

Kevan Porter, Alphington



Ben Carroll certainly isn’t Daniel Andrews.

Michael McKenna, Warragul How can we ask politicians to step down, when often they’ve never actually stepped up?

Ron Mather, Melbourne CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby deserves a statue.

Richard Sykes, Bell Park Opponents of the government, such as senator Andrew Bragg, can call it many things but communist is not one of them.

Garry Meller, Bentleigh Maybe Andrew Bragg could supply us with a list of those communists.

Andrew O’Brien, South Yarra



Furthermore

Yet another excellent Wilcox (31/7) illustrating the chasm between reality and the Hanson perspective on domestic violence.

Dorothy Galloway, Mentone Cathy Wilcox once again encapsulates the inequality and power some men wield over women and children.

Jane Ross, San Remo Wouldn’t it be nice if FIFA announced that tickets at the next World Cup will be capped at $100 a seat for all games?

Luigi Cosma, Rosanna Yes, Steve Martinuzzo (Comment, 31/7) my pet hate: A red right turn arrow at 3am in the morning!

Peter McGill, Lancefield Finally

Collingwood will need post-game hugs rather than pre-game.

John Bye, Elwood

World.title: Families of men killed in ADF helicopter crash launch class action
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAir accident Families of men killed in ADF helicopter crash launch class action Courtney Kruk July 31, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The families of four Australian Defence Force members killed in a helicopter crash in North Queensland during a training exercise have launched a class action against the Commonwealth and aerospace manufacturer Airbus, alleging failings led to their death. Captain Danniel Lyon, Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent, Warrant Officer Class 2 Joseph “Phillip” Laycock and Corporal Alexander Naggs died when a MRH-90 Taipan helicopter crashed at 259km/h into the water off Queensland’s Whitsunday Islands in July 2023. The crew were flying in a nighttime training exercise, and were killed instantly. Warrant Officer Class 2 Joseph “Phil” Laycock (left), Corporal Alexander Naggs, Troop Commander Captain Danniel Lyon and Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent were all killed in the crash. In October 2023, the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force launched an independent inquiry into the incident to understand the causes of deaths and determine whether actions or inactions by ADF personnel were contributing factors.



The 15-month inquiry heard evidence from dozens of witnesses, including the men’s families and ADF personnel, and raised issues around fatigue and operational equipment, namely the software upgrade of “TopOwl” night vision goggles. Related Article Exclusive

ADF ‘Cover-up’: Families, pilot demand justice for dead Australian soldiers Lyon and Nugent were both wearing TopOwl helmets at the time of the crash. Retired test pilot Major Ian Wilson told this masthead he had warned the army in 2020 that it risked “industrial manslaughter” by putting TopOwl 5.1 into service after discovering serious faults in the software. He also found the helmet’s night vision to be deficient, with 50 per cent less visibility compared with other systems.



A draft report of the 15-month inquiry has been shared with the families of the men but has not been released publicly. Four other investigations have been launched in the three years since the tragedy, including a Senate inquiry and a probe by the Defence Flight Safety Bureau. The latter, released in May last year and described as “one of the most complex conducted by defence in recent history”, found the accident was primarily caused by “an unrecognised loss of spatial orientation” or spatial disorientation. Loading It found it was “very unlikely” the known hazards relating to the TopOwl helmet contributed to the loss of spatial orientation.



This week marked three years since the tragedy, with the families of the four men travelling to the Whitsundays to unveil a permanent memorial. Related Article ADF Families briefed on safety report into army chopper crash Caitland Lyon, the widow of Danniel Lyon, is leading the federal court class action against the Commonwealth and Airbus. In a statement on Friday, lawyers said the lawsuit was filed now to “stop the clock” so that families wouldn’t lose their right to sue. It’s understood the class action will allege failings led to the men’s deaths. A Defence spokesperson said the department is currently considering the claim, but that would not be appropriate to comment further as the matter is subject to legal proceedings.

World.title: Police officer shot by Tom Phillips returns to work

The officer who was shot in the head by Tom Phillips is returning to work.

The officer, who has not been named, was critically injured when Phillips shot him several times last September.

Phillips died shortly after a shootout with another officer, when police were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025, after 1358 days in the bush with his children.

It is understood the officer who was shot underwent numerous surgeries at Waikato Hospital, after being hit in his skull and his right shoulder.

World.title: Weekend weather: Snow warnings and strong wind watches as chilly days ahead
World.content:
The country is set to face a chilly weekend as subantarctic winds move up the country, MetService says.

In the South Island, temperatures will start to drop in the south on Friday morning as the southerly pushes through Otago, and then into Canterbury this afternoon, with colder temperatures expected overnight Friday and Saturday.

MetService has road snowfall warnings in place for South Island mountain passes on Friday and the Desert Road on Saturday, with motorists told to avoid travel.

The mountain passes include Crown Range Road, Lindis Pass, Milford Road, Arthur's, Porters and Lewis Pass.

The Civil Defence said just a few centimetres of snow would make driving dangerous on Desert Road, and said to only do so if necessary.

MetService forecasted snow showers lowering to 800 metres and 1 to 2cm of snow could accumulate about the summit.

Meanwhile, the northern Cook Strait and the North Taranaki Bight have experienced thunderstorms.

Strong wind watches are also in place for parts of the South Island.

Coastal Otago's watch is in place from noon to 10pm on Friday, where southwest winds may approach severe gale in exposed places.

A watch for Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains kicks off from 5pm Friday until 1am Saturday.

The watch for coastal Southland and southern Fiordland kicked in late Thursday and continues until 5pm Friday.

All watches have a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

MetService said subantarctic air was being dragged north by southerly winds - resulting in "bitterly cold conditions".

It would make temperatures feel close to -2C in Invercargill on Friday afternoon "and even colder for higher elevations".

The cold weather would move up to the North Island during Saturday, it said, "with the wind chill cooling things to a feels-like temperature of just 1C in Wellington".

For those running or on the sidelines at the Taupō marathon, meteorologist Braydon While suggested dressing warm.

"Those preparing for the marathon, whether competing or cheering on the sidelines, will want to wrap up warm and bring a cosy jacket in case a few showers manage to sneak over the hills."

Sunday would bring clear skies for most of the country, MetService said, and "widespread frosts".

World.title: Silver Ferns to meet England in Commonwealth Games semi-finals
World.content:
The Silver Ferns will have to beat England in the semi-finals in Glasgow if they are to make their first Commonwealth Games gold medal match since 2014.

England will have their tails up after putting up their best performance in Glasgow by far with a 58-54 win over the fifth-ranked South Africa on Friday morning.

Anticipation was high that South Africa would pull off an upset over the third ranked England Roses in the last pool match of the tournament.

Earlier in the week, the Diamonds posted a 19-goal win over England, before beating South Africa by a 10-goal margin.

With South Africa beating England 2-1 in a series earlier in the year, Pool A was always considered the 'Pool of Death'.

The Silver Ferns topped Pool B earlier in the day after demolishing Trinidad and Tobago 83-23 to make it five straight wins.

Australia went through Pool A unbeaten, and will meet Jamaica in the second semi-final at midnight Saturday evening. The Silver Ferns and England will meet at 8pm Saturday New Zealand time.

The New Zealanders were reduced to 10 players for their final pool match with young defender Catherine Hall awaiting a MRI scan to determine the extent of a knee injury suffered in the previous match against Wales.

Shooter Georgia Heffernan was also left off the team sheet after suffering an ankle knock in the same match but coach Dame Noeline Taurua said Heffernan would be available for selection for the semi-final.

At the 2023 Netball World Cup, the Silver Ferns suffered a massive blow when strike shooter Grace Nweke suffered a tournament ending injury in pool play. The Ferns finished outside of the medals in fourth.

Taurua said selectors picked a versatile squad.

"We're always looking at the depth and making sure that if an injury happens or people can't take the court, we've already got the depth and we knew that in each position we've got three deep," Taurua said.

"The positive is that we're in towards the business end. We're not at the beginning, so we've got fresh legs and that's why those combinations and the changes that we've made earlier in the tournament, we've got something in our back pocket."

The 10 players were rotated throughout the match as New Zealand went on to post their highest score and biggest winning margin in 24 outings against a poor Trinidad & Tobago.

The Silver Ferns went through pool play unbeaten, with earlier wins over Scotland, Jamaica, Uganda, and Wales.

The Proteas boast one of the best shooters in the world in Elmeré van der Berg, who scored the most goals in her debut season in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition this year.

South Africa came out strong to win the first quarter 17-11 but a defensive change for England saw them mount a fight-back in the second spell.

Coming on at goal keep Halimat Adio applied all kinds of pressure on van der Berg and put doubt into the feeders minds.

At half-time, South Africa held a slim 29-28 goal lead.

South Africa lost their starting wing attack to a head knock in the third quarter, which disrupted the Proteas attacking end.

England ramped up their efforts in the third quarter, to lead by four going into the final turn.

Liv Tchine and Lois Pearson combined brilliantly in the England shooting end.

Pearson has stepped up brilliantly into the goal attack position, with the England Roses missing the experienced Helen Housby through injury.

The Roses also lost impressive defender Jaz Brown in the lead-up to the event to injury but Adio's efforts against South Africa show what she is capable of.

The Silver Ferns and England have played out some tight matches in recent years.

England beat New Zealand on their way to finishing runners up at the 2023 World Cup to Australia.

World.title: El Niño could bring a 'highly unusual warm' spring
World.content:
A scientist says El Niño could bring an 'highly unusual warm' spring to New Zealand.

El Niño was officially declared at the start of July and could strongly influence the upcoming seasons.

Earth Sciences New Zealand's chief scientist Chris Brandolino said they expect more profound and more noticeable weather conditions beyond 1 September.

"We're expecting to see more westerly pipe winds, so that could be maybe northwest or southwest or somewhere in between," he told RNZ.

"We're expecting it to become more persistent, more regular, and more intense with time."

Rainfall for lower South Islands, dry spells for North

He said that did favour increased rainfall for the western and lower part of the South Island.

Meanwhile, Brandolino said the upper North Island and many other parts of the country were at risk of dryness.

He said areas such as Northland, the Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Waikato, Auckland would most likely receive below normal rainfall.

"In terms of temperatures over the next three months, we think in spite of a pretty cold start to the August month, there will be some pretty chilly mornings over the next, probably four to nine days, the first week of August roughly," Brandolino said.

"But that won't be a theme, we think, when we look at the three-month period as a collective, as in its totality. We think temperatures are probably going to end up being somewhere between the average or even above average category for the next three months."

Brandolino said the hottest temperature recorded in New Zealand was 42.4 degrees in 1973.

He said that was during a "super El Niño", which is what we are experiencing now.

"El Niño is expected to become very strong, or so-called super El Niño in intensity. So, I'm not predicting a new national record, don't get me wrong, that's not my prediction," Brandolino said.

"But I'm just sort of making the linkage that when we have these westerly winds and we have El Niño, because of these westerly winds, that does cause Australia to go through these hum spells, or at least increased risk of these hot spells of weather or heat waves.

"When our air or our wind does come from Australia, that will bring it into New Zealand, that will happen."

Weather events harder to predict

Brandolino said there would be an increase in spiky temperatures.

He said that could see periods of one to three days of "highly unusually warm" temperatures for September, October and beyond.

"That's followed up by perhaps a big sharp downturn in temperature. So, big variability, roller coaster type weather.

"But when our winds align, so that it's kind of plugging air from Australia, and if their air is warm, we're going to get that warm air."

Brandolino said the odds particularly favoured spells of unusually warm temperatures for eastern areas of both islands.

Whether or not that translates into a record or not, we'll have to wait and see, but it certainly loads the dice for those outcomes, he said.

He said climate change was making it harder to use historical weather events to predict the future.

"Ordinarily we'd like to say we know the average outcome of El Niño, but no El Niño is average," Brandolino said.

"So, we know the average outcome and when you throw in climate change, that does tend to underscore that statement.

World.title: Almost 1000 medals reunited with families yet Ian's own search continues
World.content:
Returning medals to the relatives of New Zealand servicemen First Up Download MP3 4m

Ian Martyn has returned almost a thousand military medals to the relatives of New Zealand servicemen, but the medals that started his quest continue to elude him.

Despite his own extensive military record that stretches from 1970 to 2007, Martyn didn't get involved in returning medals until after he retired.

His initial interest was sparked in 2010, when he discovered the identity of his great-grandfather, Private Jack Sullivan.

Sullivan served in the Australian Army during the First World War. He survived the Gallipoli campaign but was killed at the Battle of the Somme in 1916.

"I was pretty keen to know whether or not any medals or any of his paraphernalia or memorial bits and pieces still existed because all the family were dead, bar me."

Martyn's search resulted in him founding Medals Reunited New Zealand, after encountering a massive volume of medals belonging to Australian and NZ servicemen.

"There was probably a hell of a lot of people like me out there that would dearly love to have their own family's medals return, and so I thought I could link both projects together," he said.

"If I was in the business of returning medals, that might spawn somebody offering up medals that perhaps were my great-grandfather's."

However, while Martyn has now successfully returned almost a thousand medals to the families of former service personnel, Private Sullivan's have remained out of reach.

"Nothing has turned up to date in 15 odd years, but I remain ever hopeful."

Medals come to Martyn in a variety of ways, and some he even uses his own money to secure.

"I'm of the opinion you can't take it with you," he said.

"If I spent it all and it meant the medals went back to families, and that they cherish having them, that to me is a total win."

Some are sent in to Martyn, people finding them anywhere from op shops to auction sites or even old cars.

Martyn said a World War II Memorial Cross had just been sent to him by a person who had came into its possession when they bought a car via Trade Me.

He said the medal had been awarded to an airman who was killed in a bomber aged 22. "So that is now off on its way back into the hands of his nephew, who's about 92 at this point."

One of his highlights had been returning another Memorial Cross, awarded to an airman who died in the same action that saw the Victoria Cross awarded to Flying Officer Lloyd Trigg.

Only nine New Zealanders had been awarded Victoria Crosses - the military's highest award for valour - during World War II.

Trigg's was awarded for sinking a German submarine despite his Liberator bomber aircraft being heavily damaged and on fire. Trigg and his crew died when they crashed into the sea.

"It was as a result of the submarine commander's after-action report, that actually secured the VC posthumously for Trigg," Martyn said.

The Memorial Cross was returned to a relative, who still had the paperwork that had been issued with it.

"When I took the Memorial Cross down to meet him and he produced the certificate, I was absolutely blown away."

Martyn doesn't just return medals and paraphernalia either. He's also helped expose people for wearing military medals they're not entitled to - a deception known as "stolen valour".

"It's kind of grown out of my own distaste for these people, and the fact that I was a disciplinarian in the military myself and had a significant background in the knowledge of that.

"I certainly don't pull any punches when I 'out' somebody, and we had a particularly successful one down at the Rolleston RSA. But that sort of thing, really irks me."

Fortunately, Martyn believes the practice is declining, despite New Zealand having lighter penalties than elsewhere.

As for his commitment to returning medals to their rightful owners, Martyn says won't stop when he reaches a thousand.

"That would be a nice milestone to reach" he said. "I think the last post I put on was 982. Well, it's 988 now. I'm closing in.

World.title: Unions fear Lyttelton Port privatisation despite rejection of unsolicited bid
World.content:
Union protesters say a decision to reject an unsolicited bid by global port operator DP World and three Canterbury rūnanga to run Lyttelton Port does nothing to allay their concerns about privatisation.

On Thursday the city council's investment arm Christchurch City Holdings Limited (CCHL) announced that it had declined to proceed with the Tōnui consortium's proposal to lease the port's operations.

Protesters rallied outside CCHL's Cambridge Terrace office on Friday morning, saying they still wanted to emphasise their call to keep the port in public hands.

Maritime Union Lyttelton branch secretary Gerard Loader said the decision was good news but he feared the next tempting offer would not be far away.

"This would be in my short career the fourth time we have had to beat this down. It has happened in Auckland and they beat it down there. The private interests are always trying to get in through the ports because as we know everything initially comes through a port and if we get privatisation in the port it will just flow through to every other asset that we have," he said.

Maritime Union Lyttelton branch secretary Gerard Loader. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Rail and Maritime Transport Union's Lyttelton branch secretary Mark Wilson said the port company's $800 million plan for an expansion and modernisation project remained a concern.

"We have concerns around the potential of holding on to a significant amount of debt on to a company, with someone else coming on later on and saying lets partially privatise this to get rid of the debt. That's generally how things go. We're not saying no but we're saying you need to involve mana whenua, you need to involve the community, you need to involve Christchurch in this," he said.

Wilson said the proposal should go out for public consultation.

Rail and Maritime Transport Union's Lyttelton branch secretary Mark Wilson. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Keep Our Assets spokesman Murray Horton said it was an ongoing battle fending off the sale of CCHL assets despite community feedback repeatedly showing people did not want assets privatised.

"It's not just us. We are not just speaking on our behalf or for a couple of unions. The public of Christchurch have made it very clear that they want the assets that they own and paid for to remain in public ownership," he said.

CCHL did not respond to a request for further comment on Friday.

Keep Our Assets spokesman Murray Horton. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

In a statement announcing its decision, chair Bryan Pearson said the council's 2026/2027 letter of expectation to CCHL did not support leasing the port and encouraged retention of a directly employed workforce.

"Our assessment of the proposal, as presented, is it does not meet the threshold for ongoing consideration and is not sufficiently compelling to warrant further detailed investigation by CCHL, or additional consultation with council given its letter of expectation," he said.

Pearson said CCHL had considered the port company's improving operational and financial performance, as well as its advice about infrastructure resilience and maintaining a culture of safety and efficiency.

"CCHL maintains full confidence in the LPC [Lyttelton Port Company] board and management and their operation of the port, and continues to work closely with LPC in considering the port's long-term development and associated investment," he said.

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Tōnui spokesperson Dr Liz Brown said the consortium was disappointed by CCHL's decision.

"Our concern is not simply that the proposal was rejected. Our concern is whether it was ever given a genuine opportunity to be assessed on its commercial merits," she said.

Brown said the proposal would have retained public ownership while bringing together Christchurch, three Ngāi Tahu papatipu rūnanga and one of the world's leading port operators in a partnership that shared investment, risk and international expertise.

"CCHL says it carefully considered the proposal and concluded it did not meet the threshold for ongoing consideration. That raises an obvious governance question. What was that threshold, how was it established, and how was this proposal assessed against it," she said.

If assessment was robust, there should be no difficulty explaining at a high level the process the board followed and why it concluded that the proposal did not warrant further consideration, Brown said.

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Given the scale and significance of the proposal, we also believe there is a legitimate question as to whether it should have been considered more broadly by Christchurch's elected representatives before the process came to an end," she said.

Brown said CCHL's response raised governance questions.

World.title: Live: Storm at risk of rare NRL finals failure after loss to surging Bulldogs
World.content:
The Melbourne Storm are at risk of missing the NRL finals for the first time in 16 years, and just the fourth time in club history, following a 36-22 loss to the Canterbury Bulldogs on Friday night.

The Storm entered the round 22 clash needing to win all five of their remaining games to finish the season on 32 points, which has been needed to make two of the past three finals series.

Missing captain Harry Grant, five-eighth Cameron Munster, and halfback Jahrome Hughes ruled out 90 minutes before kick-off, the Storm threatened a famous upset win when they led 22-16 early in the second half.

But the Bulldogs rallied with the final four tries of the match to record a sixth win in their last seven matches, and leapfrog North Queensland into the NRL top-eight.

The Storm have only missed finals three times since their inaugural season in 1998. The Victorian club missed finals in 2001 and 2002, the two season prior to Craig Bellamy becoming head coach.

The only time the Storm have not made finals under Bellamy was in 2010, when the club was not allowed to earn premiership points as punishment for salary cap breaches which led to the stripping of the 2007 and 2009 premierships.

Earlier, the Dolphins consolidated fifth place on the NRL ladder with a nervous 28-22 win over the last-placed St George Illawarra Dragons.

World.title: Magpies coach throws support behind Bobby Hill as star exits
World.content:
Collingwood's Bobby Hill has exited the club amid support from coach Craig McRae after the premiership hero was racially abused on social media.

Meanwhile Geelong has confirmed its own mutually arranged split with 2022 flag forward Tyson Stengle.

The Magpies have formally split with Hill, cutting short the 26-year-old's bumper contract, which was due to expire at the end of 2030.

"I'm going to take a break from football to keep working on myself and regain my passion for the game," Hill said in a statement released by the Magpies today.

Hill was the star of Collingwood's 2023 premiership under coach Craig McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal for a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But having taken stretches of personal leave, he hasn't played at AFL level for almost a year — making just three VFL appearances in 2026.

On Thursday, before the Pies lost to Geelong at the MCG, Hill shared on Instagram a vile direct message from a Collingwood supporter that included a racist slur among other insults.

"You have disappointed this whole club and it's (sic) 100 thousand plus fans what you have done the last 18 months," the account also posted.

"… I hope nothing but the worst for you."

Hill posted a screenshot of the message and captioned it "anyone know this tough guy?"

The Magpies have publicly supported Hill throughout his turbulent period, and McRae again expressed his care for the forward's wellbeing — and disgust at those posting abusive comments on social media.

"Bobby, our thoughts are with you," McRae said after the MCG defeat on Thursday night.

"Not just for Bobby — what's going on? It's a crazy place at times, isn't it?

"I don't do social media, so bear with me, but I did look on a website which had feedback, and the feedback is unbelievable.

"It's just a cesspool for people just to vent. I find it fascinating that's actually something that people would be interested in.

"If Bobby's listening there, I'm sorry to hear that's the case. We'll always love him. It's sad to hear that."

This morning, the Pies' football manager Charlie Gardiner confirmed the end of Hill's contract.

"The club has been working with Bobby over the past 12 months to put support structures in place to help him work through some personal matters," Gardiner said in a statement.

"Despite this, Bobby has unfortunately struggled to meet his commitments to the club consistently this year and agreed that taking a break from football is the best decision for him and his family."

Meanwhile, the Magpies are counting the cost of Thursday night's loss with veteran defender Jeremy Howe suffering a fractured arm.

It is the same arm that he broke horrifically after a nasty landing from an aerial contest, also against Geelong, in 2023.

"The likelihood is he'll probably need an operation," McRae said post-game.

Utility Harry Perryman suffered a left hamstring injury — having strained his right hamstring earlier in the season.

And Brownlow medal favourite Nick Daicos has a bruised right foot, but he played out the game.

Stengle agrees Cats departure

Geelong meanwhile formally cut ties with Stengle, who said he has chosen to step away from AFL football and return home to South Australia after a difficult year.

Stengle, 27, still had three years left on a bumper five-year extension signed in 2024.

Tyson Stengle's last AFL game for Geelong was the 2025 grand final defeat to Brisbane. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But the Cats confirmed on Friday they had reached a mutual agreement with Stengle and finalised it with his management and the AFL Players' Association.

The forward played only one VFL game this season amid off-field issues, and last played at the top level in Geelong's 2025 AFL grand final loss.

"Geelong Football Club gave me another chance to play at the highest level and achieve a lot of highs and lows and to win a premiership and All Australian in 2022 will forever be my greatest achievements I would have never thought I would have done," Stengle said in a post on Instagram.

"But after a tough year or so I have made the decision to step away from AFL football and move home and be with family where I feel more comfortable. It was a tough decision but it was the best decision for me mentally.

"I will always be grateful for playing at the top level and playing in the biggest games of them all, it was always fun and exciting.

"Thank you to everyone who has supported along the way."
